## Assistant

Yes—the equality of the odd parts is the right additional constraint. In the notes’ original subscripts, it is

```text
2^M − 1 = q^n₁ · odd(q^N − 1),
odd(q^N − 1) = A.
```

Thus every prime other than q dividing 2^M − 1 must divide q^N − 1 **with the same valuation**. Your rejection of the 461 example is correct: its 461-adic valuation is zero.

Pushing this through the cyclotomic factorization gives a useful restriction, although it does not yet prove coprimality.

Write

```text
U = 2^(M/d),  V = q^(N/d),
B = UV − 1,  A = BC,  Cp = Φ_d(UV),
```

where d ≥ 5 is prime.

**Zsigmondy guarantees primitive factors on both sides.** There are no exceptional cases in this range. A primitive Mersenne factor ℓ at exponent M satisfies ord_ℓ(2) = M, hence ℓ ≡ 1 modulo M. A primitive factor at exponent N for base q satisfies ord_ℓ(q) = N, hence ℓ ≡ 1 modulo 2N. The Mersenne factor could be q itself; otherwise both kinds must belong to A. [Zsigmondy’s theorem, as stated by Győry–Smyth, Theorem 13](https://www.pure.ed.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/530468/Gyory_Smyth_Integers.pdf).

The important distinction is **where these factors land**. For ℓ dividing A, ℓ ≠ d, the orders of U and V modulo ℓ are each either 1 or d:

| ord_ℓ(U) | ord_ℓ(V) | Where the entire ℓ-power in A goes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | B |
| 1 | d | C |
| d | 1 | C |
| d | d | B if UV ≡ 1 modulo ℓ; otherwise C |

This follows from gcd(B, C) dividing d. In the last row, two elements of order d can be inverses. So being primitive for both bases does permit a shared factor in B.

There is a stronger consequence of the full equations. Put

```text
G = gcd(U − 1, V − 1).
```

Then

```text
B = G·H,
gcd(G, H) = 1,
H > U,
```

and **every prime dividing H is primitive at exponent d for both bases U and V**.

To see this, any prime dividing B makes U and V inverses, so their orders agree. If their order is 1, the equal valuations in the original equations force its entire contribution to B into G. At the exceptional prime d, the single factor d in Φ_d(UV) gives the same conclusion after lifting. Everything left belongs to H, and

```text
H = (UV − 1)/G ≥ (UV − 1)/(V − 1) > U.
```

Thus a hypothetical solution requires a substantial product of simultaneous primitive factors with the inverse relation.

The complementary route is to **force factors into C**. For example, take a primitive Mersenne factor ℓ ≠ q at exponent M and let t = ord_ℓ(q). If

```text
v_d(t) < v_d(N),
```

then V ≡ 1 modulo ℓ while U has order d. Therefore the entire ℓ-power goes into C. There is a symmetric criterion starting from a primitive factor of q^N − 1.

Those forced contributions must satisfy

```text
C < (UV)^(d/2) / [2^(m₂/2) · q^(n₁/2) · (UV − 1)].
```

That gives two concrete targets: restrict the simultaneous primitive product H enough to contradict H > U, or force enough factors into C to exceed its upper bound. Zsigmondy supplies existence; the additional work is controlling their orders at the other base and the inverse relation.

I added these deductions and their proofs to the [notes](/home/erpage159/fluid/research/math/nt/prime-power-sum-pf/prime_power_notes.tex).

Yes. The useful point is that n₁ controls **how much of the Mersenne factorization can be removed before everything else must match q^N − 1**.

Since M = 2k,

```text
(2^k − 1)(2^k + 1) = q^n₁ A,
gcd(2^k − 1, 2^k + 1) = 1.
```

The entire q^n₁ divides exactly one factor. The other factor goes into A intact. Moreover, its location is determined by r = ord_q(2):

```text
r divides k:      q^n₁ divides 2^k − 1;
r does not divide k: q^n₁ divides 2^k + 1.
```

That gives us a definite collection of factors to test against the q-side, with no freedom to discard any of them into q^n₁.

For each prime power ℓ^e in that collection, the requirement is

```text
ord_(ℓ^e)(q) divides N.
```

We should combine this with the established residue restrictions on q and the restrictions on N—particularly that N is odd and 3 does not divide N. An order containing either 2 or 3 immediately excludes the configuration. Surviving factors then face the finer allocation between B and C.

So I would organize the next argument around **which half contains q^n₁**, then use congruences on the intact half first. The size bound on n₁ also controls the remainder of the half containing q. This keeps both the size and congruence arguments attached to actual forced divisors, rather than relying only on the existence of an unspecified primitive factor.

## Assistant

Yes. **The minimum admissible smaller terms already force long returns in the exponents.** The question is whether those returns can occur before the size bounds prohibit them. I was focusing too much on bounding the smaller exponents themselves.

There is a precise way to express your point. Put

```text
r = ord_q(2),
ρ = v_q(2^r − 1).
```

Already n₁ ≥ 2 requires 2^M to return to 1 modulo q². When ρ = 1,

```text
ord_(q²)(2) = qr.
```

So even the smallest permitted n₁ forces

```text
qr divides M.
```

With a common prime divisor d, we require

```text
lcm(2, d, qr) divides M,
d divides N.
```

If d does not already divide 2qr, it multiplies the minimum possible M by d. This is exactly the tension you mean: **the minimum multiplicity demands a large exponent, before we increase n₁ at all.**

The size requirement also starts high. With c = m₂ = v₂(q − 1), n₁ ≥ 2 and N ≥ d give

```text
2^M = 1 + q^n₁(q^N − 1)/2^c
     ≥ 1 + q²(q^d − 1)/2^c.
```

M must therefore clear this threshold **and** lie among the multiples of that required return period. Our logarithmic estimate supplies an upper bound on M for each q. This is a concrete comparison between the earliest possible return and the latest allowable one.

The case ρ = 1 is already part of our q-divides-M reduction. What remains harder is when the period does not grow upon passing from q to q². More generally, the exact condition

```text
n₁ = ρ + v_q(M), with n₁ even,
```

means that **every odd ρ forces q to divide M**. The branch without that large factor q requires ρ itself to be even and at least 2.

There is also a useful congruence strengthening that we should exploit. We established that N has no factor 2 or 3. Consequently, whenever ℓ divides A and ℓ − 1 has only prime factors 2 and 3,

```text
ord_ℓ(q) divides gcd(N, ℓ − 1) = 1,
```

so q ≡ 1 modulo ℓ. In particular:

- If 3 divides M, then **q ≡ 1 modulo 7**.
- If 12 divides M and q ≠ 13, then **q ≡ 1 modulo 13**.

These improve the earlier residue lists. Several such factors force a product of distinct primes to divide q − 1. If that product reaches q, we have a contradiction. This connects the required large return M to congruences that q itself cannot accommodate.

I read the relevant parts of the [doubling-map preprint](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.29130v1). Its Theorem A identifies divisibility by an odd integer Q with periodicity of 1/Q under doubling. Section 4 compresses the orbit into returns with recorded “flying times.” Its period is precisely ord_Q(2); those results do not themselves impose a new restriction on simultaneous returns for two bases.

But the perspective fits your idea particularly well **at prime-power denominators**: passing from 1/q to 1/q² usually demands a longer orbit, and our minimum n₁ already requires that second orbit to close. For the factors of A, the same denominator must support a doubling period dividing M and a multiplication-by-q period dividing N. The congruence argument above excludes some of those simultaneous periods outright.

That is the direction I would prioritize: **minimum required return lengths, plus forced factors whose permitted q-periods are too short or have forbidden prime divisors**. It gives a way to turn the density intuition into explicit incompatibilities.

## Assistant

There’s a useful new restriction: 2 must be a cubic residue modulo q.

We have v₃(M) = v₃(q − 1) − 1, and ord_q(2) divides M. Therefore ord_q(2) divides (q − 1)/3, so

2^((q − 1)/3) ≡ 1 modulo q.

This excludes any q that fails the test, for every p. It also gives an exact constraint on the multiples of the return period that M can use.

    \appendix
    \section{Auxiliary calculations and comparison with MSS}
    \label{sec:auxiliary}
    % Added in discussion: comparison with MSS and the two adaptations below.
    
    \subsection{The full common divisor}
    \label{sec:full-gcd}
    % Restored from even_odd_case.tex, Section 6.3; totient restriction added here.
    Let $d=\gcd(M,N)>1$, $U=2^{M/d}$, $V=q^{N/d}$, and $Y=UV$.
    Then $Ap=Y^d-1$. The sharper size bound gives
    \[
    p>2q(1-Y^{-d})Y^{d/2}>Y^{d/2}.
    \]
    For any proper divisor $e$ of $d$, $\Phi_e(Y)\mid Y^e-1<Y^{d/2}$.
    Hence $p$ divides only the factor $\Phi_d(Y)$, and
    \[
    H_d:=\frac{Y^d-1}{\Phi_d(Y)}\mid A,\qquad
    \operatorname{ord}_p(Y)=d,\qquad p\equiv1\pmod d.
    \]
    The M\"obius product gives
    \[
    \left|\log\Phi_d(Y)-\varphi(d)\log Y\right|
    \leq\sum_{j\geq1}-\log(1-Y^{-j})
    \leq\frac{Y}{(Y-1)^2}<\log2.
    \]
    Thus $\Phi_d(Y)<2Y^{\varphi(d)}$. Comparing the resulting lower bound
    on $H_d$ with $A<Y^{d/2}/(2q)$ proves
    \[
    \boxed{\varphi(d)>d/2.}
    \]
    Equivalently, the prime factors of $d$ must satisfy
    $\prod_{\ell\mid d}(1-1/\ell)>1/2$; every odd prime power passes this test.
    In addition, $3\nmid d$ by the preceding
    argument, and the valuation identity at $3$ then gives
    \[
    3\nmid N,\qquad v_3(q-1)=1+v_3(M).
    \]
    
    \subsection{The proposed descent}
    \label{sec:descent}
    % User's proposed direction, worked out here. The obstruction below is to
    % the reduced integrality system, not a counterexample to the original problem.

This produced two concrete exclusions and a stronger restriction on q. I added the proofs and the minimum-return argument to the [notes](/home/erpage159/fluid/research/math/nt/prime-power-sum-pf/prime_power_notes.tex).

**First, 2 must be a cubic residue modulo q:**

```text
ord_q(2) divides (q − 1)/3,
2^((q−1)/3) ≡ 1 modulo q.
```

This follows from our exact identity v₃(M) = v₃(q − 1) − 1. It excludes q outright when the congruence fails.

**Second, forced Mersenne factors can collectively make q too large.** Since N has no factors 2 or 3, any prime ℓ dividing A whose ℓ − 1 contains only those factors forces q ≡ 1 modulo ℓ. Combining these congruences gives:

| Required divisibility | Forced lower bound |
|---|---:|
| 36 divides M | q ≥ 3,838,381 |
| 48 divides M | q ≥ 9,003,541 |

Therefore, in the q-divides-M branch, where we proved q < 10⁶, **neither 36 nor 48 can divide M**. These are exclusions for all p, with no enumeration.

The mechanism is the one you were pointing toward: a required return period forces factors into the Mersenne number; their allowed periods at base q force congruences; together those congruences demand a q larger than the height bound permits.

I also made the iteration precise:

1. Start with the minimum forced divisor of M, including the multiplicity needed for n₁ ≥ 2 and the common divisor d.
2. Use its Mersenne factors to force orders dividing N.
3. Use those divisors of N and the exact valuation identities to force further divisors of M.
4. Compare the resulting minimum size with the logarithmic upper bound, while accumulating the forced congruences on q.

The remaining task is to find families where this propagation necessarily reaches a contradiction. The two exclusions above show that the combined restrictions can already do more than the individual order tests.

    -- Exact finite check for M = 2^a q^b, using the external bound q < 10^6.
    -- Run with: lua check_power_two_orders.lua
    
    local LIMIT = 1000000
    
    local function filter(values, predicate)
        local result = {}
        for _, value in ipairs(values) do
            if predicate(value) then
                result[#result + 1] = value
            end
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function primes_below(limit)
        -- Sieve of Eratosthenes; mutation stays local to the sieve.
        local composite = {}
        for p = 2, math.floor(math.sqrt(limit - 1)) do
            if not composite[p] then
                for multiple = p * p, limit - 1, p do
                    composite[multiple] = true
                end
            end
        end
    
        local primes = {}
        for n = 2, limit - 1 do
            if not composite[n] then
                primes[#primes + 1] = n
            end
        end
        return primes
    end
    
    local function valuation_at_two(n)
        local exponent = 0
        while n % 2 == 0 do
            n = math.floor(n / 2)
            exponent = exponent + 1
        end
        return exponent
    end
    
    local function power_modulo(base, exponent, modulus)
        -- Repeated squaring. With modulus < 10^6, products stay below 10^12,
        -- so the arithmetic is exact even in Lua versions using doubles.
        local result = 1
        base = base % modulus
        while exponent > 0 do
            if exponent % 2 == 1 then
                result = (result * base) % modulus
            end
            base = (base * base) % modulus
            exponent = math.floor(exponent / 2)
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function is_one_modulo_three(q)
        return q % 3 == 1
    end
    
    local function has_even_two_valuation(q)
        return valuation_at_two(q - 1) % 2 == 0
    end
    
    local function has_power_of_two_order(q)
        -- For prime q, ord_q(2) divides q - 1. It is a power of two
        -- exactly when it divides the largest power of two dividing q - 1.
        local two_part = 2 ^ valuation_at_two(q - 1)
        return power_modulo(2, two_part, q) == 1
    end
    
    local function is_one_modulo_five(q)
        return q % 5 == 1
    end
    
    local function display(label, values)
        local entries = {}
        for i, value in ipairs(values) do
            entries[i] = string.format("%.0f", value)
        end
        print(label .. ": [" .. table.concat(entries, ", ") .. "]")
    end
    
    local function main()
        -- Apply the restrictions in the order of the mathematical argument.
        local primes = primes_below(LIMIT)
        local one_modulo_three = filter(primes, is_one_modulo_three)
        local even_valuation = filter(one_modulo_three, has_even_two_valuation)
        local candidates = filter(even_valuation, has_power_of_two_order)
        local survivors = filter(candidates, is_one_modulo_five)
    
        display("Power-of-two order, q = 1 mod 3, even v2(q-1)", candidates)
        display("Also q = 1 mod 5", survivors)
    
        assert(#candidates == 1 and candidates[1] == 274177,
            "Expected exactly the candidate 274177")
        assert(#survivors == 0, "Expected no survivors")
    end
    
    main()

    -- Finite proof check for the branch q | M in prime_power_notes.tex.
    -- Analytic inputs proved there: q < 10^6 and M < 4 * 10^6.
    -- Every rejection applies to all M, N and p satisfying the gap equations.
    -- Run with Lua 5.5, Lua 5.4, or LuaJIT; no external libraries are needed.
    
    local Q_LIMIT = 1000000
    local M_LIMIT = 4000000
    
    local function filter(values, predicate)
        local result = {}
        for _, value in ipairs(values) do
            if predicate(value) then result[#result + 1] = value end
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function primes_below(limit)
        local composite, primes = {}, {}
        for p = 2, math.floor(math.sqrt(limit - 1)) do
            if not composite[p] then
                for n = p * p, limit - 1, p do composite[n] = true end
            end
        end
        for n = 2, limit - 1 do
            if not composite[n] then primes[#primes + 1] = n end
        end
        return primes
    end
    
    local function valuation(n, prime)
        local exponent = 0
        while n % prime == 0 do
            n = math.floor(n / prime)
            exponent = exponent + 1
        end
        return exponent
    end
    
    local function gcd(a, b)
        while b ~= 0 do a, b = b, a % b end
        return a
    end
    
    local function lcm(a, b)
        return (a / gcd(a, b)) * b
    end
    
    local function power_modulo(base, exponent, modulus)
        local result = 1
        base = base % modulus
        while exponent > 0 do
            if exponent % 2 == 1 then result = result * base % modulus end
            base = base * base % modulus
            exponent = math.floor(exponent / 2)
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function prime_factors(n, primes)
        local factors = {}
        for _, prime in ipairs(primes) do
            if prime * prime > n then break end
            if n % prime == 0 then
                factors[#factors + 1] = prime
                repeat n = math.floor(n / prime) until n % prime ~= 0
            end
        end
        if n > 1 then factors[#factors + 1] = n end
        return factors
    end
    
    local function order_of_two(prime, primes)
        local order = prime - 1
        for _, factor in ipairs(prime_factors(order, primes)) do
            while order % factor == 0
                and power_modulo(2, order / factor, prime) == 1 do
                order = math.floor(order / factor)
            end
        end
        return order
    end
    
    local function meets_base_restrictions(q)
        return q > 3
            and q % 3 == 1
            and valuation(q - 1, 2) % 2 == 0
            and power_modulo(2, (q - 1) / 3, q) == 1
    end
    
    local function forced_gap_divisor(q, primes)
        -- r | M, q | M, 2 | M, and v3(M) = v3(q-1) - 1.
        local r = order_of_two(q, primes)
        local three_part = 3 ^ (valuation(q - 1, 3) - 1)
        local L = q * lcm(lcm(2, r), three_part)
        if L >= M_LIMIT then return L end
    
        -- The odd part of q-1 divides A. Each of its primes therefore
        -- forces its order at base 2 to divide M as well.
        for _, prime in ipairs(prime_factors(q - 1, primes)) do
            if prime > 2 then
                L = lcm(L, order_of_two(prime, primes))
                if L >= M_LIMIT then return L end
            end
        end
        return L
    end
    
    local witnesses = {
        -- ell, ord_ell(2), largest divisor of ell-1 coprime to 6.
        { prime = 5,  two_order = 4, allowed_q_order = 1 },
        { prime = 7,  two_order = 3, allowed_q_order = 1 },
        { prime = 31, two_order = 5, allowed_q_order = 5 },
    }
    
    local function first_obstruction(q, primes)
        local L = forced_gap_divisor(q, primes)
        if L >= M_LIMIT then return "minimum M exceeds height bound" end
        if valuation(L, 3) > valuation(q - 1, 3) - 1 then
            return "incompatible valuation at 3"
        end
    
        -- If ord_ell(2) | L and ell ~= q, then ell | A.
        -- Since gcd(N,6)=1, the order of q modulo ell must divide
        -- the largest divisor of ell-1 coprime to 6.
        for _, witness in ipairs(witnesses) do
            if q ~= witness.prime and L % witness.two_order == 0
                and power_modulo(q, witness.allowed_q_order, witness.prime) ~= 1 then
                return "incompatible order modulo " .. witness.prime
            end
        end
        return nil
    end
    
    local function main()
        local primes = primes_below(Q_LIMIT)
        local candidates = filter(primes, meets_base_restrictions)
        local survivors, counts = {}, {}
        for _, q in ipairs(candidates) do
            local obstruction = first_obstruction(q, primes)
            if obstruction then
                counts[obstruction] = (counts[obstruction] or 0) + 1
            else
                survivors[#survivors + 1] = q
            end
        end
    
        print("Primes satisfying the base restrictions: " .. #candidates)
        for _, reason in ipairs({
            "minimum M exceeds height bound",
            "incompatible valuation at 3",
            "incompatible order modulo 5",
            "incompatible order modulo 7",
            "incompatible order modulo 31",
        }) do
            print(reason .. ": " .. (counts[reason] or 0))
        end
        print("Survivors: " .. #survivors)
        for _, q in ipairs(survivors) do print(q) end
        assert(#survivors == 0, "The stated restrictions did not exclude every q")
    end
    
    -- Exact arithmetic also on LuaJIT: modular products are below 10^12.
    -- The initial L is below 10^12; subsequent lcm products are below
    -- 4 * 10^12 because we stop as soon as L reaches M_LIMIT.
    -- All integer intermediates are therefore below 2^53.
    main()

**This closes the q-divides-M branch by a finite exact check, covering all p.**

The decisive addition was to include the orders forced by the odd factors of q − 1. Each such prime ℓ divides A, so ord_ℓ(2) must divide M. Combined with qr dividing M, these requirements make the minimum possible M too large.

The argument now gives:

- q < 1,000,000 from the existing logarithmic bound.
- A uniform bound M < 4,000,000.
- Of 4,347 primes passing the initial restrictions, the minimum return excludes 4,332.
- The exact valuation at 3 excludes five more; congruences modulo 5, 7, and 31 exclude the remaining ten.

The [Lua check](/home/erpage159/fluid/research/math/nt/prime-power-sum-pf/check_q_divides_gap.lua) uses exact arithmetic and enumerates only q. It gives identical results under Lua 5.5, 5.4, and LuaJIT.

I added the proof to the [notes](/home/erpage159/fluid/research/math/nt/prime-power-sum-pf/prime_power_notes.tex:935). Every remaining hypothetical solution therefore satisfies

```text
q does not divide M,
n₁ = v_q(2^r − 1) is even and at least 2,
r divides (q − 1)/3,
2^((q−1)/3) ≡ 1 modulo q².
```

That leaves the branch where the required multiplicity is already present at the primitive Mersenne exponent r. Coprimality of M and N remains open.

## User

So, what can we apply to the remaining branch that we've learned?

## Assistant

The main gain is that **n₁ is now fixed by q’s first return**. Increasing M cannot increase it:

```text
r = ord_q(2),
n₁ = v_q(2^r − 1),
q does not divide M.
```

That lets us distinguish the factors needed for the first return from those introduced by additional returns.

**1. Every additional return contributes its entire quotient to A.**

Write M = rh. Since q does not divide h,

```text
(2^M − 1)/(2^r − 1)
```

is coprime to q and therefore divides A. More precisely,

```text
A = [(2^r − 1)/q^n₁] · [(2^M − 1)/(2^r − 1)].
```

In the cyclotomic factorization, q occurs only in Φ_r(2). Every Φ_e(2) with e dividing M and e ≠ r goes into A intact.

So additional multiples of the return period supply increasingly many mandatory factors whose orders at base q must divide N. This is where the congruence propagation should concentrate.

**2. We can sharpen the height comparison when M contains additional returns.**

Let E = lcm(2, r), the smallest even return exponent. The same difference-of-squares argument gives

```text
q^n₁ ≤ 2^(E/2) + 1.
```

The previous bound used M in place of E. Substituting this into the gap equation gives the stronger inequality

```text
N·log(q) > (M − E/2)·log(2).
```

Thus, if M = hE,

```text
N·log(q) > (1 − 1/(2h))·M·log(2).
```

For five or more returns, the coefficient is at least 9/10, compared with our previous 1/2. We can use this directly in the logarithmic argument. Additional returns make the required closeness of the large powers substantially more restrictive.

**3. A common divisor d now gives a useful case split.**

For a prime d dividing both gaps, we know d ≠ q.

If E divides M/d, then M contains at least d even returns. Consequently,

```text

```

There is no q-factor to remove from that entire cyclotomic quotient. Its factors must satisfy the q-order restrictions and the allocation conditions for B and C.

Otherwise, d already occurs in r to its full multiplicity in M. In that case d divides r, so

```text

```

This gives a restriction on q itself. We should treat these two cases separately: they impose different kinds of pressure.

**4. All the congruence machinery remains available.**

In particular:

```text

v₃(M) = v₃(q − 1) − 1,
2^((q−1)/3) ≡ 1 modulo q².
```

The orders forced by the odd factors of q − 1 still divide M. Every additional forced divisor of M can introduce more factors of A, which then restrict N or force further residues of q.

The second case requires exploiting the fact that the common divisor is already built into q’s primitive return period. Neither case is eliminated yet, but we now have a sharper division of the problem.

```text
h < (N + n₁)/(2n₁ − 1/2) ≤ 2(N + 2)/7.
```

Thus N = 5 forces M = E; N = 7 allows at most two returns, and N = 11 at most three.

For a common prime divisor d, the two cases give:

**If dE divides M:**

- The entire Φ_d(2^(M/d)) divides A.
- N ≥ 5d.
- At the smallest possibility, N = 5d, we necessarily have **n₁ = 2 and M = dE**.
- The height inequality strengthens to  
  N·log(q) > (1 − 1/(2d))·M·log(2).

For d = 5, the coefficient is 9/10 instead of the previous 1/2. I also reduced the logarithmic term in the corresponding Baker bound.

**If dE does not divide M:**

d already occurs in ord_q(2) to its full multiplicity in M. Put

```text
η = v_d(2^ord_d(2) − 1).
```

Then

```text
v_d(N) ≤ η.
```

When η = 1, this sharpens to

```text
v_d(N) = 1,
v_d(M) = v_d(ord_q(2)) = v_d(q − 1).
```

This applies to d = 5, 7, 11, and 13. Consequently, for example, **N = 25 with 5 dividing M forces n₁ = 2 and M = 5E**.

These give substantially smaller cases to attack with the full equations. They do not yet eliminate every common divisor. The proofs and follow-up exercises are included, and the PDF rebuilds cleanly.

    +\subsection{A finite target when q is bounded in terms of d}
    +% Added from the question about whether large common divisors are prohibitive.
    +\begin{lemma}
    +If a prime $d\mid\gcd(M,N)$ satisfies $q\le d^2$, then $d<10^6$.
    +\end{lemma}
    +\begin{proof}
    +Suppose $d\ge10^6$, and put $t=\log d$, $\lambda=\log q\le2t$.
    +Write $H_\lambda(x)=\max\{\log(3x/\lambda)+0.38,10\}$.
    +The function
    +\[
    +\frac{x\log2/2-\log(27/26)}{H_\lambda(x)^2}
    +\]
    +is increasing for the positive $x$ used below. Also
    +$\lambda H_\lambda(x)$ is increasing in $\lambda$.
    +These allow the lower bounds on $M$ to be substituted into
    +\eqref{eq:baker-M}.
    +
    +If $dE\mid M$, then
    +$M\ge2d\log_2(q^2-1)>3d\lambda/\log2$.
    +At $x=3d\lambda/\log2$, $H_\lambda(x)<t+3$.
    +Consequently \eqref{eq:baker-M} implies
    +\[
    +d<34t(t+3)^2.
    +\]
    +At $d=10^6$ the right side is less than $133000$; moreover
    +$d/[\log d(\log d+3)^2]$ increases thereafter, a contradiction.
    +
    +Otherwise $d\mid r\mid q-1$. Put $f=\operatorname{ord}_d(2)$.
    +Since $f\mid M$, $d\mid M$ and $\gcd(d,f)=1$,
    +\[
    +M\ge df>\frac{d\log d}{\log2}.
    +\]
    +Using $\lambda\le2t$ and
    +$H_{2t}(dt/\log2)<t+1.2$, \eqref{eq:baker-M} implies
    +\[
    +d<202t(t+1.2)^2.
    +\]
    +At $d=10^6$ the right side is less than $630000$, and
    +$d/[\log d(\log d+1.2)^2]$ increases thereafter. This is again
    +a contradiction.
    +\end{proof}
    +Thus $d\ge10^6$ requires $q>d^2$. More generally, imposing
    +$q\le d^K$ for any fixed $K>0$ gives an effective finite bound
    +on $d$ by the same argument. In the first case the necessary bound
    +has the form $d=O_K((\log d)^3)$; the second case does also.
    +This is a finite target for a specified family, not an absolute bound
    +on common divisors when $q$ is unrestricted.
    +

## Assistant

Yes—**larger d forces larger minimum return exponents in both cases**, and this gives a finite target once q is bounded in terms of d.

If dE divides M, we have

```text
M ≥ 2d·log₂(q² − 1),
N ≥ 5d.
```

If d is already present in the primitive return period, then d divides q − 1. Consequently f = ord_d(2) also divides M. Since d and f are coprime,

```text
M ≥ d·f > d·log₂(d).
```

That second lower bound is useful: the common divisor forces another return period, and their contributions multiply.

Comparing these lower bounds with our logarithmic upper bound gives a concrete result:

**If q ≤ d², then d < 1,000,000.**

I added the proof to the [notes](/home/erpage159/fluid/research/math/nt/prime-power-sum-pf/prime_power_notes.tex). The cutoff is deliberately conservative. More generally, **for any fixed K, the family q ≤ d^K has an effective finite bound on d**.

This does not bound d absolutely. What remains outside those finite families is the possibility that q grows much faster than d. The result tells us what a large common divisor would demand: q must also be sufficiently large to accommodate its forced return periods within the height bound.

One limitation matters here: the upper bound on C itself grows rapidly with d. Merely producing another primitive factor need not exceed that bound. The more promising pressure comes from forcing **additional orders to divide M or N**, particularly orders coprime to factors already required. Their lcm can grow much faster than either requirement individually.

    \begin{lemma}
    If a prime $d\mid\gcd(M,N)$ satisfies $q\le d^2$, then $d<10^6$.
    \end{lemma}
    \begin{proof}
    Suppose $d\ge10^6$, and put $t=\log d$, $\lambda=\log q\le2t$.
    Write $H_\lambda(x)=\max\{\log(3x/\lambda)+0.38,10\}$.
    The function
    \[
    \frac{x\log2/2-\log(27/26)}{H_\lambda(x)^2}
    \]
    is increasing for the positive $x$ used below. Also
    $\lambda H_\lambda(x)$ is increasing in $\lambda$.
    These allow the lower bounds on $M$ to be substituted into
    \eqref{eq:baker-M}.
    
    If $dE\mid M$, then
    $M\ge2d\log_2(q^2-1)>3d\lambda/\log2$.
    At $x=3d\lambda/\log2$, $H_\lambda(x)<t+3$.
    Consequently \eqref{eq:baker-M} implies
    \[
    d<34t(t+3)^2.
    \]
    At $d=10^6$ the right side is less than $133000$; moreover
    $d/[\log d(\log d+3)^2]$ increases thereafter, a contradiction.
    
    Otherwise $d\mid r\mid q-1$. Put $f=\operatorname{ord}_d(2)$.
    Since $f\mid M$, $d\mid M$ and $\gcd(d,f)=1$,
    \[
    M\ge df>\frac{d\log d}{\log2}.
    \]
    Using $\lambda\le2t$ and
    $H_{2t}(dt/\log2)<t+1.2$, \eqref{eq:baker-M} implies
    \[
    d<202t(t+1.2)^2.
    \]
    At $d=10^6$ the right side is less than $630000$, and
    $d/[\log d(\log d+1.2)^2]$ increases thereafter. This is again
    a contradiction.
    \end{proof}
    Thus $d\ge10^6$ requires $q>d^2$. More generally, imposing
    $q\le d^K$ for any fixed $K>0$ gives an effective finite bound
    on $d$ by the same argument. In the first case the necessary bound
    has the form $d=O_K((\log d)^3)$; the second case does also.
    This is a finite target for a specified family, not an absolute bound
    on common divisors when $q$ is unrestricted.

## Assistant

**The congruence on p was decisive. It eliminates the entire second case from our previous split.**

For every common prime divisor d of M and N, we have p ≡ 1 modulo d. If d also divided q − 1, then

```text
p = 2^m₂ + q^n₂ ≡ 2^m₂ + 1 modulo d,
```

which contradicts p ≡ 1. Therefore

```text
gcd(gcd(M,N), q − 1) = 1.
```

Since ord_q(2) divides q − 1, every common divisor must contribute an additional factor to M beyond that order. The alternative I had been retaining is impossible.

Also, **5 cannot divide both gaps**: p = 2^m₁ + q^n₁ is a sum of two nonzero squares modulo 5, so p cannot be 1 modulo 5.

Keeping the smaller-term ratio central, write

```text
R = q^n₁ / 2^m₂,
u = (q − 1)/2^m₂,
M = ad, N = bd.
```

Then the exact relation is

```text
d·[a log(2) − b log(q)] = log(R) − Λ,

log(R) = (n₁ − 1)log(q) + log(u) + log(q/(q − 1)),
0 < Λ < (27/26)q^(−N).
```

Here u is precisely where the congruences on q enter the ratio: every odd product forced to divide q − 1 also divides u. Even at n₁ = 2, we have R > 3q.

The new coprimality restriction also strengthens those congruences. For an odd prime ℓ dividing q − 1, whenever

```text
v_ℓ(2^ord_ℓ(2) − 1) = 1,
```

we now obtain

```text
ℓ does not divide N,
v_ℓ(M) = v_ℓ(q − 1) − 1,
2^((q−1)/ℓ) ≡ 1 modulo q².
```

This applies to ℓ = 3, 5, 7, 11, and 13 whenever they divide q − 1.

There are concrete consequences for the gaps:

- If g = gcd(M,N) > 1, then **N ≥ 5g**, and every prime factor of g is at least 7.
- Hence the gaps are coprime whenever N is prime or a power of 5.
- The first possible noncoprime case, N = 35, is contradicted modulo 7. Thus **N < 49 implies coprime gaps**.

## Assistant

It follows from two congruences we already had:

```text
q ≡ 1 modulo 3,
q ≡ 1 modulo 4.
```

The second comes from m₂ = v₂(q − 1) being even and at least 2. Together they give **q ≡ 1 modulo 12**, whose smallest possible prime is 13.

So q ≥ 13 was just a convenient coarse bound, not a new deduction about size. **13 itself is excluded** by the stronger condition

```text
2^((q−1)/3) ≡ 1 modulo q,
```

since 2⁴ ≡ 3 modulo 13.

        -- Necessary local equations for m2=2, hence m1=2 mod 4.
        for _,d in ipairs({7,13,17}) do

            and (4+pow(q,e+N,d))%d==1 then count=count+1 end
          end
         end end end
         print('common divisor',d,'compatible residue tuples',count)
        end

    +\subsection{Using the two classes modulo eight}
    +\label{sec:mod-eight-families}
    +If $7\mid g$, reducing the two representations modulo $7$ gives
    +\[
    +\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
    +q\bmod7&m_2\bmod6&m_1\bmod6&n_1\bmod6&N\bmod6\\\hline
    +3&4&2&4&5\\
    +5&4&2&2&1
    +\end{array}
    +\]
    +Indeed $p\equiv1\pmod7$ requires
    +$2^{m_1}\equiv q^{n_1}\equiv4\pmod7$. Substituting the possible
    +residues into $2^{m_2}+q^{n_1+N}\equiv1$, with $\gcd(N,6)=1$,
    +leaves the two rows. In particular $M\equiv4\pmod6$ and
    +$n_2\equiv3\pmod6$.
    +
    +Now suppose $q\equiv5\pmod8$. Then
    +\[
    +m_2=2,\quad v_2(r)=2,\quad4\mid M,\quad m_1\equiv2\pmod4,
    +\quad q\equiv1\pmod5,\quad5\nmid N.
    +\]
    +The last assertion follows from \eqref{eq:ordinary-q-minus-one}.
    +Thus $\gcd(N,30)=1$. The preceding table excludes $7\mid g$.
    +Two more common prime factors are excluded:
    +\begin{itemize}
    +\item If $13\mid g$, then $p\equiv1\pmod{13}$ and
    +$q^{n_2}\equiv-3\equiv10\pmod{13}$. As $n_2$ is odd, $q$ is
    +a square modulo $13$, so $q^{n_1}$ is a fourth power, in
    +$\{1,3,9\}$. But a sum of two nonzero squares equal to $1$ modulo
    +$13$ requires the two residues $4,10$, a contradiction.
    +\item If $17\mid g$, then $p\equiv1\pmod{17}$ and
    +$m_1\equiv2\pmod4$ give $2^{m_1}\equiv4$ or $13$.
    +Thus $q^{n_1}\equiv14$ or $5$, neither a square modulo $17$.
    +\end{itemize}
    +Consequently the least possible prime factor of $g>1$ is $11$,
    +and $13,17$ are also excluded. Since $N/g$ is coprime to $30$
    +and at least $5$, it is at least $7$.
    +
    +If $11\mid g$, the same calculation yields
    +\begin{equation}\label{eq:eleven-congruences}
    +\boxed{q^N\equiv7\pmod{11},\qquad
    +n_1\equiv8N\pmod{10},\qquad M\equiv6\pmod{10}.}
    +\end{equation}
    +To prove this, $p\equiv1\pmod{11}$ gives $q^{n_2}\equiv8$ and
    +$q^{n_1}\in\{3,9\}$. The first choice would give $q^N\equiv-1$;
    +since $8$ has order $10$, this would require $5\mid N$.
    +Hence $q^{n_1}\equiv9$, $2^{m_1}\equiv3$ and $q^N\equiv7$.
    +Now $9\equiv7^8\pmod{11}$ and $q$ has order $10$, proving the
    +exponent congruence; $m_1\equiv8\pmod{10}$ gives the last one.
    +
    +\begin{lemma}\label{lem:coprime-133}
    +If $q\equiv5\pmod8$ and $N<133$, then $\gcd(M,N)=1$.
    +\end{lemma}
    +\begin{proof}
    +If $g>1$, then $N\ge7g$, and its prime factors exclude
    +$2,3,5,7,13,17$. Thus $N<133$ forces $g=11$.
    +The only possible values of $N/g$ are $7,11$, giving $N=77,121$.
    +The bound
    +\[
    +N/11>\frac{21}{11}n_1-\frac12
    +\]
    +gives $n_1=2$ when $N=77$, whereas
    +\eqref{eq:eleven-congruences} requires $n_1\equiv6\pmod{10}$.
    +When $N=121$, it gives $n_1\le6$, whereas the congruence requires
    +$n_1\equiv8\pmod{10}$. Both cases are impossible.
    +\end{proof}
    +This is a coprimality result, not an exclusion of the values $N=77,121$
    +themselves. In the class $q\equiv1\pmod8$, the present guaranteed
    +range remains $N<49$.
    +
    +\subsection{Forcing a common factor}
    +\label{sec:forcing-common-factor}
    +Let $\ell=jM+1>q$ be a primitive Mersenne factor at exponent $M$.
    +If $\gcd(j,N)=1$, then
    +\[
    +1<\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)\mid\gcd(M,N).
    +\]
    +Indeed, $\ell\mid A$ gives $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)\mid N$,
    +while the order also divides $\ell-1=jM$. Coprimality with $j$
    +forces it to divide $M$, and $1<q<\ell$ excludes order $1$.
    +Thus such a factor contradicts $N<49$, or $N<133$ in the class
    +$q\equiv5\pmod8$. A multiplier $j$ supported on $2,3$ automatically
    +passes the coprimality test; in the latter class, factors of $5$ in
    +$j$ are allowed as well.
    +The missing general step is to force a primitive factor with this
    +multiplier condition and $\ell>q$. Zsigmondy's theorem alone does
    +not supply either condition.
    +
    +The actual alternatives are $g=1$ and $g>1$ within each class of $q$.
    +The bounds $49,133$ identify ranges where only $g=1$ is possible;
    +they do not bound $N$, and larger $N$ may still have coprime gaps.
    +For a fixed common prime $d$ and $b=N/d$, the inequality
    +$n_1<d(b+1/2)/(2d-1)$ leaves finitely many even values of $n_1$.
    +Reducing both representations modulo $d$ can then exclude those
    +values, as above. This gives a way to eliminate families; it does
    +not yet give a uniform exclusion of all common divisors.
    +

## Assistant

There is a simpler contradiction that eliminates the whole q ≡ 5 modulo 8 class, so the intermediate N < 133 bound is unnecessary.

That class forces m₂ = 2 and 4 dividing M, hence m₁ ≡ 2 modulo 4. It also forces q ≡ 1 modulo 5. The original representation then gives

p = 2^m₁ + q^n₁ ≡ 4 + 1 ≡ 0 modulo 5,

contradicting primality. So only q ≡ 1 modulo 8 remains—and more precisely q ≡ 1 modulo 48.

    \label{sec:mod-eight-families}
    If $7\mid g$, reducing the two representations modulo $7$ gives
    \[
    \begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
    q\bmod7&m_2\bmod6&m_1\bmod6&n_1\bmod6&N\bmod6\\\hline
    3&4&2&4&5\\
    5&4&2&2&1
    \end{array}
    \]
    Indeed $p\equiv1\pmod7$ requires
    $2^{m_1}\equiv q^{n_1}\equiv4\pmod7$. Substituting the possible
    residues into $2^{m_2}+q^{n_1+N}\equiv1$, with $\gcd(N,6)=1$,
    leaves the two rows. In particular $M\equiv4\pmod6$ and
    $n_2\equiv3\pmod6$.
    
    \begin{lemma}\label{lem:q-one-mod-eight}
    In the remaining case, $q\equiv1\pmod{48}$ and $m_2$ is even and
    at least $4$.
    \end{lemma}
    \begin{proof}
    Suppose $q\equiv5\pmod8$. Then $m_2=2$ and
    $v_2(\operatorname{ord}_q(2))=2$, so $4\mid M$.
    Thus $5\mid A$ and $q^N\equiv1\pmod5$. Since $N$ is odd,
    $q\equiv1\pmod5$. But $m_1=M+2\equiv2\pmod4$, giving
    $p=2^{m_1}+q^{n_1}\equiv4+1\equiv0\pmod5$, impossible.
    The remaining class $q\equiv1\pmod8$, together with even
    $m_2=v_2(q-1)$, gives $q\equiv1\pmod{16}$.
    Combine this with $q\equiv1\pmod3$.
    \end{proof}
    
    \begin{lemma}\label{lem:mod-five-split}
    The congruences modulo $5$ split as follows:
    \[
    \begin{array}{c|c|c}
     &q\bmod5&\text{further conditions}\\\hline
    4\mid M&1&m_2\equiv0\pmod4,\quad5\nmid N,\quad p\equiv2\pmod5\\
    M\equiv2\pmod4&2,3&q^N\equiv3\pmod5,\quad m_2+n_1\equiv2\pmod4
    \end{array}
    \]
    Consequently
    \[
    q\equiv1,97,193\pmod{240},\qquad
    q^2\equiv1,49\pmod{240}.
    \]
    \end{lemma}
    \begin{proof}
    When $4\mid M$, we have $q\equiv1\pmod5$, as above.
    Then $p\equiv2^{m_2}+1\pmod5$ excludes $m_2\equiv2\pmod4$.
    The assertion $5\nmid N$ follows from \eqref{eq:ordinary-q-minus-one}.
    When $M\equiv2\pmod4$, put $P=2^{m_2}$ and $Q=q^{n_1}$.
    Both are $\pm1$ modulo $5$, and $p\equiv Q-P$ cannot vanish.
    Hence $Q\equiv-P\pmod5$. Since $AQ\equiv2^M-1\equiv3$,
    \[
    q^N=AP+1\equiv-3+1\equiv3\pmod5.
    \]
    Thus $q\equiv2$ or $3\pmod5$. The relation $Q\equiv-P$ gives
    $m_2+n_1\equiv2\pmod4$. Combining the three possible residues
    of $q$ modulo $5$ with $q\equiv1\pmod{48}$ gives the last assertions.
    \end{proof}
    In the second row, $q\equiv2\pmod5$ requires $N\equiv3\pmod4$,
    and $q\equiv3\pmod5$ requires $N\equiv1\pmod4$.
    Also
    \[
    p\equiv65\pmod{96},\qquad p\equiv257\text{ or }353\pmod{480}.
    \]
    Indeed $q^{n_1}\equiv1\pmod{96}$ and
    $2^{m_1}\equiv64\pmod{96}$, while $p\equiv2,3\pmod5$.
    
    For $N=49$, a nontrivial common divisor would have to be $g=7$.
    The modulo-$7$ table and the size bounds give
    \[
    n_1=2,\qquad M/E\in\{7,14\},\qquad
    q\equiv5\pmod7,\qquad m_2\equiv4\pmod{12},\qquad M\equiv4\pmod6.
    \]
    Here the bound with $N/7=7$ first gives $n_1\le4$; the table then
    forces $n_1=2$. The congruence on $m_2$ follows by combining
    $m_2\equiv4\pmod6$ with Lemma~\ref{lem:mod-five-split}.
    These restrictions have not yet excluded the family $N=49$, $g=7$.
    
    \subsection{Forcing a common factor}
    \label{sec:forcing-common-factor}
    Let $\ell=jM+1>q$ be a primitive Mersenne factor at exponent $M$.
    If $\gcd(j,N)=1$, then
    \[
    1<\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)\mid\gcd(M,N).
    \]
    Indeed, $\ell\mid A$ gives $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)\mid N$,
    while the order also divides $\ell-1=jM$. Coprimality with $j$
    forces it to divide $M$, and $1<q<\ell$ excludes order $1$.
    Thus such a factor contradicts $N<49$. A multiplier $j$ supported
    on $2,3$ automatically passes the coprimality test; if $4\mid M$,
    then $5\nmid N$, so factors of $5$ in $j$ are allowed as well.
    The missing general step is to force a primitive factor with this
    multiplier condition and $\ell>q$. Zsigmondy's theorem alone does
    not supply either condition.
    
    The remaining class is $q\equiv1\pmod{48}$, with alternatives
    $g=1$ and $g>1$. The bound $49$ identifies a range where only
    $g=1$ is possible; it does not bound $N$, and larger $N$ may still
    have coprime gaps. Neither alternative has been eliminated.
    For a fixed common prime $d$ and $b=N/d$, the inequality
    $n_1<d(b+1/2)/(2d-1)$ leaves finitely many even values of $n_1$.
    Reducing both representations modulo $d$ can then exclude those
    values, as above. This gives a way to eliminate families; it does
    not yet give a uniform exclusion of all common divisors.
    
    \subsection{A finite target when q is bounded in terms of d}
    % Added from the question about whether large common divisors are prohibitive.
    \begin{lemma}
    If a prime $d\mid\gcd(M,N)$ satisfies $q\le d^2$, then $d<10^5$.
    \end{lemma}

## Assistant

**The modulo-8 restriction now eliminates the entire q ≡ 5 (mod 8) branch.** Previously we retained both 1 and 5; combining it with modulo 5 gives more:

- If q ≡ 5 (mod 8), then m₂ = 2 and v₂(ord_q(2)) = 2. Hence 4 divides M.
- Consequently 5 divides A, so q^N ≡ 1 (mod 5). Since N is odd, q ≡ 1 (mod 5).
- But m₁ = M + 2 ≡ 2 (mod 4), giving p ≡ 4 + 1 ≡ 0 (mod 5), a contradiction.

Thus **q ≡ 1 (mod 8)** remains. Since m₂ is even, this strengthens to q ≡ 1 (mod 16), and together with q ≡ 1 (mod 3), to **q ≡ 1 (mod 48)**.

There is a further useful split:

| Condition | q modulo 5 | Additional restrictions |
|---|---|---|
| 4 divides M | 1 | m₂ ≡ 0 (mod 4), 5 ∤ N |
| M ≡ 2 (mod 4) | 2 or 3 | q^N ≡ 3 (mod 5), m₂ + n₁ ≡ 2 (mod 4) |

These give q ≡ 1, 97, or 193 (mod 240).

The remaining structural split is **g = gcd(M,N) = 1 versus g > 1**. The statement N < 49 ⇒ g = 1 does not bound N; both alternatives remain possible above that threshold. Neither alternative has been eliminated. I agree that gcd is presently a lever: a common divisor supplies stronger factorization and congruence conditions, while coprimality restricts which orders the Mersenne factors can support.

There is a concrete way to force a common factor. Suppose a primitive Mersenne factor at exponent M has the form

`ℓ = jM + 1 > q`, with `gcd(j,N) = 1`.

Since ℓ divides A, ord_ℓ(q) divides N. It also divides jM, hence M. And ℓ > q excludes order 1. Therefore

`1 < ord_ℓ(q) divides gcd(M,N)`.

For example, a primitive factor ℓ = 2M + 1 > q would suffice, since N is odd. **That would contradict N < 49.** What we lack is a reason such a factor must exist; Zsigmondy alone does not supply the multiplier restriction or ℓ > q.

There is also a systematic way to push the coprime range: for each possible common prime d, put b = N/d. Our inequality

`n₁ < d(b + 1/2)/(2d − 1)`

leaves finitely many even values of n₁. Then p ≡ 1 (mod d), applied to both representations, can eliminate those values. This explains the N = 35 exclusion. At N = 49 it narrows the surviving family to g = 7 and n₁ = 2, with additional congruences, but **does not yet exclude it**. So the general cutoff remains 49.

I added these arguments and an appendix reference table to [the notes](/home/erpage159/fluid/research/math/nt/prime-power-sum-pf/prime_power_notes.tex:1641). The table separates residues, valuations, and orders, and updates the obsolete classes in your earlier table. The PDF compiles cleanly.

    \subsection{A finite target when q is bounded in terms of d}
    % Added from the question about whether large common divisors are prohibitive.
    \begin{lemma}
    If a prime $d\mid\gcd(M,N)$ satisfies $q\le d^2$, then $d<10^5$.
    \end{lemma}
    \begin{proof}
    Suppose $d\ge10^5$, and put $t=\log d$, $\lambda=\log q\le2t$.
    Write $H_\lambda(x)=\max\{\log(3x/\lambda)+0.38,10\}$.
    The function
    \[
    \frac{x\log2/2-\log(27/26)}{H_\lambda(x)^2}
    \]
    is increasing for the positive $x$ used below. Also
    $\lambda H_\lambda(x)$ is increasing in $\lambda$.
    These allow the lower bounds on $M$ to be substituted into
    \eqref{eq:baker-M}.
    
    We have $dE\mid M$, so
    $M\ge2d\log_2(q^2-1)>3d\lambda/\log2$.
    At $x=3d\lambda/\log2$, $H_\lambda(x)<t+3$.
    Consequently \eqref{eq:baker-M} implies
    \[
    d<34t(t+3)^2.
    \]
    At $d=10^5$ the right side is less than $83000$; moreover
    $d/[\log d(\log d+3)^2]$ increases thereafter, a contradiction.
    \end{proof}
    Thus $d\ge10^5$ requires $q>d^2$. More generally, imposing
    $q\le d^K$ for any fixed $K>0$ gives an effective finite bound
    on $d$ by the same argument: the necessary bound has the form
    $d=O_K((\log d)^3)$.
    This is a finite target for a specified family, not an absolute bound
    on common divisors when $q$ is unrestricted.
    
    \section{Factorization results and their use here}
    \label{sec:factor-results}
    % Original notes Sections 8.2, 8.4, 9.5--9.6 restored; new consequences marked.
    For $u=(q-1)/2^{m_2}$, the original factorization $A=u\Psi$ gives
    \[
    \operatorname{lcm}\left(\operatorname{ord}_q(2),
     \{\operatorname{ord}_\ell(2):\ell\mid u\text{ prime}\}\right)\mid M.
    \]
    Also $M/r<2N$ for $r=\operatorname{ord}_q(2)$, since
    $2^{M/2}<q^N<2^{rN}$.
    Zsigmondy's theorem applied to $q^N-1$, with odd $N\geq3$, has no
    exception. It supplies a prime $\ell_0\mid\Psi$ such that
    \[
    \operatorname{ord}_{\ell_0}(q)=N,\qquad
    \ell_0\equiv1\pmod{2N},\qquad\operatorname{ord}_{\ell_0}(2)\mid M.
    \]
    Conversely, a primitive Mersenne factor at $M\neq6$ has order $M$
    and lies among the primes dividing $q(q^N-1)$. Thus fixing $(q,N)$
    restricts $M$ to the orders at base $2$ of those primes, with $6$
    as the primitive-divisor exception.
    
    \subsection{Gcd identities and primitive-factor counts}
    Cambraia et al.\ \cite[\S2, Proposition 9]{Cambraia} collect the
    same-base gcd and valuation facts used here. In particular,
    \[
    \gcd(2^a-1,2^b-1)=2^{\gcd(a,b)}-1,
    \]
    \[
    \gcd\left(2^a-1,\frac{2^{ab}-1}{2^a-1}\right)=\gcd(2^a-1,b).
    \]
    The second follows by reducing the geometric sum modulo $2^a-1$.
    Their Proposition 2 uses coprime exponents and a primitive factor at
    the product exponent to force an additional prime.
    
    Write $\omega(n)$ for the number of distinct prime factors and
    $\tau(n)$ for the number of positive divisors. The primitive-factor
    argument in Kova\v{c}--Luca \cite[\S3]{KL} gives, more precisely,
    \[
    \omega(2^M-1)\geq\tau(M)-1-\mathbf1_{6\mid M},\qquad
    \omega(A)\geq\tau(M)-2-\mathbf1_{6\mid M}.
    \]
    Choose a primitive prime at every divisor of $M$ except $1,6$;
    different orders give different primes. Removing $q$ loses one prime.
    
    \begin{lemma}
    For the remaining case $A>1$, $q>3$,
    \[
    \omega(2^M-1)\geq4,\qquad\omega(A)\geq3.
    \]
    \end{lemma}
    \begin{proof}
    Suppose $\omega(2^M-1)\leq3$. The preceding count, with $M$ even,
    leaves $M=2,4,6,8$ or $M=2s$ for an odd prime $s$.
    The size bound excludes $2,4$; $2^6-1=3^2\cdot7$ and
    $2^8-1=3\cdot5\cdot17$ exclude $6,8$ since $q>3$ and $n_1\geq2$.
    For $s\geq5$, the three primes are $3$, a primitive factor at $s$,
    and a primitive factor at $2s$. Hence
    \[
    2^s-1=P^f,\qquad2^s+1=3Q^e
    \]
    for distinct primes $P,Q$, using $v_3(2^s+1)=1$.
    A Mersenne number $2^s-1$ is not a nontrivial perfect power:
    an even exponent is excluded modulo $4$, and an odd exponent greater
    than $1$ makes $P^f+1$ have an odd factor greater than $1$.
    Thus $f=1$, so $q=Q$ and $e=n_1$ is even.
    But $2^s+1=3Q^e$ is then impossible modulo $8$.
    \end{proof}
    % This consequence is derived here; the low-factor classification also
    % appears in Cambraia et al., Theorems 14--15.
    
    \subsection{Transferring factors into C}
    For a prime $s\mid\gcd(M,N)$, put $a=M/s$, $b=N/s$,
    $Y=2^a q^b$ and $C=A/(Y-1)$. Then
    \[
    Cp=\Phi_s(Y),\qquad C<\frac{Y^{s/2}}{2q(Y-1)},\qquad
    \gcd(C,Y-1)\mid s.
    \]
    For any divisor $D\mid A$,
    \[
    \frac{D}{\gcd(D,Y-1)}\mid C.
    \]
    Taking $D=(2^a-1)/q^{v_q(2^a-1)}$ gives
    \[
    \boxed{\frac{D}{\gcd(D,q^b-1)}\mid C,}
    \]
    since $Y-1\equiv q^b-1\pmod D$.
    Thus a useful lower bound on $C$ requires control of a mixed-base gcd.
    For $\ell\mid C$, $\ell\neq s$, we have $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(Y)=s$;
    therefore, with $r_\ell=\operatorname{ord}_\ell(2)$ and
    $t_\ell=\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)$,
    \[
    v_s(r_\ell)=v_s(M)\quad\text{or}\quad v_s(t_\ell)=v_s(N).
    \]
    If both valuations were smaller, both factors of $Y$ would be $1$
    modulo $\ell$. The converse need not hold because of cancellation.
    
    \subsection{Primitive factors on the two sides}
    % Added from the discussion of Zsigmondy's theorem and the full odd-part equality.
    Let $d\ge5$ be a prime dividing both gaps, $U=2^{M/d}$,
    $V=q^{N/d}$, $B=UV-1$, and $C=A/B$. The full equality is
    \[
    2^M-1=q^{n_1}\operatorname{odd}(q^N-1),\qquad
    \operatorname{odd}(q^N-1)=A.
    \]
    Thus every prime power in $2^M-1$ outside the base $q$ occurs
    with exactly the same valuation in $q^N-1$.
    
    Zsigmondy's theorem \cite[Theorem 13]{GyorySmyth} supplies a prime
    of order $M$ at base $2$ and a prime of order $N$ at base $q$.
    Here $M\ge10$ and $N\ge5$ is odd, so there are no exceptions.
    The former prime belongs to $A$ unless it is $q$ itself; the latter
    always belongs to $A$. Such primes satisfy respectively
    $\ell\equiv1\pmod M$ and $\ell\equiv1\pmod{2N}$.
    If the same prime has both full orders, then
    $\ell\equiv1\pmod{\operatorname{lcm}(M,N)}$.
    
    For $\ell\mid A$, $\ell\ne d$, put
    $\alpha=\operatorname{ord}_\ell(U)$ and
    $\beta=\operatorname{ord}_\ell(V)$. Both lie in $\{1,d\}$.
    The factor allocation is
    \[
    \begin{array}{c|c|c}
    \alpha&\beta&\text{location of the full }\ell\text{-part of }A\\\hline
    1&1&B\\
    1&d&C\\
    d&1&C\\
    d&d&B\text{ if }UV\equiv1\pmod\ell;\ C\text{ otherwise}.
    \end{array}
    \]
    Indeed $Cp=\Phi_d(UV)$ and $\gcd(B,C)\mid d$.
    In the last row, $U,V$ lie in the same subgroup of order $d$;
    their product can be $1$. Primitivity at two different bases does
    not exclude this cancellation.
    
    \begin{lemma}
    Put $G=\gcd(U-1,V-1)$. Then $B=GH$ with
    \[
    \gcd(G,H)=1,\qquad H>U,
    \]
    and every prime $\ell\mid H$ satisfies
    $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(U)=\operatorname{ord}_\ell(V)=d$.
    \end{lemma}
    \begin{proof}
    For $\ell\mid B$, the residues $U,V$ are inverse, so their orders
    are equal. If this order is $1$ and $\ell\ne d$, lifting and the
    full gap equations give
    \[
    v_\ell(B)=v_\ell(A)=v_\ell(U-1)=v_\ell(V-1).
    \]
    If $d\mid B$, then $U\equiv V\equiv1\pmod d$ and
    $v_d(\Phi_d(UV))=1$. Since $p>d$, $v_d(C)=1$.
    Lifting again gives
    $v_d(B)=v_d(U-1)=v_d(V-1)$.
    Thus the entire part of $B$ whose primes have order $1$ is exactly
    $G$, with no such primes left in $H$. Finally $G\le V-1$ gives
    $H\ge(UV-1)/(V-1)>U$.
    \end{proof}
    
    For a primitive Mersenne factor $\ell\ne q$ at exponent $M$,
    $\alpha=d$. Writing $t=\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)$, if
    $v_d(t)<v_d(N)$ then $\beta=1$, so the full $\ell$-part of $A$
    is forced into $C$. Symmetrically, a primitive factor at exponent
    $N$ for base $q$ is forced into $C$ if
    $v_d(\operatorname{ord}_\ell(2))<v_d(M)$.
    Products of distinct forced prime powers must fit below
    \[
    C<\frac{(UV)^{d/2}}{2^{m_2/2}q^{n_1/2}(UV-1)}.
    \]
    The remaining target is to force enough such factors into $C$, or
    to bound the simultaneous primitive part $H$ below its required
    size. Zsigmondy's existence assertion alone does neither.
    
    \subsection{Reading and limits of the cited results}
    Pomerance \cite[\S2]{PomCycl} supplies the primitive/intrinsic
    cyclotomic decomposition, bounds for $\Phi_d(2)$, and the Aurifeuilian
    splitting for $d\equiv4\pmod8$. These concern individual factors.
    Cambraia et al.\ \cite[\S\S2--4]{Cambraia} give the gcd identities,
    valuation formula, and classification when $\omega(2^M-1)\leq3$;
    the preceding lemma specializes that classification to our equations.
    Their final section studies a different sum of Mersenne numbers.
    
    Kova\v{c}--Luca \cite{KL} study sums of divisor counts over exponents;
    their pointwise primitive-factor bound is what we use above.
    Erd\H{o}s--Kiss--Pomerance \cite{EKP} study reciprocal sums of prime
    divisors, including averages and consecutive exponents. Neither result
    currently controls the particular mixed-base gcd needed for $C$.
    Pomerance's earlier paper \cite{PomPrim} treats reciprocal sums over
    divisors of prescribed order.
    
    For the proposed descent, compare Bilu \cite[\S2, Proposition 2.1 and
    Corollary 2.2]{Bilu}: coprimality and a perfect-power product force powers
    of ideals. The identity $\Phi_s(Y)=Cp$ does not provide that
    perfect-power hypothesis. A transfer of the argument would need to
    supply it.

    \subsection{Congruences on p}
    \label{sec:p-common-gap}
    Let $g=\gcd(M,N)>1$. Section~\ref{sec:full-gcd} gives
    $p\equiv1\pmod g$. If a prime $d\mid g$ also divided $q-1$,
    then $p=2^{m_2}+q^{n_2}$ would give
    $1\equiv2^{m_2}+1\pmod d$, impossible. Thus
    \[
    \gcd(g,q-1)=1.
    \]
    Also $p=2^{m_1}+q^{n_1}$ is a sum of two nonzero squares modulo $5$.
    Since $p>5$ and $q\ne5$, $p\equiv2$ or $3\pmod5$.
    Consequently $5\nmid g$. Together with the previous exclusions,
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:common-gap-coprimality}
    \boxed{\gcd(g,30q(q-1))=1,\qquad \gcd(g,E)=1,\qquad gE\mid M.}
    \end{equation}
    Every prime factor of $g$ is at least $7$.
    The case in which a common prime has its full multiplicity already
    in $r$ is therefore excluded: such a prime would divide $q-1$.
    
    More generally, let $\ell$ be an odd prime dividing $q-1$, and put
    $\eta_\ell=v_\ell(2^{\operatorname{ord}_\ell(2)}-1)$.
    If $\eta_\ell=1$, the valuation identity and
    $\gcd(g,q-1)=1$ imply
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:ordinary-q-minus-one}
    \boxed{\ell\nmid N,\qquad v_\ell(M)=v_\ell(q-1)-1.}
    \end{equation}
    Indeed, $\ell\mid N$ would make
    $v_\ell(M)=v_\ell(q-1)+v_\ell(N)-1\ge1$, contradicting
    $\gcd(g,q-1)=1$. The same conclusion holds when $g=1$.
    Since $r\mid M$, we obtain the stronger condition on $q$
    \[
    r\mid(q-1)/\ell,\qquad
    2^{(q-1)/\ell}\equiv1\pmod{q^2}.
    \]
    This applies to $\ell=3,5,7,11,13$ whenever $\ell\mid q-1$.

    Thus $1<U/V<R^{1/d}$. More precisely, with
    $\delta=a\log2-b\log q>0$,

    \boxed{d\delta=\log R-\Lambda,\qquad

    \end{equation}
    For fixed $q$, both $n_1$ and $m_2$ are fixed, so $R$ is fixed.
    Increasing $d$ requires a closer ratio $2^a/q^b$ and the
    exponentially accurate equality \eqref{eq:smaller-ratio}.
    
    The congruences on $q$ also constrain $R$. With

    local Q_LIMIT = 1000000
    local M_LIMIT = 4000000
    
    local function filter(values, predicate)
        local result = {}
        for _, value in ipairs(values) do
            if predicate(value) then result[#result + 1] = value end
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function primes_below(limit)
        local composite, primes = {}, {}
        for p = 2, math.floor(math.sqrt(limit - 1)) do
            if not composite[p] then
                for n = p * p, limit - 1, p do composite[n] = true end
            end
        end
        for n = 2, limit - 1 do
            if not composite[n] then primes[#primes + 1] = n end
        end
        return primes
    end
    
    local function valuation(n, prime)
        local exponent = 0
        while n % prime == 0 do
            n = math.floor(n / prime)
            exponent = exponent + 1
        end
        return exponent
    end
    
    local function gcd(a, b)
        while b ~= 0 do a, b = b, a % b end
        return a
    end
    
    local function lcm(a, b)
        return (a / gcd(a, b)) * b
    end
    
    local function power_modulo(base, exponent, modulus)
        local result = 1
        base = base % modulus
        while exponent > 0 do
            if exponent % 2 == 1 then result = result * base % modulus end
            base = base * base % modulus
            exponent = math.floor(exponent / 2)
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function prime_factors(n, primes)
        local factors = {}
        for _, prime in ipairs(primes) do
            if prime * prime > n then break end
            if n % prime == 0 then
                factors[#factors + 1] = prime
                repeat n = math.floor(n / prime) until n % prime ~= 0
            end
        end
        if n > 1 then factors[#factors + 1] = n end
        return factors
    end
    
    local function order_of_two(prime, primes)
        local order = prime - 1
        for _, factor in ipairs(prime_factors(order, primes)) do
            while order % factor == 0
                and power_modulo(2, order / factor, prime) == 1 do
                order = math.floor(order / factor)
            end
        end
        return order
    end
    
    local function meets_base_restrictions(q)
        return q > 3
            and q % 3 == 1
            and valuation(q - 1, 2) % 2 == 0
            and power_modulo(2, (q - 1) / 3, q) == 1
    end
    
    local function forced_gap_divisor(q, primes)
        -- r | M, q | M, 2 | M, and v3(M) = v3(q-1) - 1.
        local r = order_of_two(q, primes)
        local three_part = 3 ^ (valuation(q - 1, 3) - 1)
        local L = q * lcm(lcm(2, r), three_part)
        if L >= M_LIMIT then return L end
    
        -- The odd part of q-1 divides A. Each of its primes therefore
        -- forces its order at base 2 to divide M as well.
        for _, prime in ipairs(prime_factors(q - 1, primes)) do
            if prime > 2 then
                L = lcm(L, order_of_two(prime, primes))
                if L >= M_LIMIT then return L end
            end
        end
        return L
    end
    
    local witnesses = {
        -- ell, ord_ell(2), largest divisor of ell-1 coprime to 6.
        { prime = 5,  two_order = 4, allowed_q_order = 1 },
        { prime = 7,  two_order = 3, allowed_q_order = 1 },
        { prime = 31, two_order = 5, allowed_q_order = 5 },
    }
    
    local function first_obstruction(q, primes)
        local L = forced_gap_divisor(q, primes)
        if L >= M_LIMIT then return "minimum M exceeds height bound" end
        if valuation(L, 3) > valuation(q - 1, 3) - 1 then
            return "incompatible valuation at 3"
        end
    
        -- If ord_ell(2) | L and ell ~= q, then ell | A.
        -- Since gcd(N,6)=1, the order of q modulo ell must divide
        -- the largest divisor of ell-1 coprime to 6.
        for _, witness in ipairs(witnesses) do
            if q ~= witness.prime and L % witness.two_order == 0
                and power_modulo(q, witness.allowed_q_order, witness.prime) ~= 1 then
                return "incompatible order modulo " .. witness.prime
            end
        end
        return nil
    end
    
    local function main()
        local primes = primes_below(Q_LIMIT)
        local candidates = filter(primes, meets_base_restrictions)
        local survivors, counts = {}, {}
        for _, q in ipairs(candidates) do
            local obstruction = first_obstruction(q, primes)
            if obstruction then
                counts[obstruction] = (counts[obstruction] or 0) + 1
            else
                survivors[#survivors + 1] = q
            end
        end
    
        print("Primes satisfying the base restrictions: " .. #candidates)
        for _, reason in ipairs({
            "minimum M exceeds height bound",
            "incompatible valuation at 3",
            "incompatible order modulo 5",
            "incompatible order modulo 7",
            "incompatible order modulo 31",
        }) do
            print(reason .. ": " .. (counts[reason] or 0))
        end
        print("Survivors: " .. #survivors)
        for _, q in ipairs(survivors) do print(q) end
        assert(#survivors == 0, "The stated restrictions did not exclude every q")
    end
    
    -- Exact arithmetic also on LuaJIT: modular products are below 10^12.
    -- The initial L is below 10^12; subsequent lcm products are below
    -- 4 * 10^12 because we stop as soon as L reaches M_LIMIT.
    -- All integer intermediates are therefore below 2^53.
    main()

    % Source map: the abstract and opening setup retain diophantine_analysis.tex.

    % even_odd_case.tex. Later additions are marked at their source locations below.
    \section*{Abstract}
    
    Let $p > 5$ be a prime. We ask how many solutions exist where $p = 2^m + q^n$ for $m, n \geq 1$ and $q$ a fixed prime.
    We know of a single example where $p$ has two solutions, $p =  11$. Do others exist? First we proceed by
    considering basic arithmetic obstructions that prevent certain solutions. This breaks down to two main cases,
    based on whether a common factor of putative solutions, $A$, is either greater than or equal to 1.
    
    
    {\small\tableofcontents}
    \clearpage
    \section{Two representations and the common factor}
    \label{sec:setup}
    
    Let $p$ be prime with two prime power solutions sharing the same base $q$. So, we have
    \[
    p = 2^{m_1} + q^{n_1} = 2^{m_2} + q^{n_2}, \qquad m_1 > m_2, \quad n_2 > n_1.
    \]
    So then writing $\Delta m = m_1 - m_2, \Delta n = n_2 - n_1$, then just following our noses we
    wind up with a coprime quantity to our bases, which is our central obstacle. That is, with
    
    \[
    2^{m_2}\left(2^{\Delta m} - 1\right) = q^{n_1}\left(q^{\Delta n} - 1\right).
    \]
    and  $\gcd(2,q) = 1$, we have $2^{m_2} \mid q^{\Delta n} - 1$ and $q^{n_1} \mid 2^{\Delta m} - 1$.
    
    And so we define
    \[
    A = \frac{2^{\Delta m} - 1}{q^{n_1}} = \frac{q^{\Delta n} - 1}{2^{m_2}},
    \]
    Now we consider
    \[
    A\,q^{n_1} = 2^{\Delta m} - 1, \qquad A\,2^{m_2} = q^{\Delta n} - 1, \qquad A < 2^{\Delta m}, \quad A < q^{\Delta n}.
    \]
    
    The coprimality of $A$ with the bases follows directly:
    $Aq^{n_1}=2^{\Delta m}-1$ makes $A$ odd, and
    $A2^{m_2}=q^{\Delta n}-1$ gives $q\nmid A$. Thus
    \[
    \gcd(A,2q)=1.
    \]
    In particular $A$ is a positive integer, so the two cases are $A=1$ and
    $A>1$.
    
    \subsection{The quadratic form and gap parity}
    \operatorname{ord}_p(2)\nmid T.
    \]
    These are necessary conditions involving the prime $p$ itself.
    They have not yet been combined into a new bound.
    The normalization of orders used elsewhere in MSS should not be assumed
    to preserve our fixed base $2$ without checking the change of variables.

    ## When To Use
    
    - Read or review PDF content where layout and visuals matter.
    - Create PDFs programmatically with reliable formatting.
    - Fill and validate interactive PDF forms.
    - Validate final rendering before delivery.

    1. Prefer visual review: render PDF pages to PNGs and inspect them.
       - Use `pdftoppm` from the bundled runtime or system Poppler when available.
       - If unavailable, install Poppler or ask the user to review the output locally.
    2. Use `reportlab` to generate PDFs when creating new documents.
    3. Use `pdfplumber` or `pypdf` for text extraction and quick checks; do not rely on text extraction for layout fidelity.
    4. After each meaningful update, re-render pages and verify alignment, spacing, and legibility.
    
    ## Fill And Validate AcroForms
    
    Visual review alone is not a correctness check for a fillable PDF. A page `/Widget` annotation can render a value from its appearance stream while the canonical `/AcroForm/Fields` tree is missing or contains a stale value.
    
    1. Keep the result interactive by default; set `flatten=True` only when the user explicitly requests a completed, static form. Preserve the source PDF, and do not flatten a signed PDF without an explicit workflow decision.
    2. Inspect both representations before filling: enumerate fields from `reader.get_fields()` and `/Widget` annotations from every page's `/Annots`, following `/Parent` and `/Kids`. If a widget and a canonical field have the same name but are distinct objects with no `/Parent` relationship, do not call `reattach_fields()` blindly: it can create a second top-level field with the same name. Report the ambiguity or produce a static result.
    3. Recover genuinely orphaned widgets, fill all pages, and write the result with `pypdf`:
    
    ```python
    from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter
    from pypdf.generic import NameObject
    
    reader = PdfReader(input_pdf)
    writer = PdfWriter()
    writer.clone_document_from_reader(reader)
    
    # Restores widgets that are missing from /AcroForm/Fields.
    writer.reattach_fields()
    fields = writer.get_fields() or {}
    missing = set(expected_values) - set(fields)
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"Form fields not found after repair: {sorted(missing)}")
    
    values_to_write = dict(expected_values)
    if flatten:
        # Paint every existing value before removing every widget.
        values_to_write = {
            name: field.get("/V", "/Off" if field.get("/FT") == "/Btn" else "")
            for name, field in fields.items()
        }
        values_to_write.update(expected_values)
    
    writer.update_page_form_field_values(
        None, values_to_write, auto_regenerate=False, flatten=flatten
    )
    
    if flatten:
        # pypdf's flatten=True paints appearances but does not remove widgets.
        writer.remove_annotations(subtypes="/Widget")
        writer.root_object.pop(NameObject("/AcroForm"), None)
    
    with open(output_pdf, "wb") as stream:
        writer.write(stream)
    ```

    Laurent's estimate, quoted in Miyazaki--Scott--Styer
    \cite{MSS} (\texttt{prop-comp} in the local source), gives
    \[
    \log|b_2\log\alpha_2-b_1\log\alpha_1|
    >-25.2H_1H_2\bigl(\max\{\log b'+0.38,10\}\bigr)^2,
    \qquad b'=b_1/H_2+b_2/H_1,
    \]
    under its height and independence hypotheses.
    Use $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=(2,q)$, $(b_1,b_2)=(m_1,n_2)$.
    The bases are multiplicatively independent because they are distinct primes.
    For a conservative application choose $H_1=H_2=\log q>1$;
    these dominate both rational heights, both logarithms, and $1$.
    This choice also avoids any issue with the mismatched index in the height
    condition printed in the local copy. Sharper admissible heights could
    improve the constants, but are not needed for the deduction below.
    
    Put $\lambda=\log q$ and
    \[
    \mathcal H=\max\left\{\log\frac{m_1+n_2}{\lambda}+0.38,10\right\}.
    \]
    Combining the quoted lower bound with \eqref{eq:lambda-upper} gives
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:baker-gap}
    N\lambda<25.2\lambda^2\mathcal H^2+\log(27/26).
    \end{equation}
    
    The dependence on $m_1,n_2$ can be removed in favor of $M,q$.
    Since $m_2\leq M/2$, $m_1\leq3M/2$. Also
    $q^{n_2}<p<2^{m_1+1}$, so
    \[
    n_2<\frac{(3M/2+1)\log2}{\lambda}.
    \]
    Since $\lambda\geq\log3$, $\log2/\log3<2/3$, and $M\geq6$,
    these inequalities give $m_1+n_2<3M$.
    Together with $N\lambda>M\log2/2$, this proves
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:baker-M}
    \boxed{
    \frac{M\log2}{2}
    <25.2(\log q)^2
    \left(\max\left\{\log\frac{3M}{\log q}+0.38,10\right\}\right)^2
    +\log(27/26).}
    \end{equation}
    
    For each fixed $q$, the right side grows like $(\log M)^2$ whereas the
    left side grows like $M$. It therefore gives an effective upper bound
    on $M$ for that fixed $q$, and then bounds all four exponents by the
    identities and bounds in Section~\ref{sec:bounds}. By itself this does not bound $q$
    absolutely; the next step supplies such a bound in one branch.

    Add: /home/erpage159/fluid/research/math/nt/prime-power-sum-pf/check_common_gap_residues.lua
    -- Necessary residue conditions for d | gcd(M,N), with d prime.
    -- Inputs from prime_power_notes.tex: p = 1 mod d, n1 even,
    -- M = hE with E even, d | h, and (2h-1)n1 < N.
    -- The modulo-5 split retains the exponent classes modulo 4.
    -- This checks whole residue classes, not primes q below a search bound.
    -- Lua 5.5, 5.4 and LuaJIT; no external libraries.
    
    local function gcd(a, b)
        while b ~= 0 do a, b = b, a % b end
        return a
    end
    
    local function lcm(a, b)
        return math.floor(a / gcd(a, b)) * b
    end
    
    local function power_modulo(base, exponent, modulus)
        local result = 1
        while exponent > 0 do
            if exponent % 2 == 1 then result = result * base % modulus end
            base = base * base % modulus
            exponent = math.floor(exponent / 2)
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function primes_through(limit)
        local result = {}
        for n = 2, limit do
            local prime = true
            for divisor = 2, math.floor(math.sqrt(n)) do
                if n % divisor == 0 then prime = false; break end
            end
            if prime then result[#result + 1] = n end
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function even_exponents_by_value(d, period)
        local result = {}
        for exponent = 0, period - 1, 2 do
            local value = power_modulo(2, exponent, d)
            result[value] = result[value] or {}
            result[value][#result[value] + 1] = exponent
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function passes_modulo_five(c, m1, e, N)
        if (m1 - c) % 4 == 0 then
            return c % 4 == 0 and N % 5 ~= 0
        end
        return (c + e) % 4 == 2
    end
    
    local function possible_even_E(c, m1, h, period)
        -- hE = m1-c mod period is soluble with E even exactly in this case.
        return (m1 - c) % gcd(2 * h, period) == 0
    end
    
    local function local_residues(d, N, e, h)
        local period = lcm(4, d - 1)
        local exponents = even_exponents_by_value(d, period)
        local result = {}
        for q = 2, d - 1 do
            -- q = 0,1 mod d are already excluded by gcd(g,q(q-1))=1.
            local small_power = (1 - power_modulo(q, N + e, d)) % d
            local large_power = (1 - power_modulo(q, e, d)) % d
            local found = false
            for _, c in ipairs(exponents[small_power] or {}) do
                for _, m1 in ipairs(exponents[large_power] or {}) do
                    if passes_modulo_five(c, m1, e, N)
                        and possible_even_E(c, m1, h, period) then
                        found = true
                        break
                    end
                end
                if found then break end
            end
            if found then result[#result + 1] = q end
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function surviving_families(d, N)
        local result = {}
        local e = 2
        while (2 * d - 1) * e < N do
            local h = d
            while (2 * h - 1) * e < N do
                local residues = local_residues(d, N, e, h)
                if #residues > 0 then
                    result[#result + 1] = {e = e, h = h, residues = residues}
                end
                h = h + d
            end
            e = e + 2
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function check_global_seventeen()
        -- All relevant exponents are periodic modulo 16 (also a multiple of 4).
        -- Ignoring 3 | N and allowing h=17 enlarges the necessary residue set.
        for e = 2, 16, 2 do
            for N = 1, 15, 2 do
                assert(#local_residues(17, N, e, 17) == 0,
                    "Unexpected residue class for 17 | gcd(M,N)")
            end
        end
    end
    
    local function main()
        check_global_seventeen()
        print("17 | gcd(M,N): no residue classes")
    
        local excluded = {}
        for _, d in ipairs(primes_through(200)) do
            if d >= 7 and #surviving_families(d, 5 * d) == 0 then
                excluded[#excluded + 1] = d
            end
        end
        print("N=5d forces coprime gaps for d in: " .. table.concat(excluded, ", "))
    
        for _, pair in ipairs({{49, 7}, {55, 11}, {65, 13}, {77, 7},
            {77, 11}, {85, 17}, {91, 7}, {91, 13}, {121, 11}}) do
            local N, d = pair[1], pair[2]
            local families = surviving_families(d, N)
            print(string.format("N=%d, d=%d: %d local families", N, d, #families))
            for _, family in ipairs(families) do
                print(string.format("  n1=%d, h=%d, q mod d in {%s}",
                    family.e, family.h, table.concat(family.residues, ",")))
            end
        end
    end
    
    main()

For your reading, there is a less restrictive target than ℓ > q: it is enough that ℓ does not divide q − 1. We can also combine several qualifying primitive factors and compare their product with the odd part of q − 1.

    +% New deductions from the common-divisor residue calculations.
    +\begin{lemma}\label{lem:exclude-seventeen}
    +$17\nmid\gcd(M,N)$. Consequently gaps are coprime whenever
    +$N=5^a17^b$, with $a,b\ge0$.
    +\end{lemma}
    +\begin{proof}
    +Suppose $17\mid g$. The nonzero squares modulo $17$ are
    +$1,2,4,8,9,13,15,16$, and
    +$\langle4\rangle=\{1,4,16,13\}$.
    +In $2^{m_1}+q^{n_1}\equiv1$, only
    +$2^{m_1}\equiv16$, $q^{n_1}\equiv2$ are possible.
    +Thus $m_1\equiv4\pmod8$. Since $\operatorname{ord}_{17}(2)=8$
    +and $n_1$ is even, $q$ has order $16$ and $n_1\equiv2\pmod4$.
    +The odd power $q^{n_2}$ also has order $16$.

    +In the remaining case,

    +\[
    +2.97h\lambda-\beta

    +for $h\ge q^2$. Hence

    +This proves $h<q^2$.

    +Write $e=n_1$, $c=m_2$, $Q=q^e$. Since $c\ge4$, $e\ge2$,
    +\[

    +\]
    +Thus $(2h-1)e<N$. Now use $e\ge2$ and $g\mid h$.
    +\end{proof}

    \subsection{Scope of the MSS results}
    
    The system is a special case of $a^x+b^y=c^z$ with
    $(a,b,c)=(2,q,p)$ and $z=Z=1$. MSS's complete results for
    $c=7,13,97$ exclude those values of $p$ here. Their more general effective
    results fix $c$ in specified families, so a bound depending on $c=p$
    does not supply a global bound for our problem. Their Pillai theorem
    concerns a difference of powers and is not directly a theorem about
    our sum. See the theorem statements and outline in \cite{MSS}.
    
    Their polynomial-exponential equation matches our equality exactly:
    \[
    X^a-X^b=q^{y_1}-q^{y_2},\qquad
    (X,a,b,y_1,y_2)=(2,m_1,m_2,n_2,n_1).
    \]
    But the proposition labeled \texttt{prop-EuAl} in the local MSS source
    assumes $(a-b)/E$ odd, where $E$ is the least positive exponent for which
    $X^E\equiv\pm1\pmod q$. This is a signed order, unlike our ordinary orders.
    For $X=2$ put $r=\operatorname{ord}_q(2)$. If $r$ is odd, $E=r$,
    and $M/E$ is even. If $r$ is even, $E=r/2$, and $M/E=2(M/r)$ is even.
    Thus the proposition as stated never applies to this specialization.
    The polynomial argument below is a separate adaptation, not an invocation
    of that proposition.

    \subsection{Reading and limits of the cited results}
    Pomerance \cite[\S2]{PomCycl} supplies the primitive/intrinsic
    cyclotomic decomposition, bounds for $\Phi_d(2)$, and the Aurifeuilian
    splitting for $d\equiv4\pmod8$. These concern individual factors.
    Cambraia et al.\ \cite[\S\S2--4]{Cambraia} give the gcd identities,
    valuation formula, and classification when $\omega(2^M-1)\leq3$;
    the preceding lemma specializes that classification to our equations.
    Their final section studies a different sum of Mersenne numbers.
    
    Kova\v{c}--Luca \cite{KL} study sums of divisor counts over exponents;
    their pointwise primitive-factor bound is what we use above.
    Erd\H{o}s--Kiss--Pomerance \cite{EKP} study reciprocal sums of prime
    divisors, including averages and consecutive exponents. Neither result
    currently controls the particular mixed-base gcd needed for $C$.
    Pomerance's earlier paper \cite{PomPrim} treats reciprocal sums over
    divisors of prescribed order.
    
    For the proposed descent, compare Bilu \cite[\S2, Proposition 2.1 and
    Corollary 2.2]{Bilu}: coprimality and a perfect-power product force powers
    of ideals. The identity $\Phi_s(Y)=Cp$ does not provide that
    perfect-power hypothesis. A transfer of the argument would need to
    supply it.

## Assistant

Yes—the useful object is Φ_M(2) = Norm(2 − ζ_M), where ζ_M is a primitive M-th root of unity. Its prime factors come from reducing 2 − ζ_M modulo prime ideals. That gives a more structural starting point than the residual-index terminology I focused on.

And you’re right about ℓ > q: a size theorem could be much more tractable than proving ℓ ∤ q − 1. I’ll keep those as separate approaches and look at what cyclotomic norms, subfields, and factorization identities can actually contribute.

## Assistant

This gives a concrete improvement. When r ≡ 4 (mod 8), an Aurifeuillean factorization splits 2^(r/2) + 1 into two coprime integers of roughly size 2^(r/4). The whole q^n₁ must fit into one of them. That strengthens the size constraint enough to exclude r ≡ 4 (mod 8) in the remaining N = 49 family.

Brent’s *On computing factors of cyclotomic polynomials* looks like a better first recommendation: it develops these factorizations from roots of unity and gives algorithms for computing them.
