    +\begin{lemma}\label{lem:aurifeuillean-height}
    +Suppose $r\equiv4\pmod8$. If

    +\frac{8h}{q^{n_1/2}-1}\le m_2\log2,
    +\]
    +then $(4h-1)n_1<N$. The hypothesis holds whenever $h\le32$.
    +Consequently the noncoprime $N=49$ family requires
    +$r\not\equiv4\pmod8$.
    +\end{lemma}
    +\begin{proof}
    +Write $r=8a+4$. Since $q^{n_1}\mid2^r-1$ and
    +$\operatorname{ord}_q(2)=r$, the full power $q^{n_1}$ divides
    +\[
    +2^{r/2}+1
    +=(2^{2a+1}-2^{a+1}+1)(2^{2a+1}+2^{a+1}+1).
    +\]
    +The two factors are odd and their difference is a power of $2$,
    +so they are coprime. Hence
    +\[
    +q^{n_1}\le2^{r/4}+2^{(r+4)/8}+1
    + <(2^{r/8}+1)^2,
    +\qquad 2^r>(q^{n_1/2}-1)^8.

    +Here $E=r$. Put $e=n_1$, $c=m_2$. The hypothesis and
    +$\log(1+x)<x$ give

    +8h\log\frac{q^{e/2}}{q^{e/2}-1}<c\log2.
    +\]

    + >2^c(q^{e/2}-1)^{8h}>q^{4he}.

    +For $N=49$ we have $h=7$, $e=2$, which would require $54<49$.
    +\end{proof}

## Assistant

The cyclotomic approach produced a useful additional restriction. I’ve added it, the residue calculations, and revised reading notes.

The main new results are:

- **17 cannot divide gcd(M,N).** Combining the two representations modulo 17 with our modulo-5 restrictions gives a contradiction. Consequently, gaps are coprime whenever N = 5^a·17^b.
- With E = lcm(2,r) and M = hE, the sharper height bound is **(2h − 1)n₁ < N**, hence h < (N + 2)/4.
- For the noncoprime N = 49 case, this leaves **n₁ = 2 and M = 7E**, removing the previous h = 14 possibility.

The further gain comes from the factorization, for r = 8a + 4:

```text
2^(r/2) + 1
  = (2^(2a+1) − 2^(a+1) + 1)
    (2^(2a+1) + 2^(a+1) + 1).
```

Those factors are coprime. Since q has order r, **the entire q^n₁ must divide one of them**. Therefore:

```text
q^n₁ ≤ 2^(r/4) + 2^((r+4)/8) + 1.
```

This is substantially tighter than placing q^n₁ in the whole half-factor. Combining it with the original equality gives **(4h − 1)n₁ < N** whenever h ≤ 32; the notes give the more general condition too. For N = 49, h = 7 and n₁ = 2 would require 54 < 49. Thus **r ≡ 4 (mod 8) is excluded from that family**.

That is a concrete reason to study how the roots group into factors: it can reduce the space available for q^n₁ before we know the prime factorization. Brent’s §§2.2–2.3 develop the root groupings behind the identities; §3 supplies algorithms. [Brent’s paper](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/brent/pd/rpb135.pdf)

For the systematic residue work, the notes now contain a finite-field polynomial criterion for N = 5d. It proves coprimality for:

```text
d = 7, 17, 29, 41, 43, 73, 89, 109, 113.
```

The calculation is in [the Lua script](/home/erpage159/fluid/research/math/nt/prime-power-sum-pf/check_common_gap_residues.lua). These are exclusions of whole families, with q unrestricted.

On the reading direction, I’ve retained **ℓ > q as a substantive size target**. Stewart’s *On divisors of Lucas and Lehmer numbers*, especially Theorem 1.1 and §5, is relevant: it combines the size of cyclotomic values with bounds on prime-adic multiplicities to force large primitive factors. We would still need to compare its lower bound with q and control the resulting multiplier j. [Stewart’s paper](https://uwaterloo.ca/pure-mathematics/sites/default/files/uploads/documents/s11511-013-0105-y.pdf)

The q − 1 alternative now has a precise target in the notes: the qualifying factors must fit into the odd part of q − 1, or that quantity times N in the version using E. Establishing that they cannot fit requires an actual bound on shared factors; I haven’t treated it as easier merely because its hypothesis is weaker.

The updated PDF compiles cleanly, and I checked the new proof and reading pages.

- [Brent — On computing factors of cyclotomic polynomials](/home/erpage159/fluid/research/math/nt/prime-power-sum-pf/Brent-1992-On-computing-factors-of-cyclotomic-polynomials.pdf)
- [Brent — Computing Aurifeuillian factors](/home/erpage159/fluid/research/math/nt/prime-power-sum-pf/Brent-Computing-Aurifeuillian-factors.pdf), his shorter exposition.
- [Stewart — On divisors of Lucas and Lehmer numbers](/home/erpage159/fluid/research/math/nt/prime-power-sum-pf/Stewart-2013-On-divisors-of-Lucas-and-Lehmer-numbers.pdf)

Brent’s starting point is that **the primitive roots can be grouped according to a quadratic character**. For an odd prime exponent, for example, group ζ^a according to whether a is a quadratic residue or nonresidue. Multiplying within each group gives two conjugate polynomials over a quadratic field. Their product is the cyclotomic polynomial.

For n = 5, this gives:

```text
4Φ₅(x) = (2x² + x + 2)² − 5x².
```

The square root of 5 appears because the two root groups are exchanged by the nontrivial automorphism of Q(√5). This is how the organization of the roots becomes an algebraic factorization. [Brent, §2.2](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/brent/pd/rpb135.pdf)

The Aurifeuillean construction uses a related grouping, involving roots of order 2n and a parity condition. The resulting identity has a variable inside the square-root term. For example:

```text
Φ₅(x) = (x² + 3x + 1)² − 5x(x + 1)².
```

Now a suitable specialization makes that square root an integer. At x = 5:

```text
Φ₅(5) = 41² − 30² = 11 · 71.
```

So the useful question becomes: **which substitutions make these algebraic factors into integer factors?** This is the source of the special factorizations. [Brent’s shorter exposition, §§1–2](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/brent/pd/rpb127.pdf)

His computational step is also appealing. He computes sums of powers of the selected roots using Gauss sums, then recovers the polynomial coefficients through Newton’s identities. The algorithms work with exact integer arithmetic; one needn’t numerically approximate and multiply a collection of complex roots. [Brent, §3](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/brent/pd/rpb135.pdf)

For our problem, the payoff is already visible in the specialization

```text
x = 2t²:

x² + 1 = (2t² − 2t + 1)(2t² + 2t + 1).
```

When r ≡ 4 (mod 8), take x = 2^(r/2). The two integer factors are coprime, so q^n₁ must occur entirely in one. Their size then constrains our exponents without requiring their prime factorizations.

What I’d pursue next is **other groupings or relative norms that constrain where q^n₁ can occur for the remaining orders r**. The useful output could be a smaller factor, a restriction on its prime divisors, or control of the gcd between factors. Brent supplies concrete constructions and algorithms with which to investigate those possibilities.

**Neither process currently has a proved terminal point.** The congruence calculations can keep removing families, and the cyclotomic factorizations can keep tightening size restrictions. What we need is a reason those restrictions eventually overwhelm every remaining possibility.

There is, however, a more concrete route to termination than I made explicit earlier: **use the factorization to force growth that exceeds what the logarithmic bound permits.**

Recall E = lcm(2,r). We have the integer

```text
(2^E − 1) / q^n₁.
```

Our existing bound q^n₁ ≤ 2^(E/2) + 1 implies

```text
(2^E − 1) / q^n₁ ≥ q^n₁ − 2 ≥ q² − 2.
```

So even at n₁ = 2, there is already roughly q² of factorization left after removing q’s contribution.

Now let D_E be the part of that integer supported on primes ℓ for which

```text
gcd((ℓ − 1)/ord_ℓ(2), N) = 1.
```

We proved that this part must satisfy

```text
D_E divides uN,     where u = (q − 1)/2^m₂.
```

Since m₂ ≥ 4, that gives D_E < qN/16.

**This creates a possible terminal mechanism.** Suppose we could prove, throughout the remaining families, a lower bound

```text
D_E ≥ q^(1 + δ)
```

for some fixed δ > 0. Then necessarily

```text
N > 16q^δ.
```

But solving our existing logarithmic estimate gives an effective upper bound on N of the shape

```text
N ≤ C log(q) · (log log(q) + C₀)²,
```

with absolute constants. Those two bounds are incompatible for sufficiently large q. That would leave a finite range of q, and the logarithmic estimate would then bound the exponents for the final computation.

The missing step is substantial: **we know the whole remaining factorization has size at least q² − 2, but we do not know that enough of it belongs to D_E.** For example, forcing slightly more than half its logarithmic size into D_E would suffice. This is a quantitative target for the root-grouping approach: produce factors whose size we control *and* whose prime divisors satisfy the needed order restrictions. Splitting into smaller factors alone does not supply that second property.

The congruence process has a different prospect. A list of excluded common primes or exponent classes has no inherent endpoint. To become decisive, it needs either:

- a structural contradiction covering all common primes d in a specified family; or
- a bound on d or N independent of q, followed by complete treatment of the remaining families.

The exclusion of 17 is an example of the first kind: it removes that common divisor for every N. The isolated N = 5d exclusions have less reach unless their underlying polynomial conditions admit a general characterization.

So I would put more weight on **factor allocation combined with the logarithmic bound** as a route to a finite endpoint. The congruence work remains useful for restricting which allocations are possible. Brent’s constructions could contribute by identifying whole factors that must go to a particular place; a sufficiently strong result of that sort would do much more than add another excluded residue class.

We do not yet have that result. But we now have a specific growth comparison that would turn such a result into a finite computational target.

## Assistant

**Gauss sums connect the rule used to group the roots with the coefficients of the resulting factors.** They also help estimate those factors. Control of their prime divisors requires another step.

Take n = 5. Split the primitive roots into the quadratic-residue exponents {1,4} and nonresidue exponents {2,3}. The Gauss sum is their difference:

```text
τ = ζ + ζ⁴ − ζ² − ζ³ = √5.
```

Their total is −1, so the two group sums are (−1 + √5)/2 and (−1 − √5)/2. This gives the factors

```text
G₊(x) = x² + (1 − √5)x/2 + 1
G₋(x) = x² + (1 + √5)x/2 + 1,

Φ₅(x) = G₊(x)G₋(x).
```

For larger n, Brent evaluates the sums of successive powers of each group’s roots using Gauss sums. Newton’s identities then recover the coefficients. The quadratic character determines the grouping; the Gauss sums make it computable. [Brent, §§2.2–3](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/brent/pd/rpb135.pdf)

For **sizes**, those same power sums enter the expansion

```text
log(G(x)/x^degree(G))
    = −sum over k≥1 of [sum of k-th powers of its roots]/(k x^k).
```

Thus their cancellation controls how far G(x) lies from its leading term. Brent uses this approach to estimate the factors and their relative sizes. [Brent, §4](https://maths-people.anu.edu.au/brent/pd/rpb135.pdf)

For **prime divisors’ residue classes**, the connection is through how reduction modulo ℓ acts on the root groups. Raising ζ to the ℓ-th power sends an exponent a to ℓa. A quadratic character therefore tells us whether this operation preserves the groups or exchanges them. That is the splitting information expressed by the quadratic field appearing in the coefficients.

But there is a limitation particularly relevant to us: **this information can already be contained in the primitive-order condition.** If ℓ is primitive at exponent t, then ℓ ≡ 1 (mod t), so it fixes every t-th root. A quadratic grouping within that cyclotomic field need not impose any additional restriction on ℓ.

Our D_E condition concerns something further:

```text
ℓ ≠ 1 (mod s) for every prime s dividing N.
```

Since gcd(E,N) = 1, these moduli s lie outside the exponents t dividing E. So I should not suggest that Brent’s Gauss sums automatically classify factors into D_E and its complement. **We still need a connection between the root grouping and these additional moduli.**

There are therefore two distinct ways this machinery could help us:

- **Size and allocation:** produce coprime integer factors small enough that q^n₁ cannot fit into either. This is exactly what our Aurifeuillean argument uses; it needs no classification of their other prime divisors.
- **Residue control:** show that a structured factor has a sufficiently large contribution from primes outside the classes ℓ ≡ 1 (mod s). That would feed into D_E, but we have not established such a result.

The first use is already productive. The second is a research direction, and the Gauss sums provide a way to describe the factors precisely—not, by themselves, the missing restriction on their prime divisors.

“Root group” was imprecise. I meant **an orbit of primitive roots under a subgroup of the Galois group**.

For example, put K = Q(ζ₅). Identify Gal(K/Q) with (Z/5Z)×. The subgroup H = {1,4} has fixed field Q(√5) and two orbits:

```text
{ζ₅, ζ₅⁴},    {ζ₅², ζ₅³}.
```

The products over these orbits are conjugate polynomials over Q(√5). The Gauss sum

```text
ζ₅ + ζ₅⁴ − ζ₅² − ζ₅³ = √5
```

determines their coefficients. Their product is Φ₅(x). **That is the structural role:** explicit relative norms and their conjugates.

Brent’s related Aurifeuillean construction gives

```text
Φ₅(x) = (x² + 3x + 1)² − 5x(x + 1)².
```

At x = 5 this yields integer factors:

```text
Φ₅(5) = (41 − 30)(41 + 30) = 11 · 71.
```

The construction supplies the factors and their sizes. Their prime divisors can then be studied separately.

By “additional moduli,” I meant **the primes s dividing N**. For N = 49, the relevant modulus is 7: D_E retains primes ℓ ≠ 1 (mod 7). In the numerical example, 11 qualifies and 71 does not. That conclusion comes from checking their residues, not from the Gauss-sum identity.

For our actual integer a, the task is to obtain structured factors, then determine—by inspection, congruences, or another argument—which contributions belong to D_E. You’re right: whether the construction immediately supplies a new congruence is not the criterion for its usefulness.

    -- Exact finite check for M = 2^a q^b, using the external bound q < 10^6.
    -- Run with: lua check_power_two_orders.lua
    
    local LIMIT = 1000000
    
    local function filter(values, predicate)
        local result = {}
        for _, value in ipairs(values) do
            if predicate(value) then
                result[#result + 1] = value
            end
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function primes_below(limit)
        -- Sieve of Eratosthenes; mutation stays local to the sieve.
        local composite = {}
        for p = 2, math.floor(math.sqrt(limit - 1)) do
            if not composite[p] then
                for multiple = p * p, limit - 1, p do
                    composite[multiple] = true
                end
            end
        end
    
        local primes = {}
        for n = 2, limit - 1 do
            if not composite[n] then
                primes[#primes + 1] = n
            end
        end
        return primes
    end
    
    local function valuation_at_two(n)
        local exponent = 0
        while n % 2 == 0 do
            n = math.floor(n / 2)
            exponent = exponent + 1
        end
        return exponent
    end
    
    local function power_modulo(base, exponent, modulus)
        -- Repeated squaring. With modulus < 10^6, products stay below 10^12,
        -- so the arithmetic is exact even in Lua versions using doubles.
        local result = 1
        base = base % modulus
        while exponent > 0 do
            if exponent % 2 == 1 then
                result = (result * base) % modulus
            end
            base = (base * base) % modulus
            exponent = math.floor(exponent / 2)
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function is_one_modulo_three(q)
        return q % 3 == 1
    end
    
    local function has_even_two_valuation(q)
        return valuation_at_two(q - 1) % 2 == 0
    end
    
    local function has_power_of_two_order(q)
        -- For prime q, ord_q(2) divides q - 1. It is a power of two
        -- exactly when it divides the largest power of two dividing q - 1.
        local two_part = 2 ^ valuation_at_two(q - 1)
        return power_modulo(2, two_part, q) == 1
    end
    
    local function is_one_modulo_five(q)
        return q % 5 == 1
    end

    \section{Auxiliary calculations and comparison with MSS}

    % Added in discussion: comparison with MSS and the two adaptations below.
    
    \subsection{Scope of the MSS results}
    
    The system is a special case of $a^x+b^y=c^z$ with
    $(a,b,c)=(2,q,p)$ and $z=Z=1$. MSS's complete results for
    $c=7,13,97$ exclude those values of $p$ here. Their more general effective
    results fix $c$ in specified families, so a bound depending on $c=p$
    does not supply a global bound for our problem. Their Pillai theorem
    concerns a difference of powers and is not directly a theorem about
    our sum. See the theorem statements and outline in \cite{MSS}.
    
    Their polynomial-exponential equation matches our equality exactly:
    \[
    X^a-X^b=q^{y_1}-q^{y_2},\qquad
    (X,a,b,y_1,y_2)=(2,m_1,m_2,n_2,n_1).
    \]
    But the proposition labeled \texttt{prop-EuAl} in the local MSS source
    assumes $(a-b)/E$ odd, where $E$ is the least positive exponent for which
    $X^E\equiv\pm1\pmod q$. This is a signed order, unlike our ordinary orders.
    For $X=2$ put $r=\operatorname{ord}_q(2)$. If $r$ is odd, $E=r$,
    -- Exact finite check for M = 2^a q^b, using the external bound q < 10^6.
    -- Run with: lua check_power_two_orders.lua
    
    local LIMIT = 1000000
    
    local function filter(values, predicate)
        local result = {}
        for _, value in ipairs(values) do
            if predicate(value) then
                result[#result + 1] = value
            end
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function primes_below(limit)
        -- Sieve of Eratosthenes; mutation stays local to the sieve.
        local composite = {}
        for p = 2, math.floor(math.sqrt(limit - 1)) do
            if not composite[p] then
                for multiple = p * p, limit - 1, p do
                    composite[multiple] = true
                end
            end
        end
    
        local primes = {}
        for n = 2, limit - 1 do
            if not composite[n] then
                primes[#primes + 1] = n
            end
        end
        return primes
    end
    
    local function valuation_at_two(n)
        local exponent = 0
        while n % 2 == 0 do
            n = math.floor(n / 2)
            exponent = exponent + 1
        end
        return exponent
    end
    
    local function power_modulo(base, exponent, modulus)
        -- Repeated squaring. With modulus < 10^6, products stay below 10^12,
        -- so the arithmetic is exact even in Lua versions using doubles.
        local result = 1
        base = base % modulus
        while exponent > 0 do
            if exponent % 2 == 1 then
                result = (result * base) % modulus
            end
            base = (base * base) % modulus
            exponent = math.floor(exponent / 2)
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function is_one_modulo_three(q)
        return q % 3 == 1
    end
    
    local function has_even_two_valuation(q)
        return valuation_at_two(q - 1) % 2 == 0
    end
    
    local function has_power_of_two_order(q)
        -- For prime q, ord_q(2) divides q - 1. It is a power of two
        -- exactly when it divides the largest power of two dividing q - 1.
        local two_part = 2 ^ valuation_at_two(q - 1)
        return power_modulo(2, two_part, q) == 1
    end
    
    local function is_one_modulo_five(q)
        return q % 5 == 1
    end
    
    local function display(label, values)
        local entries = {}
        for i, value in ipairs(values) do
            entries[i] = string.format("%.0f", value)
        end
        print(label .. ": [" .. table.concat(entries, ", ") .. "]")
    end
    
    local function main()
        -- Apply the restrictions in the order of the mathematical argument.
        local primes = primes_below(LIMIT)
        local one_modulo_three = filter(primes, is_one_modulo_three)
        local even_valuation = filter(one_modulo_three, has_even_two_valuation)
        local candidates = filter(even_valuation, has_power_of_two_order)
        local survivors = filter(candidates, is_one_modulo_five)
    
        display("Power-of-two order, q = 1 mod 3, even v2(q-1)", candidates)
        display("Also q = 1 mod 5", survivors)
    
        assert(#candidates == 1 and candidates[1] == 274177,
            "Expected exactly the candidate 274177")
        assert(#survivors == 0, "Expected no survivors")

    \label{sec:p-common-gap}

    -- Necessary residue conditions for d | gcd(M,N), with d prime.
    -- Inputs from prime_power_notes.tex: p = 1 mod d, n1 even,
    -- M = hE with E even, d | h, and (2h-1)n1 < N.
    -- The modulo-5 split retains the exponent classes modulo 4.
    -- This checks whole residue classes, not primes q below a search bound.
    -- Lua 5.5, 5.4 and LuaJIT; no external libraries.
    
    local function gcd(a, b)
        while b ~= 0 do a, b = b, a % b end
        return a
    end
    
    local function lcm(a, b)
        return math.floor(a / gcd(a, b)) * b
    end
    
    local function power_modulo(base, exponent, modulus)
        local result = 1
        while exponent > 0 do
            if exponent % 2 == 1 then result = result * base % modulus end
            base = base * base % modulus
            exponent = math.floor(exponent / 2)
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function primes_through(limit)
        local result = {}
        for n = 2, limit do
            local prime = true
            for divisor = 2, math.floor(math.sqrt(n)) do
                if n % divisor == 0 then prime = false; break end
            end
            if prime then result[#result + 1] = n end
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function even_exponents_by_value(d, period)
        local result = {}
        for exponent = 0, period - 1, 2 do
            local value = power_modulo(2, exponent, d)
            result[value] = result[value] or {}
            result[value][#result[value] + 1] = exponent
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function passes_modulo_five(c, m1, e, N)
        if (m1 - c) % 4 == 0 then
            return c % 4 == 0 and N % 5 ~= 0
        end
        return (c + e) % 4 == 2
    end
    
    local function possible_even_E(c, m1, h, period)
        -- hE = m1-c mod period is soluble with E even exactly in this case.
        return (m1 - c) % gcd(2 * h, period) == 0
    end
    
    local function local_residues(d, N, e, h)
        local period = lcm(4, d - 1)
        local exponents = even_exponents_by_value(d, period)
        local result = {}
        for q = 2, d - 1 do
            -- q = 0,1 mod d are already excluded by gcd(g,q(q-1))=1.
            local small_power = (1 - power_modulo(q, N + e, d)) % d
            local large_power = (1 - power_modulo(q, e, d)) % d
            local found = false
            for _, c in ipairs(exponents[small_power] or {}) do
                for _, m1 in ipairs(exponents[large_power] or {}) do
                    if passes_modulo_five(c, m1, e, N)
                        and possible_even_E(c, m1, h, period) then
                        found = true
                        break
                    end
                end
                if found then break end
            end
            if found then result[#result + 1] = q end
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function surviving_families(d, N)
        local result = {}
        local e = 2
        while (2 * d - 1) * e < N do
            local h = d
            while (2 * h - 1) * e < N do
                local residues = local_residues(d, N, e, h)
                if #residues > 0 then
                    result[#result + 1] = {e = e, h = h, residues = residues}
                end
                h = h + d
            end
            e = e + 2
        end
        return result
    end
    
    local function check_global_seventeen()
        -- All relevant exponents are periodic modulo 16 (also a multiple of 4).
        -- Allow the 4 | M branch regardless of 5 | N. Ignoring 3 | N
        -- and allowing h=17 also enlarge the necessary residue set.
        for e = 2, 16, 2 do
            for N = 1, 15, 2 do
                local representative = N % 5 == 0 and N + 16 or N
                assert(#local_residues(17, representative, e, 17) == 0,
                    "Unexpected residue class for 17 | gcd(M,N)")
            end
        end
    end
    
    local function main()
        check_global_seventeen()
        print("17 | gcd(M,N): no residue classes")
    
        local excluded = {}
        for _, d in ipairs(primes_through(200)) do
            if d >= 7 and #surviving_families(d, 5 * d) == 0 then
                excluded[#excluded + 1] = d
            end
        end
        print("N=5d forces coprime gaps for d in: " .. table.concat(excluded, ", "))
    
        for _, pair in ipairs({{49, 7}, {55, 11}, {65, 13}, {77, 7},
            {77, 11}, {85, 17}, {91, 7}, {91, 13}, {121, 11}}) do
            local N, d = pair[1], pair[2]
            local families = surviving_families(d, N)
            print(string.format("N=%d, d=%d: %d local families", N, d, #families))
            for _, family in ipairs(families) do
                print(string.format("  n1=%d, h=%d, q mod d in {%s}",
                    family.e, family.h, table.concat(family.residues, ",")))
            end
        end
    end
    
    main()

    PPValuation := function(n, prime)
        local exponent;
        if n <= 0 then Error("valuation requires a positive integer"); fi;
        exponent := 0;
        while n mod prime = 0 do
            n := QuoInt(n, prime);
            exponent := exponent + 1;
        od;
        return exponent;
    end;
    
    # Compute v_prime(base^exponent - 1) without constructing base^exponent.
    PPPowerValuation := function(base, exponent, prime)
        local valuation, modulus;
        valuation := 0;
        modulus := prime;
        while PowerModInt(base, exponent, modulus) = 1 do
            valuation := valuation + 1;
            modulus := modulus * prime;
        od;
        return valuation;
    end;
    
    PPProvenPrime := function(n)
        local proof;
        if not IsPrimeInt(n) then return false; fi;
        if n < 2^64 then return true; fi;
        proof := PrimalityProof(n);
        if proof = fail or proof = false then
            Error("primality not certified for ", n);
        fi;
        return PrimalityProof_Verify(n, proof);
    end;
    
    PPFactorization := function(n)
        local factors;
        if n = 1 then return []; fi;
        factors := FactorsInt(n);
        if Product(factors) <> n or not ForAll(Set(factors), PPProvenPrime) then
            Error("factorization not certified");
        fi;
        return Collected(factors);
    end;
    
    PPFactorText := factors -> JoinStringsWithSeparator(
        List(factors, pair -> Concatenation(String(pair[1]), "^", String(pair[2]))), " * ");
    
    # Primes ell | q-1 for which the valuation identity in the notes applies.

    PPBaseData := function(q)

    PPBaseCompatible := function(b)
        local condition, Q, ceiling;

        local a, result, pair, ell, t;
        a := QuoInt(2^b.E-1,b.q^b.e);
        if a*b.q^b.e <> 2^b.E-1 then Error("incorrect q valuation"); fi;
        result := [];
        for pair in PPFactorization(a) do
            ell := pair[1];
            t := OrderMod(2,ell);
            Add(result,rec(ell := ell, f := pair[2], t := t,
                j := QuoInt(ell-1,t), orderQ := OrderMod(b.q,ell),
                orderQPower := OrderMod(b.q,ell^pair[2]),
                phiIndices := Filtered(DivisorsInt(b.E), d ->
                    Value(CyclotomicPolynomial(Rationals,d),2) mod ell = 0)));
        od;
        return result;
    end;
    
    PPSelectedProduct := function(factors,N)
        return Product(Filtered(factors,f -> Gcd(f.j,N)=1), f -> f.ell^f.f);
    end;
    
    # N must accommodate every prime-power order in a, not only selected factors.
    PPGapCompatible := function(b,factors,N)
        if N < 5 or Gcd(N,6*b.E) <> 1 then return false; fi;
        if not ForAll(b.ordinary,ell -> N mod ell <> 0) then return false; fi;
        if not ForAll(factors,f -> N mod f.orderQPower = 0) then return false; fi;
        return (QuoInt(b.q-1,2^b.c)*N) mod PPSelectedProduct(factors,N) = 0;
    end;
    
    PPMultiplierCompatible := function(b,N,h)
        local M,g,ell,condition,smallP,largeP;
        M := h*b.E;
        g := Gcd(M,N);
        if M < 6 or h >= b.q^2 or M mod b.q = 0 or
            (2*h-1)*b.e >= N then return false; fi;
        if b.r mod 8 = 4 and h <= 32 and (4*h-1)*b.e >= N then return false; fi;
        if Gcd(g,510*b.q*(b.q-1)*b.E) <> 1 then return false; fi;
        if g > 1 and (N < 5*g or 2*Phi(g) <= g) then return false; fi;
        if N=5*g and g>1 and (b.e<>2 or h<>g) then return false; fi;
        for ell in b.ordinary do
            if PPValuation(M,ell) <> PPValuation(b.q-1,ell)-1 then return false; fi;
        od;
        for condition in [[3,7],[4,5],[8,17],[12,13],[16,257],[18,19]] do
            if M mod condition[1]=0 and b.q mod condition[2]<>1 then return false; fi;
        od;
        if M mod 4=0 then
            if b.c mod 4<>0 or N mod 5=0 or b.q mod 5<>1 then return false; fi;
        elif (b.c+b.e) mod 4<>2 or PowerModInt(b.q,N,5)<>3 then
            return false;
        fi;
        # p = 1 modulo g, in both representations.
        if g>1 then
            smallP := (PowerModInt(2,b.c,g)+PowerModInt(b.q,N+b.e,g)) mod g;
            largeP := (PowerModInt(2,M+b.c,g)+PowerModInt(b.q,b.e,g)) mod g;
            if smallP<>1 or largeP<>1 then return false; fi;
        fi;
        # Exact comparisons, avoiding floating point logarithms.
        return 2^(M/2) < b.q^N and b.q^N < 2^M and
            2^(M+b.c) < b.q^(N+b.e);
    end;
    
    # Arithmetic Frobenius in Q(zeta_m). Here m=N is odd, or m=t divides ell-1.
    PPFrobenius := function(ell,m)
        if Gcd(ell,m)<>1 then return ["ramified","-"]; fi;
        if m=1 then return [1,1]; fi;
        return [ell mod m,OrderMod(ell,m)];
    end;
    
    PPLine := function(stream,line)
        WriteLine(stream,line);
    end;
    
    PPRow := function(stream,entries)
        PPLine(stream,Concatenation("| ",JoinStringsWithSeparator(
            List(entries,String)," | ")," |"));
    end;
    
    PPDetails := function(stream,b,config)
        local factors,N,f,hList,rows,frob;
        PPLine(stream,Concatenation("\n## q = ",String(b.q),"\n"));
        PPRow(stream,["q","c = m₂","e = n₁","r","E","ord_(q²)(2)"]);
        PPRow(stream,["---","---","---","---","---","---"]);
        PPRow(stream,[b.q,b.c,b.e,b.r,b.E,OrderMod(2,b.q^2)]);
        if b.E > config.factorE then
            PPLine(stream,"\nFactorization deferred: E exceeds factorE. This q remains in the base table.");
            return;
        fi;
        factors := PPFactorsOfA(b);
        PPLine(stream,"\n### Factors of a = (2^E − 1)/q^e\n");
        PPRow(stream,["ℓ","v_ℓ(a)","t = ord_ℓ(2)","j = (ℓ−1)/t",
            "ord_ℓ(q)","ord_(ℓ^f)(q)","indices d with ℓ dividing Φ_d(2)","ℓ > q"]);
        PPRow(stream,List([1..8],x -> "---"));
        for f in factors do
            PPRow(stream,[f.ell,f.f,f.t,f.j,f.orderQ,f.orderQPower,f.phiIndices,f.ell>b.q]);
        od;
        PPLine(stream,"\n### N and h satisfying the tested necessary conditions\n");
        PPRow(stream,["N","factorization of N","admissible h = M/E","D_E","uN / D_E"]);
        PPRow(stream,List([1..5],x -> "---"));
        rows := [];
        for N in [5..config.nMax] do
            if not PPGapCompatible(b,factors,N) then continue; fi;
            hList := Filtered([1..QuoInt(N+b.e-1,2*b.e)],
                h -> PPMultiplierCompatible(b,N,h));
            if IsEmpty(hList) then continue; fi;
            Add(rows,N);
            PPRow(stream,[N,PPFactorText(PPFactorization(N)),hList,
                PPSelectedProduct(factors,N),
                QuoInt(QuoInt(b.q-1,2^b.c)*N,PPSelectedProduct(factors,N))]);
        od;
        if IsEmpty(rows) then PPLine(stream,"\nNo N,h rows in the configured range."); fi;
        for N in rows do
            PPLine(stream,Concatenation("\n### Frobenius and D_E for N = ",String(N),"\n"));
            PPRow(stream,["ℓ","t","Frob in Q(ζ_t): exponent","ℓ mod N",
                "residue degree in Q(ζ_N)","gcd(ℓ−1,N)","ℓ^f included in D_E"]);
            PPRow(stream,List([1..7],x -> "---"));
            for f in factors do
                frob := PPFrobenius(f.ell,N);
                PPRow(stream,[f.ell,f.t,PPFrobenius(f.ell,f.t)[1],frob[1],frob[2],
                    Gcd(f.ell-1,N),Gcd(f.j,N)=1]);
            od;
        od;
    end;
    
    PPReport := function(config)
        local scan,stream,labels,i,b;
        scan := PPScan(config.qMax);
        stream := OutputTextFile(config.output,false);
        SetPrintFormattingStatus(stream,false);
        PPLine(stream,"# Mersenne factors: constrained GAP tables\n");
        PPLine(stream,Concatenation("GAP ",GAPInfo.Version,". Prime q range: 97 ≤ q ≤ ",
            String(config.qMax)," (inclusive)."));
        PPLine(stream,"The range is a computational choice, not an upper bound from the notes.");
        PPLine(stream,"Assumptions: A > 1, q > 3, q does not divide M; the remaining case of `prime_power_notes.tex`.");
        PPLine(stream,"Write c=m₂, e=n₁, r=ord_q(2), E=lcm(2,r), M=hE, N=n₂−n₁.\n");
        PPLine(stream,"## Counts after successive conditions\n");
        PPRow(stream,["Condition retained cumulatively","Number of q"]);
        PPRow(stream,["---","---"]);
        labels := ["q prime; q mod 240 in {1,97,193}","c=v₂(q−1) even (hence c≥4)",
            "2^((q−1)/6) = 1 modulo q; equivalently r divides (q−1)/6",
            "2^(q−1) = 1 modulo q²; equivalently e≥2",
            "e=v_q(2^r−1) even",
            "Remaining q-only order, residue and height tests in PPBaseCompatible"];
        for i in [1..Length(labels)] do PPRow(stream,[labels[i],scan.counts[i]]); od;
        if IsEmpty(scan.candidates) then
            PPLine(stream,"\n**No candidate q in this range.** There are consequently no candidate factor, N or Frobenius rows.");
        fi;
        for b in scan.candidates do PPDetails(stream,b,config); od;
        PPLine(stream,"\n## Table definitions and coverage\n");
        PPLine(stream,Concatenation("For surviving q, factor a when E ≤ ",String(config.factorE),
            "; test 5 ≤ N ≤ ",String(config.nMax),". All h with (2h−1)e<N are tested."));
        PPLine(stream,"A q outside the factorization limit remains listed; a missing factor table is not an exclusion.");
        PPLine(stream,"The N,h tables apply the orders modulo every prime power in a, gcd(E,N)=1, the ordinary-prime valuation identities for q−1, the gap/gcd restrictions, the modulo-5 split, the listed consequences of divisors of M, p=1 modulo gcd(M,N), and the gap inequalities. These are necessary-condition tables; the full representation equations and primality of p are not tested.");
        PPLine(stream,"Factorization products and the primality of every factor are checked. Above 2^64, a GAP primality proof is required.");
        PPLine(stream,"\n## Frobenius and the selected factors\n");
        PPLine(stream,"For ℓ not dividing m, arithmetic Frobenius in Q(ζ_m) sends ζ_m to ζ_m^ℓ; its order is ord_m(ℓ), the residue degree. See [Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, cyclotomic extensions and Frobenius](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT.pdf).");
        PPLine(stream,"For t=ord_ℓ(2), ℓ=1 modulo t, so Frobenius in Q(ζ_t) is the identity. To form D_E, use Q(ζ_s) for each prime s dividing N. Since gcd(E,N)=1 and t divides E, gcd((ℓ−1)/t,N)=gcd(ℓ−1,N).");
        PPLine(stream,"Thus ℓ^f belongs to D_E precisely when Frobenius is nonidentity in every Q(ζ_s) with s dividing N and s≠ℓ. At s=ℓ the prime is ramified; it imposes no exclusion from D_E, since ℓ does not divide ℓ−1. The table retains the full ℓ^f, and checks D_E divides ((q−1)/2^c)N.");
        PPLine(stream,"The order in Q(ζ_N) alone is insufficient to select D_E: the restrictions to each Q(ζ_s) matter. This is the exact role of the additional cyclotomic moduli here.");
        PPLine(stream,"\n## Reproduction\n\n```sh\n~/fluid/sauce/gap/gap -A -q -b mersenne_tables.g\n```\n");
        PPLine(stream,"To change the bounds, in GAP:\n\n```gap\nPPConfig := rec(qMax := 10^8, nMax := 121, factorE := 256,\n                output := \"mersenne-tables.md\");;\nRead(\"mersenne_tables.g\");\n```\n");
        PPLine(stream,"`mersenne_tables_test.g` checks the arithmetic and table helpers on independent small fixtures; those fixtures are not included as candidates.");
        CloseStream(stream);
        Print("Wrote ",config.output,"; counts = ",scan.counts,"\n");
        return scan;
    end;
    
    if not IsBound(PPLibraryOnly) or not PPLibraryOnly then
        if not IsBound(PPConfig) then
            PPConfig := rec(qMax := 10^8,nMax := 121,factorE := 256,
                output := "mersenne-tables.md");
        fi;
        PPResult := PPReport(PPConfig);;
    fi;

    Add: /home/erpage159/fluid/research/math/nt/prime-power-sum-pf/mersenne_tables_test.g
    # Run: ~/fluid/sauce/gap/gap -A -q -b --quitonbreak mersenne_tables_test.g
    PPLibraryOnly := true;;
    Read("mersenne_tables.g");
    
    PPTestCount := 0;;
    PPCheck := function(condition,message)
        if not condition then Error(message); fi;
        PPTestCount := PPTestCount+1;
    end;
    
    # Compare modular valuations with actual integer powers.
    for prime in [3,5,7,11,13,1093,3511] do
        r := OrderMod(2,prime);
        PPCheck(PPPowerValuation(2,r,prime)=PPValuation(2^r-1,prime),
            "valuation mismatch");
    od;
    PPCheck(PPPowerValuation(2,364,1093)=2,"Wieferich valuation fixture");
    PPCheck(not PPProvenPrime(341),"composite fixture");
    PPCheck(PPProvenPrime(2^89-1),"large certified prime fixture");
    
    # Include all three residue ranges, small limits, and inclusive endpoints.
    PPCheck(IsEmpty(PPStructuralScan(rec(qMax:=96,factorE:=256)).rows),"lower endpoint");
    PPCheck(IsEmpty(PPStructuralScan(rec(qMax:=432,factorE:=256)).rows),"upper endpoint");
    PPCheck(List(PPStructuralScan(rec(qMax:=433,factorE:=256)).rows,b -> b.q)=[433],
        "inclusive prime endpoint");
    scan := PPStructuralScan(rec(qMax:=10000,factorE:=256));;
    PPCheck(List(scan.rows,b -> b.q)=[433,1777,2113,2833,4177],"bounded structural scan");
    
    # A deliberately nonadmissible fixture checks that no row is relabelled a solution.
    PPCheck(not PPBaseCompatible(PPBaseData(433)),"odd rho must fail the full tests");
    PPCheck(IsEmpty(PPScan(10000).candidates),"strict scan must remain empty");
    
    for b in scan.rows do
        fs := PPFactorsOfA(b);
        a := QuoInt(2^b.E-1,b.q^b.e);
        PPCheck(Product(fs,f -> f.ell^f.f)=a,"factor product");
        PPCheck(Gcd(a,b.q)=1,"q removed completely");
        for f in fs do
            modulus := f.ell^f.f;
            PPCheck(PowerModInt(b.q,f.orderQPower,modulus)=1,"prime-power order");
            for divisor in Set(FactorsInt(f.orderQPower)) do
                PPCheck(PowerModInt(b.q,QuoInt(f.orderQPower,divisor),modulus)<>1,
                    "order minimality");
            od;
            for d in f.phiIndices do
                quotient := QuoInt(d,f.t);
                PPCheck(d mod f.t=0 and quotient=f.ell^PPValuation(quotient,f.ell),
                    "cyclotomic occurrence must have index t*ell^j");
            od;
        od;
        for N in Filtered([5..121],N -> Gcd(N,6*b.E)=1) do
            # Independently select factors by Frobenius on each prime cyclotomic field.
            selected := Filtered(fs,f -> ForAll(Set(FactorsInt(N)),s -> f.ell mod s<>1));
            PPCheck(PPSelectedProduct(fs,N)=Product(selected,f -> f.ell^f.f),
                "Frobenius selection and residual-index selection disagree");
        od;
    od;
    
    # Compute polynomial factorizations, rather than merely repeating the order formula.
    for ell in [3,5,7,11,13,17,19,31] do
        for s in [5,7,11] do
            factors := Factors(CyclotomicPolynomial(GF(ell),s));
            frob := PPFrobenius(ell,s);
            if ell=s then
                PPCheck(frob[1]="ramified" and Length(factors)=s-1 and
                    Length(Set(factors))=1 and Degree(factors[1])=1,"ramification");
            else
                PPCheck(List(factors,Degree)=List([1..QuoInt(s-1,frob[2])],i -> frob[2]),
                    "residue degrees versus finite-field factorization");
                PPCheck(GaloisCyc(E(s),ell)=E(s)^frob[1],"cyclotomic automorphism");
            fi;
        od;
    od;
    Print("Passed ",PPTestCount," checks.\n");
    QUIT;

    ## Table definitions and coverage
    
    The q rows exhaust the retained conditions with q ≤ 100000000 and E ≤ 256. The N tables cover every 5 ≤ N ≤ 121 with gcd(N,6E)=1. Neither bound is asserted for the original problem.
    The N rows display the order test L divides N and the product test D_E divides uN, even when they fail. No M, h or p is chosen. Conditions requiring those choices are not tested.
    Here L=ord_a(q), computed as the lcm of the prime-power orders. A nonunit gcd(L,6E) excludes every N with gcd(N,6E)=1 for that row.
    S_ℓ consists of primes s dividing j=(ℓ−1)/ord_ℓ(2) with s not dividing 6E. For every N with gcd(N,6E)=1, the full factor ℓ^f is omitted from D_E exactly when some s in S_ℓ divides N. Empty S_ℓ means that ℓ^f is always retained. This description has no upper bound on N.
    The Frobenius tables include all s occurring in the N evaluations and every s in every S_ℓ, including those above the N range.
    An ordinary odd prime divisor ℓ of q−1 means v_ℓ(2^ord_ℓ(2)−1)=1. Such a prime cannot divide N in a solution. The column records this test separately.
    The indices d in each factor table distinguish the primitive exponent t=ord_ℓ(2) from other cyclotomic values Φ_d(2) containing ℓ. The q factor itself is removed completely; its primitive exponent is r.
    Factorization products and the primality of every factor are checked. Above 2^64, a GAP primality proof is required.
    
    ## Frobenius and the selected factors
    
    For ℓ not dividing m, arithmetic Frobenius in Q(ζ_m) sends ζ_m to ζ_m^ℓ; its order is ord_m(ℓ), the residue degree. See [Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, cyclotomic extensions and Frobenius](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT.pdf).
    For t=ord_ℓ(2), ℓ=1 modulo t, so Frobenius in Q(ζ_t) is the identity. To form D_E, use Q(ζ_s) for each prime s dividing N. Since gcd(E,N)=1 and t divides E, gcd((ℓ−1)/t,N)=gcd(ℓ−1,N).
    Thus ℓ^f belongs to D_E precisely when Frobenius is nonidentity in every Q(ζ_s) with s dividing N and s≠ℓ. At s=ℓ the prime is ramified; it imposes no exclusion from D_E, since ℓ does not divide ℓ−1. The table retains the full ℓ^f, and checks D_E divides ((q−1)/2^c)N.
    For ℓ≠s, Φ_s over F_ℓ has (s−1)/f distinct irreducible factors of degree f=ord_s(ℓ); these correspond to the prime ideals above ℓ. At ℓ=s, Φ_s=(X−1)^(s−1) over F_s. The displayed decomposition data can therefore be checked by finite-field factorization.
    The order in Q(ζ_N) alone is insufficient to select D_E: the restrictions to each Q(ζ_s) matter. This is the exact role of the additional cyclotomic moduli here.
    
    ## Reproduction
    
    ```sh
    ~/fluid/sauce/gap/gap -A -q -b mersenne_tables.g
    ```
    
    To change the bounds, in GAP:
    
    ```gap
    PPConfig := rec(qMax := 10^8, nMax := 121, factorE := 256,
                    output := "mersenne-tables.md");;
    Read("mersenne_tables.g");
    ```
    
    `mersenne_tables_test.g` checks the arithmetic and table helpers on independent small fixtures; those fixtures are not included as candidates.

## User

Wait, so was the frobenius relevant? You didn't comment on that at all.

## Assistant

Yes—Frobenius describes **which factors enter D_E**.

For a prime s dividing N and ℓ ≠ s:

- Frobenius at ℓ in Q(ζ_s) is the identity exactly when ℓ ≡ 1 modulo s.
- That identity excludes ℓ^f from D_E.
- Thus ℓ^f enters D_E when Frobenius is nonidentity for every such s. The ramified case s = ℓ does not exclude it.

A concrete row: ℓ = 38737 has ord_ℓ(2) = 72 and

```text
(ℓ − 1)/72 = 538 = 2·269.
```

With gcd(N,6E) = 1 and E = 72, this factor enters D_E exactly when **269 does not divide N**. The relevant field is Q(ζ_269): Frobenius at 38737 is the identity there.

So the tables identify the cyclotomic fields governing each factor’s inclusion, for arbitrary N. That gives a precise structure to investigate. What I have not established is a theorem controlling these Frobenius conditions collectively across the factors of 2^E − 1—that would be the substantive next step.

    # Compute v_prime(base^exponent - 1) without constructing base^exponent.
    PPPowerValuation := function(base, exponent, prime)
        local valuation, modulus;
        valuation := 0;
        modulus := prime;
        while PowerModInt(base, exponent, modulus) = 1 do
            valuation := valuation + 1;
            modulus := modulus * prime;
        od;

        if not IsPrimeInt(n) then return false; fi;
        if n < 2^64 then return true; fi;
        proof := PrimalityProof(n);
        if proof = fail or proof = false then
            Error("primality not certified for ", n);
        fi;
        return PrimalityProof_Verify(n, proof);

        if n = 1 then return []; fi;
        factors := FactorsInt(n);

            Error("factorization not certified");
        fi;
        return Collected(factors);

    \subsection{A finite target when q is bounded in terms of d}
    % Added from the question about whether large common divisors are prohibitive.
    \begin{lemma}
    If a prime $d\mid\gcd(M,N)$ satisfies $q\le d^2$, then $d<10^5$.
    \end{lemma}
    \begin{proof}
    Suppose $d\ge10^5$, and put $t=\log d$, $\lambda=\log q\le2t$.
    Write $H_\lambda(x)=\max\{\log(3x/\lambda)+0.38,10\}$.
    The function
    \[
    \frac{x\log2/2-\log(27/26)}{H_\lambda(x)^2}
    \]
    is increasing for the positive $x$ used below. Also
    $\lambda H_\lambda(x)$ is increasing in $\lambda$.
    These allow the lower bounds on $M$ to be substituted into
    \eqref{eq:baker-M}.
    
    We have $dE\mid M$, so
    $M\ge2d\log_2(q^2-1)>3d\lambda/\log2$.
    At $x=3d\lambda/\log2$, $H_\lambda(x)<t+3$.
    Consequently \eqref{eq:baker-M} implies
    \[
    d<34t(t+3)^2.
    \]
    At $d=10^5$ the right side is less than $83000$; moreover
    $d/[\log d(\log d+3)^2]$ increases thereafter, a contradiction.
    \end{proof}
    Thus $d\ge10^5$ requires $q>d^2$. More generally, imposing
    $q\le d^K$ for any fixed $K>0$ gives an effective finite bound
    on $d$ by the same argument: the necessary bound has the form
    $d=O_K((\log d)^3)$.
    This is a finite target for a specified family, not an absolute bound
    on common divisors when $q$ is unrestricted.
    
    \section{Factorization results and their use here}
    \label{sec:factor-results}
    % Original notes Sections 8.2, 8.4, 9.5--9.6 restored; new consequences marked.
    For $u=(q-1)/2^{m_2}$, the original factorization $A=u\Psi$ gives
    \[
    \operatorname{lcm}\left(\operatorname{ord}_q(2),
     \{\operatorname{ord}_\ell(2):\ell\mid u\text{ prime}\}\right)\mid M.
    \]
    Also $M/r<2N$ for $r=\operatorname{ord}_q(2)$, since
    $2^{M/2}<q^N<2^{rN}$.
    Zsigmondy's theorem applied to $q^N-1$, with odd $N\geq3$, has no
    exception. It supplies a prime $\ell_0\mid\Psi$ such that
    \[
    \operatorname{ord}_{\ell_0}(q)=N,\qquad
    \ell_0\equiv1\pmod{2N},\qquad\operatorname{ord}_{\ell_0}(2)\mid M.
    \]
    Conversely, a primitive Mersenne factor at $M\neq6$ has order $M$
    and lies among the primes dividing $q(q^N-1)$. Thus fixing $(q,N)$
    restricts $M$ to the orders at base $2$ of those primes, with $6$
    as the primitive-divisor exception.
    
    \subsection{Gcd identities and primitive-factor counts}
    Cambraia et al.\ \cite[\S2, Proposition 9]{Cambraia} collect the
    same-base gcd and valuation facts used here. In particular,
    \[
    \gcd(2^a-1,2^b-1)=2^{\gcd(a,b)}-1,
    \]
    \[
    \gcd\left(2^a-1,\frac{2^{ab}-1}{2^a-1}\right)=\gcd(2^a-1,b).
    \]
    The second follows by reducing the geometric sum modulo $2^a-1$.
    Their Proposition 2 uses coprime exponents and a primitive factor at
    the product exponent to force an additional prime.
    
    Write $\omega(n)$ for the number of distinct prime factors and
    $\tau(n)$ for the number of positive divisors. The primitive-factor
    argument in Kova\v{c}--Luca \cite[\S3]{KL} gives, more precisely,
    \[
    \omega(2^M-1)\geq\tau(M)-1-\mathbf1_{6\mid M},\qquad
    \omega(A)\geq\tau(M)-2-\mathbf1_{6\mid M}.
    \]
    Choose a primitive prime at every divisor of $M$ except $1,6$;
    different orders give different primes. Removing $q$ loses one prime.
    
    \begin{lemma}
    For the remaining case $A>1$, $q>3$,
    \[
    \omega(2^M-1)\geq4,\qquad\omega(A)\geq3.
    \]
    \end{lemma}
    \begin{proof}
    Suppose $\omega(2^M-1)\leq3$. The preceding count, with $M$ even,
    leaves $M=2,4,6,8$ or $M=2s$ for an odd prime $s$.
    The size bound excludes $2,4$; $2^6-1=3^2\cdot7$ and
    $2^8-1=3\cdot5\cdot17$ exclude $6,8$ since $q>3$ and $n_1\geq2$.
    For $s\geq5$, the three primes are $3$, a primitive factor at $s$,
    and a primitive factor at $2s$. Hence
    \[
    2^s-1=P^f,\qquad2^s+1=3Q^e
    \]
    for distinct primes $P,Q$, using $v_3(2^s+1)=1$.
    A Mersenne number $2^s-1$ is not a nontrivial perfect power:
    an even exponent is excluded modulo $4$, and an odd exponent greater
    than $1$ makes $P^f+1$ have an odd factor greater than $1$.
    Thus $f=1$, so $q=Q$ and $e=n_1$ is even.
    But $2^s+1=3Q^e$ is then impossible modulo $8$.
    \end{proof}
    % This consequence is derived here; the low-factor classification also
    % appears in Cambraia et al., Theorems 14--15.
    
    \subsection{Transferring factors into C}
    For a prime $s\mid\gcd(M,N)$, put $a=M/s$, $b=N/s$,
    $Y=2^a q^b$ and $C=A/(Y-1)$. Then
    \[
    Cp=\Phi_s(Y),\qquad C<\frac{Y^{s/2}}{2q(Y-1)},\qquad
    \gcd(C,Y-1)\mid s.
    \]
    For any divisor $D\mid A$,
    \[
    \frac{D}{\gcd(D,Y-1)}\mid C.
    \]
    Taking $D=(2^a-1)/q^{v_q(2^a-1)}$ gives
    \[
    \boxed{\frac{D}{\gcd(D,q^b-1)}\mid C,}
    \]
    since $Y-1\equiv q^b-1\pmod D$.
    Thus a useful lower bound on $C$ requires control of a mixed-base gcd.
    For $\ell\mid C$, $\ell\neq s$, we have $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(Y)=s$;
    therefore, with $r_\ell=\operatorname{ord}_\ell(2)$ and
    $t_\ell=\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)$,
    \[
    v_s(r_\ell)=v_s(M)\quad\text{or}\quad v_s(t_\ell)=v_s(N).
    \]
    If both valuations were smaller, both factors of $Y$ would be $1$
    modulo $\ell$. The converse need not hold because of cancellation.
    
    \subsection{Primitive factors on the two sides}
    % Added from the discussion of Zsigmondy's theorem and the full odd-part equality.
    Let $d\ge5$ be a prime dividing both gaps, $U=2^{M/d}$,
    $V=q^{N/d}$, $B=UV-1$, and $C=A/B$. The full equality is
    \[
    2^M-1=q^{n_1}\operatorname{odd}(q^N-1),\qquad
    \operatorname{odd}(q^N-1)=A.
    \]
    Thus every prime power in $2^M-1$ outside the base $q$ occurs
    with exactly the same valuation in $q^N-1$.
    
    Zsigmondy's theorem \cite[Theorem 13]{GyorySmyth} supplies a prime
    of order $M$ at base $2$ and a prime of order $N$ at base $q$.
    Here $M\ge10$ and $N\ge5$ is odd, so there are no exceptions.
    The former prime belongs to $A$ unless it is $q$ itself; the latter
    always belongs to $A$. Such primes satisfy respectively
    $\ell\equiv1\pmod M$ and $\ell\equiv1\pmod{2N}$.
    If the same prime has both full orders, then
    $\ell\equiv1\pmod{\operatorname{lcm}(M,N)}$.
    
    For $\ell\mid A$, $\ell\ne d$, put
    $\alpha=\operatorname{ord}_\ell(U)$ and
    $\beta=\operatorname{ord}_\ell(V)$. Both lie in $\{1,d\}$.
    The factor allocation is
    \[
    \begin{array}{c|c|c}
    \alpha&\beta&\text{location of the full }\ell\text{-part of }A\\\hline
    1&1&B\\
    1&d&C\\
    d&1&C\\
    d&d&B\text{ if }UV\equiv1\pmod\ell;\ C\text{ otherwise}.
    \end{array}
    \]
    Indeed $Cp=\Phi_d(UV)$ and $\gcd(B,C)\mid d$.
    In the last row, $U,V$ lie in the same subgroup of order $d$;
    their product can be $1$. Primitivity at two different bases does
    not exclude this cancellation.
    
    \begin{lemma}
    Put $G=\gcd(U-1,V-1)$. Then $B=GH$ with
    \[
    \gcd(G,H)=1,\qquad H>U,
    \]
    and every prime $\ell\mid H$ satisfies
    $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(U)=\operatorname{ord}_\ell(V)=d$.
    \end{lemma}
    \begin{proof}
    For $\ell\mid B$, the residues $U,V$ are inverse, so their orders
    are equal. If this order is $1$ and $\ell\ne d$, lifting and the
    full gap equations give
    \[
    v_\ell(B)=v_\ell(A)=v_\ell(U-1)=v_\ell(V-1).
    \]
    If $d\mid B$, then $U\equiv V\equiv1\pmod d$ and
    $v_d(\Phi_d(UV))=1$. Since $p>d$, $v_d(C)=1$.
    Lifting again gives
    $v_d(B)=v_d(U-1)=v_d(V-1)$.
    Thus the entire part of $B$ whose primes have order $1$ is exactly
    $G$, with no such primes left in $H$. Finally $G\le V-1$ gives
    $H\ge(UV-1)/(V-1)>U$.
    \end{proof}
    
    For a primitive Mersenne factor $\ell\ne q$ at exponent $M$,
    $\alpha=d$. Writing $t=\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)$, if
    $v_d(t)<v_d(N)$ then $\beta=1$, so the full $\ell$-part of $A$
    is forced into $C$. Symmetrically, a primitive factor at exponent
    $N$ for base $q$ is forced into $C$ if
    $v_d(\operatorname{ord}_\ell(2))<v_d(M)$.
    Products of distinct forced prime powers must fit below
    \[
    C<\frac{(UV)^{d/2}}{2^{m_2/2}q^{n_1/2}(UV-1)}.
    \]
    The remaining target is to force enough such factors into $C$, or
    to bound the simultaneous primitive part $H$ below its required
    size. Zsigmondy's existence assertion alone does neither.
    
    \subsection{Reading and limits of the cited results}
    Pomerance \cite[\S2]{PomCycl} supplies the primitive/intrinsic
    cyclotomic decomposition, bounds for $\Phi_d(2)$, and the Aurifeuilian
    splitting for $d\equiv4\pmod8$. These concern individual factors.
    Cambraia et al.\ \cite[\S\S2--4]{Cambraia} give the gcd identities,
    valuation formula, and classification when $\omega(2^M-1)\leq3$;
    the preceding lemma specializes that classification to our equations.
    Their final section studies a different sum of Mersenne numbers.
    
    Kova\v{c}--Luca \cite{KL} study sums of divisor counts over exponents;
    their pointwise primitive-factor bound is what we use above.
    Erd\H{o}s--Kiss--Pomerance \cite{EKP} study reciprocal sums of prime
    divisors, including averages and consecutive exponents. Neither result
    currently controls the particular mixed-base gcd needed for $C$.
    Pomerance's earlier paper \cite{PomPrim} treats reciprocal sums over
    divisors of prescribed order.
    
    For the proposed descent, compare Bilu \cite[\S2, Proposition 2.1 and
    Corollary 2.2]{Bilu}: coprimality and a perfect-power product force powers
    of ideals. The identity $\Phi_s(Y)=Cp$ does not provide that
    perfect-power hypothesis. A transfer of the argument would need to
    supply it.
    
    \subsection{Cyclotomic structure and further reading}

    # Exact certificates excluding all N with gcd(N,E)=1 for a fixed q.
    # Run: ~/fluid/sauce/gap/gap -A -q -b --quitonbreak check_order_obstruction.g
    # This wider experiment does NOT impose the remaining-case conditions on q.
    PPLibraryOnly := true;;
    Read("mersenne_tables.g");
    
    PPOrderWitness := function(q,r,factors)
        local pair,ell,f,modulus,phi,s,v,w,residue;
        for pair in factors do
            ell := pair[1]; f := pair[2];
            if ell=q then continue; fi;
            modulus := ell^f;
            phi := (ell-1)*ell^(f-1);
            for s in Set(FactorsInt(r)) do
                v := PPValuation(phi,s);
                if v=0 then continue; fi;
                w := QuoInt(phi,s^v);
                residue := PowerModInt(q,w,modulus);
                if residue<>1 then
                    return rec(ell:=ell,f:=f,s:=s,w:=w,residue:=residue);
                fi;
            od;
        od;
        return fail;
    end;
    
    PPOrderExperiment := function(limit,output)
        local stream,E,factors,pair,q,r,rho,witness,count,excluded,missing,evenRho;
        stream := OutputTextFile(output,false);
        SetPrintFormattingStatus(stream,false);
        PPLine(stream,"# An order obstruction for all N\n");
        PPLine(stream,"Put r=ord_q(2), E=lcm(2,r), rho=v_q(2^r−1), a=(2^E−1)/q^rho. In the remaining case, a divides A, ord_a(q) divides N, and gcd(E,N)=1.");
        PPLine(stream,"\n## Proven certificate\n");
        PPLine(stream,"Let ℓ^f divide a, let s be a prime divisor of r, and write φ(ℓ^f)=s^v w with s not dividing w. If q^w is not 1 modulo ℓ^f, then s divides ord_(ℓ^f)(q). Consequently s divides both E and N, a contradiction. This excludes every N for that q.");
        PPLine(stream,"Proof: ord_(ℓ^f)(q) divides s^v w. If its order were coprime to s, it would divide w, contrary to the displayed residue.");
        PPLine(stream,"\n## Research question\n");
        PPLine(stream,"Can the factorization of 2^E−1 force such a certificate? Equivalently, can one prove gcd(r,ord_a(q))>1, either uniformly under our remaining assumptions or outside an effectively bounded set? This is not proved here.");
        PPLine(stream,"The experiment below first tests the stronger question for every odd prime q with E in the stated range, without imposing the q residue conditions or even rho. It distinguishes evidence for that wider question from the repeated-factor case required by the notes.");
        PPLine(stream,"\n## Kummer formulation\n");
        PPLine(stream,"For a prime-level certificate, let s divide r and ℓ−1, v=v_s(ℓ−1), w=(ℓ−1)/s^v, K=Q(ζ_(s^v)), and F=K(q^(1/s^v)). A prime P of K above ℓ has residue field F_ℓ. For α=q^(1/s^v), arithmetic Frobenius satisfies Frob_P(α)/α = q^w modulo a prime of F above P. Hence q^w≠1 detects nontrivial Frobenius in F/K and forces s to divide ord_ℓ(q). See [Stevenhagen, Kummer Theory and Reciprocity Laws](https://websites.math.leidenuniv.nl/algebra/Stevenhagen-Kummer.pdf), Sections 2 and 4.");
        PPLine(stream,"The task is to force this nontrivial Frobenius at a prime dividing the specific integer a. If the witness only appears modulo ℓ^f with f>1 and s=ℓ, use the prime-power order test above; the prime-level Kummer formulation does not cover that case.");
        PPLine(stream,"\n## Exact finite experiment\n");
        PPLine(stream,Concatenation("Enumerate every even E with 2 ≤ E ≤ ",String(limit),
            ", factor 2^E−1, and retain precisely the prime factors q with lcm(2,ord_q(2))=E. Each q therefore occurs once. Products and primality of all factors are certified. The residue column is an exact modular-power certificate; no bound on N or p is used.\n"));
        PPRow(stream,["q","r","E","rho","ℓ","f","s dividing r","w","q^w mod ℓ^f"]);
        PPRow(stream,List([1..9],x -> "---"));
        count:=0; excluded:=0; missing:=[]; evenRho:=0;
        for E in [2,4..limit] do
            factors := PPFactorization(2^E-1);
            for pair in factors do
                q:=pair[1]; rho:=pair[2]; r:=OrderMod(2,q);
                if Lcm(2,r)<>E then continue; fi;
                count:=count+1;
                if rho mod 2=0 then evenRho:=evenRho+1; fi;
                witness:=PPOrderWitness(q,r,factors);
                if witness=fail then
                    Add(missing,[q,r,E,rho,QuoInt(2^E-1,q^rho)]);
                else
                    excluded:=excluded+1;
                    PPRow(stream,[q,r,E,rho,witness.ell,witness.f,witness.s,witness.w,witness.residue]);
                fi;
            od;
        od;
        PPLine(stream,"\n## Results\n");
        PPLine(stream,Concatenation(String(count)," prime choices; ",String(excluded),
            " certified order obstructions. Cases without a certificate, as [q,r,E,rho,a]: ",String(missing),"."));
        PPLine(stream,Concatenation("Number with even rho: ",String(evenRho),". The experiment does not establish the proposed uniform statement."));
        PPLine(stream,"\nReproduce with:\n\n```sh\n~/fluid/sauce/gap/gap -A -q -b --quitonbreak check_order_obstruction.g\n```\n");
        CloseStream(stream);
        Print(count," choices; ",excluded," witnesses; missing = ",missing,
            "; even rho = ",evenRho,"\n");
    end;
    
    PPOrderExperiment(256,"order-obstructions.md");

## Assistant

There is a concrete target:

```text
a = (2^E − 1)/q^rho,   E = lcm(2,r).

Prove gcd(r, ord_a(q)) > 1.
```

Since ord_a(q) divides N and gcd(E,N) = 1, that would exclude **every N**, with no bound on M or p.

I checked every prime q with E ≤ 256: 396 choices. All 395 cases other than q = 3, a = 1 have an explicit modular-power certificate for that obstruction. All have rho = 1, so this is evidence about the broader structure, not verification of our remaining repeated-factor case. The [calculation and research question](/home/erpage159/fluid/research/math/nt/prime-power-sum-pf/order-obstructions.md) are saved.

The next abstract approach has a specific job: **power-residue reciprocity could force a factor ℓ of a where q has order divisible by a prime s dividing r.** Kummer theory expresses that as nontrivial Frobenius in an extension obtained by adjoining an s-power root of q. [Stevenhagen’s notes](https://websites.math.leidenuniv.nl/algebra/Stevenhagen-Kummer.pdf) give that formulation.

That is where I would pursue the cohomological direction first: the Kummer class of q and its local evaluations at factors of a. The missing argument is what forces one of those evaluations to be nontrivial.

**Kummer theory has a concrete reason to enter:** the obstruction we want is that q is not an sᵛ-th power modulo some prime ℓ dividing a, where s divides r and sᵛ is the full s-part of ℓ−1. Frobenius in the corresponding Kummer extension describes exactly that condition. So the connection is substantive.

But describing the obstruction does not prove that one of the prime divisors of a must exhibit it. **That existence argument is the real task.** Power-residue reciprocity is worth investigating because it could relate these local conditions across the factors of a. Calling the same conditions cohomology does not itself advance that argument.

My preference now is to examine the cyclotomic factors of a and their power-residue symbols, looking for a product relation that forces one symbol to be nontrivial. That would give a specific reason to use reciprocity. I don’t yet see a comparably specific role for ℓ-adic cohomology.

    # An order obstruction for all N
    
    Put r=ord_q(2), E=lcm(2,r), rho=v_q(2^r−1), a=(2^E−1)/q^rho. In the remaining case, a divides A, ord_a(q) divides N, and gcd(E,N)=1.
    
    ## Proven certificate
    
    Let ℓ^f divide a, let s be a prime divisor of r, and write φ(ℓ^f)=s^v w with s not dividing w. If q^w is not 1 modulo ℓ^f, then s divides ord_(ℓ^f)(q). Consequently s divides both E and N, a contradiction. This excludes every N for that q.
    Proof: ord_(ℓ^f)(q) divides s^v w. If its order were coprime to s, it would divide w, contrary to the displayed residue.
    
    ## Research question
    
    Can the factorization of 2^E−1 force such a certificate? Equivalently, can one prove gcd(r,ord_a(q))>1, either uniformly under our remaining assumptions or outside an effectively bounded set? This is not proved here.
    The experiment below first tests the stronger question for every odd prime q with E in the stated range, without imposing the q residue conditions or even rho. It distinguishes evidence for that wider question from the repeated-factor case required by the notes.
    
    ## Kummer formulation

## Assistant

Yes—this gives a concrete model for the reciprocity calculation we were discussing.

Sharifi’s useful construction is to **take a relative norm of a cyclotomic expression, then evaluate its power-residue symbol using reciprocity and local norm-residue symbols**. Section 4 does this using conductors; Section 8 gives another proof using identities between the symbols. His stated theorems concern *prime cyclotomic values*, so they don’t directly apply to arbitrary prime divisors of our Mersenne numbers. [Sharifi, §§4, 8](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/publ/cycl.pdf)

For our problem, a corresponding construction would be:

```text
Choose t | E and a prime power sᵇ | t.

L = Q(ζ_t),   K = Q(ζ_(sᵇ)),
π = Norm_{L/K}(2 − ζ_t).

Then Norm_{K/Q}(π) = Φ_t(2).
```

This retains information about the factors of Φ_t(2) **as prime ideals in K**. We would separate the factors above q and the ramified primes, then examine the sᵇ-th power-residue symbol of q against the remaining ideal factors.

At a prime ideal P above an ordinary primitive Mersenne factor ℓ of exponent t, the residue field is F_ℓ. Thus:

```text
(q/P)_(sᵇ) ≠ 1
    ⇒ q^((ℓ−1)/sᵇ) ≠ 1 modulo ℓ
    ⇒ s | ord_ℓ(q).
```

Since s divides E, that would supply the incompatibility with N we want.

**The next calculation is whether reciprocity forces the product of those remaining symbols to be nontrivial.** Sharifi gives an explicit method for evaluating such products. We still have to carry out that calculation for `2 − ζ_t`, including the contribution removed above q.

One particularly relevant detail: his proof of Theorem 2 uses Galois invariance to show that certain symbols equal 1. That makes tracking the relative norms and individual ideal factors consequential: multiplying all conjugates can erase the information we seek. [§5](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/publ/cycl.pdf)

    PPOrderFromMultiple := function(base,prime,multiple)
        local order,s;
        order:=multiple;
        if PowerModInt(base,order,prime)<>1 then Error("not an order multiple"); fi;
        for s in Set(FactorsInt(multiple)) do
            while order mod s=0 and PowerModInt(base,QuoInt(order,s),prime)=1 do
                order:=QuoInt(order,s);
            od;
        od;
        return order;
    end;
    
    PPOrderWitness := function(q,r,factors)
        local pair,ell,f,modulus,phi,s,v,w,residue;
        for pair in factors do
            ell := pair[1]; f := pair[2];
            if ell=q then continue; fi;
            modulus := ell^f;
            phi := (ell-1)*ell^(f-1);
            for s in Set(FactorsInt(r)) do
                v := PPValuation(phi,s);
                if v=0 then continue; fi;
                w := QuoInt(phi,s^v);
                residue := PowerModInt(q,w,modulus);
                if residue<>1 then
                    return rec(ell:=ell,f:=f,s:=s,w:=w,residue:=residue);
                fi;
            od;
        od;
        return fail;
    end;

    # To change the bounds without editing the script, define PPConfig before Read.
    # Setting PPLibraryOnly := true loads the functions without running the report.
    
    PPValuation := function(n, prime)
        local exponent;
        if n <= 0 then Error("valuation requires a positive integer"); fi;
        exponent := 0;
        while n mod prime = 0 do
            n := QuoInt(n, prime);
            exponent := exponent + 1;
        od;
        return exponent;
    end;
    
    # Compute v_prime(base^exponent - 1) without constructing base^exponent.
    PPPowerValuation := function(base, exponent, prime)
        local valuation, modulus;
        valuation := 0;
        modulus := prime;
        while PowerModInt(base, exponent, modulus) = 1 do
            valuation := valuation + 1;
            modulus := modulus * prime;
        od;
        return valuation;
    end;
    
    PPProvenPrime := function(n)
        local proof;
        if not IsPrimeInt(n) then return false; fi;
        if n < 2^64 then return true; fi;
        proof := PrimalityProof(n);
        if proof = fail or proof = false then
            Error("primality not certified for ", n);
        fi;
        return PrimalityProof_Verify(n, proof);
    end;
    
    PPFactorization := function(n)
        local factors;
        if n = 1 then return []; fi;
        factors := FactorsInt(n);
        if Product(factors) <> n or not ForAll(Set(factors), PPProvenPrime) then
            Error("factorization not certified");
        fi;
        return Collected(factors);
    end;
    
    PPFactorText := function(factors)
        if IsEmpty(factors) then return "1"; fi;
        return JoinStringsWithSeparator(List(factors,function(pair)
            if pair[2]=1 then return String(pair[1]); fi;
            return Concatenation(String(pair[1]),"^",String(pair[2]));
        end)," * ");
    end;
    
    # Primes ell | q-1 for which the valuation identity in the notes applies.
    PPOrdinaryDivisors := function(q)
        return Filtered(Set(FactorsInt(q-1)), ell -> ell <> 2 and
            PPPowerValuation(2, OrderMod(2, ell), ell) = 1);
    end;
    
    PPBaseData := function(q)
        local r;
        r := OrderMod(2, q);
        return rec(q := q, c := PPValuation(q-1, 2), r := r,
            E := Lcm(2, r), e := PPPowerValuation(2, r, q),
            ordinary := PPOrdinaryDivisors(q));
    end;
    
    # These restrictions depend on q alone, since E divides M.
    PPBaseCompatible := function(b)
        local condition, Q, ceiling;
        if b.e < 2 or b.e mod 2 <> 0 then return false; fi;
        if not ForAll(b.ordinary, ell -> QuoInt(b.q-1, ell) mod b.r = 0) then
            return false;
        fi;
        for condition in [[3,7], [4,5], [8,17], [12,13], [16,257], [18,19]] do
            if b.E mod condition[1] = 0 and b.q mod condition[2] <> 1 then
                return false;
            fi;
        od;
        if b.E mod 4 = 0 and b.c mod 4 <> 0 then return false; fi;
        if b.q mod 5 <> 1 and (b.c+b.e) mod 4 <> 2 then return false; fi;
        Q := b.q^b.e;
        ceiling := LogInt(Q-1, 2);
        if 2^ceiling < Q-1 then ceiling := ceiling+1; fi;
        return 2*ceiling <= b.E and 2*b.c <= b.E;
    end;
    
    PPScan := function(limit)

    \section{The smaller-term ratio and common divisors}
    \label{sec:additional-returns}
    % New deductions following the user's minimum-return and common-gap split.
    Throughout this section $q\nmid M$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:q-not-M}.
    Put $e=n_1=\rho$, $c=m_2$, $Q=q^e$, and
    \[
    E=\operatorname{lcm}(2,r),\qquad M=hE.
    \]
    Then $Q\mid2^r-1$, and lifting gives
    \[
    A=\frac{2^r-1}{Q}\,\frac{2^M-1}{2^r-1},\qquad
    \gcd\left(q,\frac{2^M-1}{2^r-1}\right)=1.
    \]
    In the cyclotomic factorization of $2^M-1$, only $\Phi_r(2)$ contains
    $q$. Every other factor $\Phi_j(2)$, $j\mid M$, enters $A$ intact.
    
    \subsection{Congruences on p}
    \label{sec:p-common-gap}
    Let $g=\gcd(M,N)>1$. Section~\ref{sec:full-gcd} gives
    $p\equiv1\pmod g$. If a prime $d\mid g$ also divided $q-1$,
    then $p=2^{m_2}+q^{n_2}$ would give
    $1\equiv2^{m_2}+1\pmod d$, impossible. Thus
    \[
    \gcd(g,q-1)=1.
    \]
    Also $p=2^{m_1}+q^{n_1}$ is a sum of two nonzero squares modulo $5$.
    Since $p>5$ and $q\ne5$, $p\equiv2$ or $3\pmod5$.
    Consequently $5\nmid g$. Together with the previous exclusions,
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:common-gap-coprimality}
    \boxed{\gcd(g,30q(q-1))=1,\qquad \gcd(g,E)=1,\qquad gE\mid M.}
    \end{equation}
    Every prime factor of $g$ is at least $7$.
    The case in which a common prime has its full multiplicity already
    in $r$ is therefore excluded: such a prime would divide $q-1$.
    
    More generally, let $\ell$ be an odd prime dividing $q-1$, and put
    $\eta_\ell=v_\ell(2^{\operatorname{ord}_\ell(2)}-1)$.
    If $\eta_\ell=1$, the valuation identity and
    $\gcd(g,q-1)=1$ imply
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:ordinary-q-minus-one}
    \boxed{\ell\nmid N,\qquad v_\ell(M)=v_\ell(q-1)-1.}
    \end{equation}
    Indeed, $\ell\mid N$ would make
    $v_\ell(M)=v_\ell(q-1)+v_\ell(N)-1\ge1$, contradicting
    $\gcd(g,q-1)=1$. The same conclusion holds when $g=1$.
    Since $r\mid M$, we obtain the stronger condition on $q$
    \[
    r\mid(q-1)/\ell,\qquad
    2^{(q-1)/\ell}\equiv1\pmod{q^2}.
    \]
    This applies to $\ell=3,5,7,11,13$ whenever $\ell\mid q-1$.
    
    \subsection{The ratio before taking d-th powers}
    For any common divisor $d>1$, write $M=ad$, $N=bd$ and
    $U=2^a$, $V=q^b$. Keep the smaller terms in the equality:
    \[
    p=2^{m_2}U^d+q^{n_1}=2^{m_2}+q^{n_1}V^d,
    \qquad
    R:=\frac{q^{n_1}}{2^{m_2}}=\frac{U^d-1}{V^d-1}.
    \]
    Thus $1<U/V<R^{1/d}$. More precisely, with
    \[
    q^{N+e}>2^{c+hr}
     >2^c(q^{e/2}-1)^{8h}>q^{4he}.
    \]
    For $h\le32$, use $q\ge97$, $e\ge2$, $c\ge4$:
    $8h/(q^{e/2}-1)\le8/3<4\log2$.
    For $N=49$ we have $h=7$, $e=2$, which would require $54<49$.
    \end{proof}
    This uses the Aurifeuillean identity before factoring its integer
    values. Its relation to grouping roots of unity is developed in
    Brent \cite[\S\S2--3]{Brent}.
    
    For a fixed prime $d\mid g$, retain the even values $e=n_1$ and
    multiples $h$ of $d$ satisfying $(2h-1)e<N$.
    For each, reduce
    \[
    2^{m_1}=1-q^e,\qquad 2^{m_2}=1-q^{N+e}\pmod d
    \]
    with $m_1,m_2,E$ even, $m_1-m_2=hE$, and the modulo-$5$ split.
    This is a finite residue calculation; no upper bound on $q$ is used.

    These are the survivors of this residue test, not asserted solutions.
    For $N=5d$, the same test proves coprimality for

    Here $g>1$ would force $g=d$, $e=2$, $h=d$.

    An algebraic version of this last test uses $t=\operatorname{ord}_d(16)$.
    Compute over $\mathbb F_d$ the gcd of
    \[
    X^{d-1}-1,\qquad (1-X^2)^t-4^t,\qquad (1-X^7)^t-1.
    \]
    If it is $1$, the family $N=5d$ is excluded. The exponent $7$ comes
    from $N+2=5d+2\equiv7\pmod{d-1}$.
    More generally use the two cosets $\langle16\rangle$ and
    $4\langle16\rangle$, retaining the permitted classes of $m_1,m_2$
    modulo $4$. A general extension would need to show that all the
    residue sets surviving the height bound are empty, possibly after
    combining further moduli. No such uniform assertion is proved here.
    
    \subsection{Forcing a common factor}
    \label{sec:forcing-common-factor}
    Let $\ell=jM+1>q$ be a primitive Mersenne factor at exponent $M$.
    If $\gcd(j,N)=1$, then
    \[
    1<\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)\mid\gcd(M,N).
    \]
    Indeed, $\ell\mid A$ gives $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)\mid N$,
    while the order also divides $\ell-1=jM$. Coprimality with $j$
    forces it to divide $M$, and $1<q<\ell$ excludes order $1$.
    Thus such a factor contradicts $N<49$. A multiplier $j$ supported
    on $2,3$ automatically passes the coprimality test; if $4\mid M$,
    then $5\nmid N$, so factors of $5$ in $j$ are allowed as well.
    The missing general step is to force a primitive factor with this
    multiplier condition and $\ell>q$. Zsigmondy's theorem alone does
    not supply either condition.
    
    The condition $\ell>q$ may be weakened to $\ell\nmid q-1$.
    There is also a product version. Put $u=(q-1)/2^{m_2}$ and
    \[
    D=\prod_{\substack{\ell\mid A,\ \operatorname{ord}_\ell(2)=M\\
                        \gcd((\ell-1)/M,N)=1}}
           \ell^{v_\ell(A)}.
    \]
    If $g=1$, every prime in this product divides $q-1$.
    Moreover $\ell>M>N$, so lifting gives
    $v_\ell(A)=v_\ell(q-1)$, and therefore
    \[
    \boxed{g=1\ \Longrightarrow\ D\mid u.}
    \]
    Thus $D\nmid u$, in particular $D>u$, forces $g>1$.
    This allows several smaller primitive factors to replace one factor
    larger than $q$. The prime $q$ is excluded from the product even when
    $\operatorname{ord}_q(2)=M$.
    
    The same test also applies inside the common-divisor branch.
    Since $\gcd(E,N)=1$, form $D_E$ from the full prime-power factors
    of $(2^E-1)/q^{n_1}$ satisfying
    \[
    \gcd\left(\frac{\ell-1}{\operatorname{ord}_\ell(2)},N\right)=1.
    \]
    Each such $\ell$ divides $q-1$, and lifting gives
    \[
    \boxed{D_E\mid uN.}
    \]
    Thus a lower bound $D_E>uN$ would exclude that family without
    first proving the gaps coprime. In the surviving $N=49$ case,
    $3\nmid E$, so $7\nmid2^E-1$. Here $D_E$ is exactly the part
    supported on primes $\ell\not\equiv1\pmod7$, after removing $q^2$,
    and the stronger conclusion is $D_E\mid u$.
    
    For $j=2$, necessarily $4\mid M$: otherwise $\ell=2M+1\equiv5\pmod8$
    and $2^M\equiv-1\pmod\ell$.
