    \\ Relative norms and power-residue symbols; PARI/GP, no optional packages.
    \\ Load with read("cyclotomic_reciprocity.gp").
    \\ Examples: reciprocity_case(1777,37,37), reciprocity_case(1093,364,13).
    
    default(parisizemax, 512000000);
    
    require(condition, message) = if(!condition, error(message));
    
    power_valuation(base, exponent, prime) = {
      my(v = 0);
      while(Mod(base, prime^(v+1))^exponent == 1, v++);
      v;
    };
    
    \\ Norm from Q(zeta_t) to Q(zeta_m), with zeta_m=zeta_t^(t/m).
    \\ Inclusion-exclusion on the exponents coprime to t.
    relative_cyclotomic_norm(t, m) = {
      require(t % m == 0 && m > 1, "m must divide t");
      my(z = Mod(x, polcyclo(m)), h = t/m, result = 1);
      fordiv(h, d,
        if(gcd(d,m) == 1 && moebius(d),
          result *= (2^(h/d) - z^lift(Mod(d,m)^(-1)))^moebius(d)
        )
      );
      result = lift(result);
      require(denominator(result) == 1, "norm must be integral");
      require(polresultant(polcyclo(m),result) == subst(polcyclo(t),x,2),
              "absolute norm mismatch");
      result;
    };
    
    \\ The logarithm is only in the small group of m-th roots of unity.
    root_exponent(value, root, m) = {
      my(power = root^0);
      for(j=0,m-1,
        if(value == power, return(j));
        power *= root
      );
      error("value is not an m-th root of unity");
    };
    
    \\ Product of the tame local symbols (pi,q)_m at all primes above q.
    \\ Rows: [embedding i, v_P(pi), unit modulo q, exponent relative to zeta_m].
    symbols_above_q(q, t, m) = {
      require(isprime(q) && (q-1)%m == 0, "q must split in Q(zeta_m)");
      my(pi = relative_cyclotomic_norm(t,m), r = znorder(Mod(2,q)));
      my(rho = power_valuation(2,r,q), precision = rho+2);
      my(z = znprimroot(q)^((q-1)/m));
      my(zlift = Mod(lift(z),q^precision)^(q^(precision-1)));
      my(rows = List(), total = 0);
      require(zlift^m == 1, "root lift failed");
      for(i=1,m-1, if(gcd(i,m)==1,
        my(value = lift(subst(pi,x,zlift^i)));
        require(value != 0, "insufficient q-adic precision");
        my(v = valuation(value,q), unit = Mod(value/q^v,q));
        my(exponent = root_exponent(((-1)^v*unit)^((q-1)/m),z^i,m));
        listput(rows,[i,v,lift(unit),exponent]);
        total = (total+exponent)%m
      ));
      [pi,Vec(rows),total];
    };
    
    \\ Independent ideal factorization and residue-field computation.
    \\ Omit primes above q and above the prime dividing m.
    \\ Rows: [ell, residue degree, ideal valuation, symbol exponent].
    symbols_away_from_q(q,t,m) = {
      my(pi = relative_cyclotomic_norm(t,m), nf = nfinit(polcyclo(m)));
      my(factors = idealfactor(nf,pi), rows = List(), total = 0);
      for(j=1,matsize(factors)[1],
        my(P=factors[j,1], multiplicity=factors[j,2], ell=P.p);
        if(ell == q || m%ell == 0, next);
        my(reduction = nfmodprinit(nf,P));
        my(z = nfmodpr(nf,x,reduction), Q = ell^P.f);
        my(value = nfmodpr(nf,q,reduction)^((Q-1)/m));
        my(exponent = root_exponent(value,z,m));
        listput(rows,[ell,P.f,multiplicity,exponent]);
        total = (total + multiplicity*exponent)%m
      );
      [Vec(rows),total];
    };
    
    \\ Sufficient condition for the ramified local symbols to vanish.
    \\ At 2, q congruent to 1 mod 2m gives an unramified Kummer extension;
    \\ pi is a 2-adic unit. For m=2, q>0 also handles the real place.
    local_correction_vanishes(q,m) = {
      my(f=factor(m));
      require(matsize(f)[1] == 1, "m must be a prime power");
      my(s=f[1,1], b=f[1,2]);
      if(s==2, return(q%(2*m)==1));
      q%(s*m)==1;
    };
    
    reciprocity_case(q,t,m) = {
      my(atq=symbols_above_q(q,t,m), away=symbols_away_from_q(q,t,m));
      my(vanishes=local_correction_vanishes(q,m));
      if(vanishes, require(atq[3]==away[2], "reciprocity check failed"));
      print("q=",q,", t=",t,", m=",m,", pi=",atq[1]);
      print("above q: ",atq[2]);
      print("away: ",away[1]);
      print("exponents: above q=",atq[3],", away=",away[2],
            "; local correction certified trivial=",vanishes);
      [atq,away,vanishes];
    };

## Assistant

There’s a useful reduction: grouping the relevant cyclotomic factors gives the single expression `2^(r/sᵇ) − ζ_(sᵇ)`. Its norm contains q^ρ.

Reciprocity lets us compute the remaining product of residue symbols using arithmetic modulo q and q^(ρ+1), without factoring that norm. A nontrivial result certifies an obstruction; a trivial product can still conceal nontrivial individual factors.

    +grouped_residue(q,m) = {
    +  my(r=znorder(Mod(2,q)), f=factor(m));

    +  my(s=f[1,1], B=2^(r/m), H=(2^r-1)/(2^(r/s)-1));
    +  my(rho=valuation(H,q), cofactor=H/q^rho, z=Mod(B,q));
    +  my(derivative=subst(deriv(polcyclo(m)),x,z));
    +  my(W=(-1)^rho*Mod(cofactor,q)/derivative);
    +  for(i=2,m-1, if(gcd(i,m)==1,
    +    W *= (z-z^i)^lift(Mod(i,m)^(-1))
    +  ));

    +          "factorization does not equal H");

    +  for(j=1,matsize(factors)[1],

    +    require(isprime(ell), "uncertified prime factor");
    +    if(ell==q || m%ell==0, next);
    +    require((ell-1)%m==0 && znorder(Mod(B,ell))==m, "wrong residue degree");
    +    my(residue=Mod(q,ell)^((ell-1)/m));
    +    my(exponent=root_exponent(residue,Mod(B,ell),m));
    +    listput(rows,[ell,multiplicity,lift(residue),exponent]);
    +    total=(total+multiplicity*exponent)%m
    +  );

    +};

    +};

        ". All three have a nontrivial product. Some permitted m supplies a nontrivial product for ",
        #witnesses," of the 18 q values. All 18 have rho=1.\n\n",
        "For rho=2, q=1093 has T=-1 at m=2. For q=3511, T=756 at m=3 ",

        "independently gives 3511^87552 = 512 modulo 262657. ",
        "Both q values already fail other remaining-case restrictions.\n");
      \\ write() appends; write the complete report through a fresh file handle.
      my(handle=fileopen(output,"w")); filewrite(handle,text); fileclose(handle);
      print("Verified ",direct_checks," factorizations, ",local_checks,
            " reciprocity equalities, q-adic/derivative agreement for ",#rows,
            " cases, and the cancellation and rho=2 examples.");
    };
    
    iferr(run_reciprocity_checks(),err,print(err);quit(1));
    quit(0);

    # Cyclotomic reciprocity calculations
    
    These calculations develop the relative-norm suggestion following [Sharifi, *On cyclotomic polynomials, power residues, and reciprocity laws*](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/publ/cycl.pdf). The reciprocity convention is his equation (5). The deductions below are for our equations; they are not applications of his prime-value theorems.
    
    ## Local conditions supplied by the equations
    
    Retain
    
    ```text
    r = ord_q(2),  E = lcm(2,r),  rho = v_q(2^r − 1),
    a = (2^E − 1)/q^rho,
    Aq^rho = 2^M − 1,  A2^m₂ = q^N − 1,
    r | M,  gcd(E,N) = 1,  rho ≥ 2 even.
    ```
    
    Let s be an odd prime dividing r. Since s divides q−1 and s does not divide N,
    
    ```text
    v_s(q−1) = v_s(A) = eta_s + v_s(M) ≥ 1 + v_s(r),
    eta_s = v_s(2^ord_s(2) − 1) ≥ 1.
    ```
    
    Here s divides A, so ord_s(2) divides M and lifting applies. No assumption eta_s=1 is needed. Consequently, for m=s^b dividing r,
    
    ```text
    q ≡ 1 (mod s^(b+1)),
    q is an m-th power in Q_s.
    ```
    
    The second assertion follows from the s-adic logarithm on 1+sZ_s. All m-th norm-residue symbols with q therefore equal 1 at primes above s.
    
    For s=2, q≡1 (mod 8) gives r | (q−1)/2. Thus m=2^b dividing r implies q≡1 (mod 2m). If q≡1 (mod 4m), q is an m-th power in Q_2. Otherwise write q=u^(m/2), where u≡5 (mod 8); adjoining an m-th root of q gives the unramified quadratic extension after adjoining the m-th roots of unity. Its norm-residue character is trivial on units. This includes b=1. The cyclotomic expressions used below are units at 2.
    
    In particular, the remaining equations imply the compact necessary condition
    
    ```text
    E rad(r) | q−1.
    ```
    
    ## A norm whose factors need not be computed
    
    Choose a prime power m=s^b dividing r. Put
    
    ```text
    B = 2^(E/m),
    H_s = Φ_m(B) = (2^E − 1)/(2^(E/s) − 1),
    a_s = H_s/q^rho.
    ```
    
    The integer H_s is independent of b. We have a_s | a, and B has order m modulo q. In K=Q(ζ_m), let β=B−ζ_m. Then Norm(β)=H_s. There is exactly one prime above q dividing β, with valuation rho: the prime where ζ_m reduces to B. Let J be the ideal obtained from (β) by removing its prime factors above q and s.
    
    At every prime P dividing J, the residue field is F_ell for some ell dividing a_s, and ζ_m reduces to B. Thus ell≡1 (mod m). If
    
    ```text
    (q/J)_m ≠ 1,
    ```
    
    some such ell satisfies s | ord_ell(q). This contradicts ord_ell(q) | N and gcd(E,N)=1.
    
    ## The calculation at q
    
    All expressions in this paragraph are modulo q. For each i with 1<i<m and gcd(i,m)=1, choose u_i satisfying i*u_i≡1 (mod m). Define
    
    ```text
    W_m = (-1)^rho · a_s / Φ'_m(B)
          · product_(1<i<m, gcd(i,m)=1) (B − B^i)^u_i,
    
    T_m = W_m^((q−1)/m).
    ```
    
    Changing the representatives u_i does not change T_m. Under the local conditions above, T_m is the reduction of (q/J)_m at ζ_m=B. Hence
    
    ```text
    T_m ≠ 1  ⇒  s | ord_ell(q) for some ell | a_s  ⇒  contradiction.
    ```
    
    **Proof of the formula.** Global reciprocity expresses (q/J)_m as the product of (β,q)_m at the primes above q; the symbols above s are trivial by the preceding local calculation. For m=2 the real symbol is also trivial, since β and q are positive.
    
    At the prime where ζ_m reduces to B^i, with i≠1, β is a unit with residue B−B^i. At the exceptional prime,
    
    ```text
    β/q^rho ≡ a_s/Φ'_m(B) (mod q).
    ```
    
    This follows by removing that factor from Φ_m(B)=product_i(B−ζ_m^i). The tame symbol (β,q)_m is the ((q−1)/m)-th power of the unit part of (-1)^v_q(β)β. Raising the contribution at the i-th embedding to u_i expresses every contribution using the same root ζ_m. Their product is the stated W_m. No generator for J is required.
    
    Thus the test uses the Mersenne quotient modulo q and cyclotomic expressions modulo q. It does not require the factorization of H_s, or a choice of M or N. The script also computes the same product independently by lifting the roots of unity modulo q^(rho+2).
    
    ## Small residue degrees
    
    For rho even, the first cases simplify to
    
    | m | W_m modulo q | necessary condition |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | 2 | a_2 | a_2 is a square modulo q |
    | 3 | a_3(2B+1) | a_3(2B+1) is a cube modulo q |
    | 4 | −4a_2 | a_2 is a fourth power modulo q |
    
    For m=3, use B²+B+1=0. For m=4, use B²=−1; since q≡1 (mod 8), −4 is a fourth power modulo q.
    
    ## Calculations
    
    The [full table](cyclotomic-reciprocity-tables.md) compares the q-adic calculation with direct power-residue symbols at the prime factors. All 23 comparisons satisfying the local condition agree. There are 41 complete-factor calculations and 46 independent comparisons between the derivative formula and the q-adic calculation.
    
    Two checks have rho=2:
    
    * **q=1093, r=E=364, m=2.** Here a_2=(2^182+1)/1093²≡101 (mod 1093), and 101^546≡−1. The complete factorization independently gives the same quadratic symbol.
    * **q=3511, r=1755, E=3510, m=3.** Here B=2^1170≡2754, a_3=(B²+B+1)/3511²≡2302, and W_3≡−14. Consequently T_3=(-14)^1170≡756≠1. No factorization of this 705-digit H_3 was used. Independently, 262657 is a primitive Mersenne factor at exponent 27 and 3511^87552≡512≠1 modulo 262657.
    
    These two primes already fail other restrictions from the notes. Their role here is to check the calculation with an even valuation, rather than extrapolate from rho=1.
    
    For **q=274177, r=128, m=128**, the local condition is the boundary case q≡1 (mod 256), q≢1 (mod 512). The calculation gives T_m=8, corresponding to ζ_128³. Directly,
    
    ```text
    2^64+1 = 274177 · 67280421310721,
    274177^((67280421310721−1)/128) ≡ 8 (mod 67280421310721).
    ```
    
    Products can cancel. For **q=433, m=8**, the individual exponents at ell=17,241,38737 are 6,2,0 modulo 8. Their sum is 0, so T_8=1 despite the two nontrivial symbols. The same q has T_9=27≠1.
    
    ## Remaining question
    
    Can all these T_m equal 1 when rho is even and the remaining conditions on q and r hold? The formula makes this a question about the residues of a_s and cyclotomic expressions modulo q, without first factoring a. Proving that some T_m is nontrivial would supply the desired obstruction for all N. No such uniform nonvanishing statement is established here.
    
    For further calculation, simplify W_m using relations between cyclotomic units, starting with m=8,9 and odd primes. A trivial product can be examined through the separate relative norms Norm_(Q(ζ_t)/Q(ζ_m))(2−ζ_t), for m | t | E; the code implements those as well.
    
    ```sh
    gp -fq -s 64M check_cyclotomic_reciprocity.gp
    ```
    
    The functions are in [cyclotomic_reciprocity.gp](cyclotomic_reciprocity.gp).

## Assistant

The calculation gives a **reciprocity test that does not require factoring the Mersenne number**.

For example, when 3 divides r, put

```text
B = 2^(E/3),
a₃ = (B² + B + 1)/q^ρ.
```

In our remaining case, I obtain the necessary condition

```text
[a₃(2B + 1)]^((q−1)/3) ≡ 1 (mod q).
```

If this fails, some prime ℓ dividing a₃ must satisfy 3 | ord_ℓ(q), contradicting gcd(E,N)=1.

The key simplification uses our existing equations: for every odd prime power sᵇ dividing r, they imply

```text
v_s(q−1) ≥ 1 + v_s(r).
```

Thus q is an sᵇ-th power in Q_s, eliminating the local correction at s. The remaining symbols can be calculated at q, including the unit left after removing q^ρ. I worked out the analogous formula for every prime power dividing r.

This remains nontrivial with **ρ even**: at q=3511, ρ=2, the cubic expression becomes `(-14)^1170 ≡ 756`, not 1. That prime was already excluded elsewhere; this checks the repeated-factor calculation.

I saved the [proof and formulas](cyclotomic-reciprocity.md), [computed tables](cyclotomic-reciprocity-tables.md), and [PARI/GP functions](cyclotomic_reciprocity.gp). All 23 applicable comparisons with directly computed factor symbols agree.

The outstanding question is now explicit: **can all these quotient-and-cyclotomic expressions be power residues simultaneously under our remaining assumptions?** Individual products can cancel; I included a concrete example of that too.

    \section*{Abstract}
    
    Let $p > 5$ be a prime. We ask how many solutions exist where $p = 2^m + q^n$ for $m, n \geq 1$ and $q$ a fixed prime.
    We know of a single example where $p$ has two solutions, $p =  11$. Do others exist? First we proceed by
    considering basic arithmetic obstructions that prevent certain solutions. This breaks down to two main cases,
    based on whether a common factor of putative solutions, $A$, is either greater than or equal to 1.
    
    
    {\small\tableofcontents}
    \clearpage
    \section{Two representations and the common factor}
    \label{sec:setup}
    
    Let $p$ be prime with two prime power solutions sharing the same base $q$. So, we have
    \[
    p = 2^{m_1} + q^{n_1} = 2^{m_2} + q^{n_2}, \qquad m_1 > m_2, \quad n_2 > n_1.
    \]
    So then writing $\Delta m = m_1 - m_2, \Delta n = n_2 - n_1$, then just following our noses we
    wind up with a coprime quantity to our bases, which is our central obstacle. That is, with
    
    \[
    2^{m_2}\left(2^{\Delta m} - 1\right) = q^{n_1}\left(q^{\Delta n} - 1\right).
    \]
    and  $\gcd(2,q) = 1$, we have $2^{m_2} \mid q^{\Delta n} - 1$ and $q^{n_1} \mid 2^{\Delta m} - 1$.
    
    And so we define
    \[
    A = \frac{2^{\Delta m} - 1}{q^{n_1}} = \frac{q^{\Delta n} - 1}{2^{m_2}},
    \]
    Now we consider
    \[
    A\,q^{n_1} = 2^{\Delta m} - 1, \qquad A\,2^{m_2} = q^{\Delta n} - 1, \qquad A < 2^{\Delta m}, \quad A < q^{\Delta n}.
    \]
    
    The coprimality of $A$ with the bases follows directly:
    $Aq^{n_1}=2^{\Delta m}-1$ makes $A$ odd, and
    $A2^{m_2}=q^{\Delta n}-1$ gives $q\nmid A$. Thus
    \[
    \gcd(A,2q)=1.
    \]
    In particular $A$ is a positive integer, so the two cases are $A=1$ and
    $A>1$.
    
    \subsection{The quadratic form and gap parity}
    
    \subsection{\texorpdfstring{The case $A=1$}{The case A=1}}
    
    \begin{lemma}\label{lem:Aone}
    If $A=1$, the two representations are
    \[
    11=2^3+3=2+3^2.
    \]
    \end{lemma}
    \begin{proof}
    Write $\Delta m=2k$ with $k\geq1$. Then
    \[
    q^{n_1}=2^{2k}-1=(2^k-1)(2^k+1).
    \]
    The two factors are odd and differ by $2$, so they are coprime.
    As their product is a power of a single prime, the smaller factor
    must be $1$. Hence $k=1$, $q=3$, and $n_1=1$.
    The other defining equation is now
    \[
    2^{m_2}=3^{\Delta n}-1.
    \]
    Since $\Delta n$ is odd, $3^{\Delta n}-1\equiv2\pmod8$.
    Thus $m_2=1$, which gives $\Delta n=1$.
    Therefore $m_1=3$, $n_2=2$, and $p=11$.
    \end{proof}
    
    \section{Valuations, size bounds, and orders}
    \subsection{Consequences for the full common divisor}
    The arguments giving $N\ge5d$ and $N=5d\Rightarrow n_1=2$, $M=dE$
    use only $dE\mid M$, $d\mid N$, $d\ne q$, and the gap equations.
    They therefore apply with $d=g=\gcd(M,N)$ as well, even when $g$
    is composite. Thus
    \[
    g>1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad N\ge5g\ge35.
    \]
    In particular the gaps are coprime when $N$ is prime, or when $N$
    is a power of $5$.
    
    The first possible value $N=35$ is also excluded from the noncoprime
    case. It would require $g=7$, $n_1=2$ and $n_2=37$.
    Since $p\equiv1\pmod7$, its representation as a sum of two nonzero
    squares gives
    \[
    2^{m_1}\equiv q^2\equiv4\pmod7.
    \]
    Hence $q\equiv2$ or $5\pmod7$. The other representation gives
    $2^{m_2}\equiv1-q^{37}\equiv1-q\pmod7$, namely $6$ or $3$.
    Neither is a power of $2$ modulo $7$. Consequently
    \[
    \boxed{N<49\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\gcd(M,N)=1.}
    \]
    Indeed, for $35<N<49$, a prime factor of a nontrivial $g$ would have
    to be $7$, since $N\ge5g$; no multiple of $7$ in this interval is
    odd and coprime to $3$.
    
    \subsection{Using congruences modulo eight and five}
    \label{sec:mod-eight-families}
    \subsection{Cyclotomic structure and further reading}
    % Further reading and open targets from the current discussion.
    For a primitive $M$-th root of unity $\zeta_M$,
    \[
    \Phi_M(2)=\operatorname{Norm}_{\mathbb Q(\zeta_M)/\mathbb Q}(2-\zeta_M).
    \]
    A primitive Mersenne factor $\ell$ corresponds to a prime ideal
    where $\zeta_M$ reduces to $2$. Subgroups of the Galois group group
    the conjugates into relative norms. This can give algebraic
    factorizations and, under suitable specialization, integer factors.
    Brent \cite[\S\S2.2--2.3,3,4.4]{Brent} develops the Gauss and
    Aurifeuillean identities from these root groupings and gives algorithms
    for computing their factors. Lemma~\ref{lem:aurifeuillean-height}
    is one use here: the whole $q^{n_1}$ must fit into one coprime factor.
    For the field structure, use Washington \cite[Chapters 2--3]{Washington};
    Chapter 6 gives the Gauss-sum background, and Chapter 8 treats
    cyclotomic units. A further target is to compute relative norms in
    small subfields and determine whether they separate the part containing
    $q^{n_1}$ from factors forced into $A$.
    
    The magnitude condition $\ell>q$ remains a separate route.
    Stewart \cite[Theorem 1.1, \S5]{Stewart} proves, for all sufficiently
    large $M$, an effective bound
    \[
    P(\Phi_M(2))>
    M\exp\!\left(\frac{\log M}{104\log\log M}\right),
    \]
    where $P$ denotes the largest prime factor. Such a factor is primitive.
    The proof combines the size of the cyclotomic value with bounds on
    prime-adic multiplicities. To use it here, one must compare its bound
    with $q$ in the family under consideration and control the multiplier
    of the resulting prime. The current general bound on $q$ in terms
    of $M$ is exponential, so this does not yet establish $\ell>q$ throughout.
    
    The alternative $\ell\nmid q-1$ asks for control of shared factors
    with $q-1$. The products $D,D_E$ above make the required divisibility
    or size statement precise; logical weakness alone does not make
    that statement easier to prove.
    For the residual index $j$, Moree \cite[\S\S1,5,6]{MoreeNear}
    provides a complementary viewpoint.
    The condition $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(2)=(\ell-1)/j$ is precisely
    his near-primitive-root problem. Lenstra--Moree--Stevenhagen
    \cite[\S\S2,5,6]{LMS} express the compatibility of the splitting
    conditions using Galois groups and character sums. Their density
    results assume GRH and vary $\ell$; they do not force a suitable
    prime divisor of a specified $\Phi_M(2)$. Here the additional target
    is the bound $D>(q-1)/2^{m_2}$ from
    Section~\ref{sec:forcing-common-factor}.
    
    For a different route to a bound on $N$, Corvaja's short survey
    \cite[\S1]{CorvajaSurvey} explains the Subspace Theorem bounds for
    gcds of powers and the extension to a fixed finitely generated
    multiplicative group. In our case
    \[
    A=\gcd(2^M-1,q^N-1)>3q^{N-1}.
    \]
    The strict inequality follows from $2^{m_2}\le(q-1)/3$.
    An effective bound, valid for our family and uniform in $q$, of the form
    \[
    \log\gcd(2^M-1,q^N-1)
     \le\theta N\log q+K\log q,\qquad \theta<1,
    \]
    with fixed $\theta,K$, would give $N<(K+1)/(1-\theta)$.
    This is a target, not a quoted theorem. Fixed-group results do not
    supply uniformity as $q$ varies, and their ineffectivity also matters
    for a finite computation. The survey connects this approach with
    complex analysis and the support problem.
    
    For computational algebraic number theory, Alvarado et al.
    \cite[\S\S3--6]{SUnitAlgorithms} give explicit archimedean and
    $\ell$-adic bounds, lattice reduction, and sieves for $S$-unit equations
    over number fields. A use here would first require a reduction to
    controlled fields and prime supports. The original equality gives a
    four-term unit relation over $S=\{2,q\}$, not directly their
    two-variable equation $x+y=1$. In a cyclotomic-field approach the
    uncontrolled primes in $A$ remain the obstacle to fixing that support.

    \label{sec:exercises}

For α=q^(1/s^v), arithmetic Frobenius satisfies Frob_P(α)/α = q^w modulo a prime of F above P. Hence q^w≠1 detects nontrivial Frobenius in F/K and forces s to divide ord_ℓ(q).     \subsection{\texorpdfstring{An effective reduction when $q\mid M$}{An effective reduction when q divides  M}}
    
    If $q\mid M$, then $qr\mid M$ because $r\mid M$ and $q\nmid r$.
    Since $q<2^r$, this gives
    \[
    M\geq qr>\frac{q\log q}{\log2}.
    \]
    Together with \eqref{eq:baker-M}, this bounds $q$ absolutely in this branch.
    A coarse cutoff is $q<10^6$.
    
    Put $\lambda=\log q$, $t=M/\lambda$, and
    $H(t)=\max\{\log(3t)+0.38,10\}$. Dividing \eqref{eq:baker-M} gives
    \[
    \frac{t}{H(t)^2}
     <\frac{50.4}{\log2}\lambda
       +\frac{2\log(27/26)}{\lambda\log2\,H(t)^2}
     <73\lambda.
    \]
    If $q\geq10^6$, then $t>q/\log2$, $H(t)=\log(3t)+0.38>2$,
    and $t/H(t)^2$ is increasing. Hence
    \[
    q<73\log2\,\lambda(\lambda+C)^2,
    \qquad C=\log(3/\log2)+0.38<1.845126.
    \]
    At $q=10^6$ the right side is less than $172000$.
    Moreover $q/[\log q(\log q+C)^2]$ is increasing thereafter:
    its logarithmic derivative with respect to $\lambda$ is
    $1-1/\lambda-2/(\lambda+C)>0$.
    Thus $q<10^6$ in this branch. For each such $q$,
    \eqref{eq:baker-M} bounds $M$ effectively. The uniform bound and
    finite exclusion below complete this branch.
    
    \begin{lemma}
    If $q\mid M$, then $36\nmid M$ and $48\nmid M$.
    \end{lemma}
    \begin{proof}
    If $36\mid M$, the primes $3,5,7,13,19,37$ divide $2^M-1$;
    their orders at base $2$ are $2,4,3,12,18,36$ respectively.
    Each has $\ell-1$ supported on $2,3$, so
    Section~\ref{sec:forbidden-periods} forces $q\equiv1\pmod\ell$
    unless $q=\ell$. The bases $3,5,7,19$ are already excluded.
    Since $4\mid M$, $q\equiv1\pmod5$, excluding $q=13,37$ as well.
    Consequently
    \[
    959595=3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot13\cdot19\cdot37\mid q-1.
    \]
    As $4\mid q-1$, this gives $q\ge3838381$, contrary to $q<10^6$.
    
    If $48\mid M$, use $3,5,7,13,17,97$, whose orders are
    $2,4,3,12,8,48$. The base $17$ is excluded modulo $3$;
    $13,97$ are excluded by $q\equiv1\pmod5$.
    Thus $2250885\mid q-1$, giving $q\ge9003541$.
    \end{proof}
    In particular, in the $q\mid M$ branch,
    \[
    \operatorname{lcm}(2,r,3^{v_3(q-1)-1})
    \quad\text{cannot be divisible by }36\text{ or }48.
    \]
    These exclusions apply to all $p$; they use no bound on $p$ and no
    enumeration. Additional prime factors in the residue product can
    strengthen the thresholds.
    
    \subsection{Excluding the branch with a finite check}
    \label{sec:q-divides-exclusion}

    \begin{lemma}
    If $q\mid M$, then $M<4\cdot10^6$.
    \end{lemma}
    \begin{proof}
    Write $H_\lambda(x)=\max\{\log(3x/\lambda)+0.38,10\}$.
    The preceding estimates give $M<73\lambda^2H_\lambda(M)^2$.
    Since $\lambda=\log q<14$ and $\lambda H_\lambda(M)$ is increasing
    in $\lambda$,
    \[
    \frac{M}{H_{14}(M)^2}<73\cdot14^2=14308.
    \]
    The function $x/H_{14}(x)^2$ is increasing: on the logarithmic
    branch its derivative has the sign of $H_{14}(x)-2>0$.
    But $H_{14}(4\cdot10^6)<15$, and
    $4\cdot10^6/15^2>14308$. Hence $M<4\cdot10^6$.
    \end{proof}

    \subsection{\texorpdfstring{The base $q=3$}{The base q=3}}
    
    \begin{lemma}\label{lem:qthree}
    For $q=3$, the only prime with two representations is $p=11$.
    \end{lemma}
    \begin{proof}
    The case $A=1$ is settled, so suppose $A>1$.
    We have $m_2=1$, $N$ odd, and
    \[
    n_1=v_3(2^M-1)=1+v_3(M).
    \]
    If $n_1>1$, then $3\mid M$. Since $\operatorname{ord}_7(2)=3$,
    we get $7\mid2^M-1$, hence $7\mid A$, hence $7\mid3^N-1$.
    But $\operatorname{ord}_7(3)=6$, contradicting $N$ odd.
    Thus $n_1=1$, and the original representations give
    \[
    3^{n_2}-1=2^{m_1},\qquad n_2=1+N\text{ even}.
    \]
    The factors $3^{n_2/2}-1$ and $3^{n_2/2}+1$ are powers of $2$
    differing by $2$, so they are $2$ and $4$. Thus $n_2=2$, $m_1=3$,
    and $p=11$, which has $A=1$.
    \end{proof}

    \begin{lemma}\label{lem:aurifeuillean-height}
    Suppose $r\equiv4\pmod8$. If
    \[
    \frac{8h}{q^{n_1/2}-1}\le m_2\log2,
    \]
    then $(4h-1)n_1<N$. The hypothesis holds whenever $h\le32$.
    Consequently the noncoprime $N=49$ family requires
    $r\not\equiv4\pmod8$.
    \end{lemma}
    \begin{proof}
    Write $r=8a+4$. Since $q^{n_1}\mid2^r-1$ and
    $\operatorname{ord}_q(2)=r$, the full power $q^{n_1}$ divides
    \[
    2^{r/2}+1
    =(2^{2a+1}-2^{a+1}+1)(2^{2a+1}+2^{a+1}+1).
    \]
    The two factors are odd and their difference is a power of $2$,
    so they are coprime. Hence
    \[
    q^{n_1}\le2^{r/4}+2^{(r+4)/8}+1
     <(2^{r/8}+1)^2,
    \qquad 2^r>(q^{n_1/2}-1)^8.
    \]
    Here $E=r$. Put $e=n_1$, $c=m_2$. The hypothesis and
    $\log(1+x)<x$ give
    \[
    8h\log\frac{q^{e/2}}{q^{e/2}-1}<c\log2.
    \]
    Therefore
    \[
    q^{N+e}>2^{c+hr}
     >2^c(q^{e/2}-1)^{8h}>q^{4he}.
    \]
    For $h\le32$, use $q\ge97$, $e\ge2$, $c\ge4$:
    $8h/(q^{e/2}-1)\le8/3<4\log2$.
    For $N=49$ we have $h=7$, $e=2$, which would require $54<49$.
    \end{proof}

    +$u\in1+4\mathbb Z_2$, using the logarithm on $1+4\mathbb Z_2$.
    +Adjoining an $m$-th root of $q$ to $K$ locally at $2$ amounts to
    +adjoining $\sqrt u$, giving a trivial or unramified extension.
    +Since $\beta$ is a unit there, the local symbol equals $1$.
    +Together the congruences give $E\operatorname{rad}(r)\mid q-1$,
    +where $\operatorname{rad}(r)$ is the product of the distinct primes dividing $r$.
    +
    +With the symbol convention of Sharifi \cite[\S3, eq.~(5)]{SharifiCycl},
    +global reciprocity expresses $(q/J)_m$ as the product of
    +$(\beta,q)_m$ over the primes above $q$. The local contribution above
    +$s$ is trivial by the preceding calculation, and for $m=2$ the real
    +contribution is trivial by positivity. This adapts the norm and
    +reciprocity calculation in Sharifi \cite[\S\S4,8]{SharifiCycl}.
    +
    +Reduce the resulting symbol modulo the prime where $\zeta_m$ maps
    +to $B$. For $1<i<m$ with $\gcd(i,m)=1$, let $u_i i\equiv1\pmod m$.
    +The result is
    +\[
    +T_m=
    +\left(
    +\frac{a_s}{\Phi'_m(B)}
    +\prod_{\substack{1<i<m\\ \gcd(i,m)=1}} (B-B^i)^{u_i}
    +\right)^{(q-1)/m}\pmod q.
    +\]
    +Indeed, at the prime above $q$ where $\zeta_m$ maps to $B$, $\beta$
    +has valuation $\rho$ and $\beta/q^\rho$ reduces to
    +$a_s/\Phi'_m(B)$, by dividing the norm by the other conjugate factors.
    +The tame symbol uses this unit with sign $(-1)^\rho=1$.
    +At the other primes the unit is $B-B^i$. Raising the corresponding
    +residue symbol to $u_i$ expresses it in the common reduction
    +$\zeta_m\mapsto B$. Thus every remaining solution must have $T_m=1$
    +for all prime powers $m\mid r$.
    +
    +For $m=2$ this requires $a_2$ to be a square modulo $q$.
    +For $m=3$ it requires $a_3(2B+1)$ to be a cube modulo $q$.
    +For example, $q=3511$ has $r=1755$ and $\rho=2$.
    +Here $a_3(2B+1)\equiv-14\pmod q$ and $T_3=756$.
    +This prime is already excluded by earlier congruences.
    +The open question is whether the remaining hypotheses force some
    +$T_m\ne1$, or an individual order obstruction when the symbols cancel.
    +
    +\subsection{Computational supplements}
    +
    +\begin{itemize}
    +\item \path{mersenne-tables.md} gives orders, the factors used in $D_E$,
    +and Frobenius in the cyclotomic fields for illustrative $q$.
    +The GAP source is \path{mersenne_tables.g}. For the cyclotomic
    +Frobenius formula see Milne \cite{MilneANT}.
    +\item \path{order-obstructions.md} checks all prime choices with
    +$E\le256$ using \path{check_order_obstruction.g} and
    +\path{mersenne-factors-256.g}. There are 395 certificates among
    +396 choices, with $q=3$, $a=1$ the exception. All have $\rho=1$.
    +\item \path{cyclotomic-reciprocity.md} gives the derivation and examples.
    +\path{cyclotomic-reciprocity-tables.md} compares the calculation at $q$
    +with direct symbols at the prime factors and includes examples
    +with $\rho=2$. The PARI/GP functions are in
    +\path{cyclotomic_reciprocity.gp}. Run
    +\path{check_cyclotomic_reciprocity.gp} to regenerate the tables.
    +\end{itemize}

    Since $r=\operatorname{ord}_q(2)$ divides both $M$ and $q-1$,
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:cubic-return}
    \boxed{r\mid(q-1)/3,\qquad 2^{(q-1)/3}\equiv1\pmod q.}
    \end{equation}
    This is a necessary condition on $q$ alone.
    
    If $\ell\mid A$ and $\ell-1=2^i3^j$, then
    $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)\mid\gcd(N,\ell-1)=1$. Hence
    \[
    q\equiv1\pmod\ell.
    \]
    In particular $3\mid M$ forces $q\equiv1\pmod7$;
    $12\mid M$, $q\ne13$, forces $q\equiv1\pmod{13}$;
    and $18\mid M$ forces $q\equiv1\pmod{19}$.
    The bases $7,19$ themselves are already excluded by $q\equiv1\pmod4$.
    For example, $q=109$ passes \eqref{eq:cubic-return}, but
    $\operatorname{ord}_{109}(2)=36$ forces $3\mid M$, while
    $109\equiv4\pmod7$. Thus it is excluded for all $p$.
    
    More generally, let $L\mid M$ be forced, and let $\mathcal S$ be
    any set of primes $\ell\ne q$ such that
    \[
    \operatorname{ord}_\ell(2)\mid L,\qquad \ell-1=2^i3^j.
    \]
    Then, writing $P=\prod_{\ell\in\mathcal S}\ell$ and $c=m_2$,
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:forced-residue-product}
    \boxed{P\mid q-1,\qquad 2^cP\le q-1.}
    \end{equation}
    A single failed residue excludes $q$; the product can exclude a whole
    specified family without computing the individual residues.
    
    When $c=2$, $q\equiv5\pmod8$ implies that $2$ is a quadratic
    nonresidue modulo $q$, so $4\mid r\mid M$. Thus $q\equiv1\pmod5$,
    and the earlier classes modulo $48$ sharpen to
    \[
    q\equiv61\text{ or }181\pmod{240}\qquad(c=2).
    \]
    
    \subsection{The full common divisor}
    \label{sec:full-gcd}
    % Restored from even_odd_case.tex, Section 6.3; totient restriction added here.
    Let $d=\gcd(M,N)>1$, $U=2^{M/d}$, $V=q^{N/d}$, and $Y=UV$.
    Then $Ap=Y^d-1$. The sharper size bound gives
    \[
    p>2q(1-Y^{-d})Y^{d/2}>Y^{d/2}.
    \]
    For any proper divisor $e$ of $d$, $\Phi_e(Y)\mid Y^e-1<Y^{d/2}$.
    Hence $p$ divides only the factor $\Phi_d(Y)$, and
    \[
    H_d:=\frac{Y^d-1}{\Phi_d(Y)}\mid A,\qquad
    \operatorname{ord}_p(Y)=d,\qquad p\equiv1\pmod d.
    \]
    The M\"obius product gives
    \[
    \left|\log\Phi_d(Y)-\varphi(d)\log Y\right|
    \leq\sum_{j\geq1}-\log(1-Y^{-j})
    \leq\frac{Y}{(Y-1)^2}<\log2.
    \]
    Thus $\Phi_d(Y)<2Y^{\varphi(d)}$. Comparing the resulting lower bound
    on $H_d$ with $A<Y^{d/2}/(2q)$ proves
    \[
    \boxed{\varphi(d)>d/2.}
    \]
    Equivalently, the prime factors of $d$ must satisfy
    $\prod_{\ell\mid d}(1-1/\ell)>1/2$; every odd prime power passes this test.
    Also $3\nmid d$ by the preceding argument.

    Notes on two prime power partitions with the same bases
    
    Abstract
    Let p > 5 be a prime. We ask how many solutions exist where p = 2m + q n for m, n ≥ 1 and q
    a fixed prime. We know of a single example where p has two solutions, p = 11. Do others exist?
    First we proceed by considering basic arithmetic obstructions that prevent certain solutions. This
    breaks down to two main cases, based on whether a common factor of putative solutions, A, is
    either greater than or equal to 1.
    
    Proof sketch
    Write M = m1 − m2 and N = n2 − n1 . Subtracting the representations gives Aq n1 = 2M − 1 and
    A2m2 = q N − 1, with gcd(A, 2q) = 1. The quadratic form gives M even and N odd. Factoring
    2M − 1 then gives p = 11 when A = 1. For q = 3, any n1 > 1 forces 7 | A, but ord7 (3) = 6. The
    case n1 = 1 again gives p = 11 (Lemmas 3 and 7).
    For A > 1 and q > 3, the parity and congruence arguments give q ≡ 1 (mod 48), m2 = v2 (q − 1)
    even, n1 even, and N ≥ 5 with gcd(N, 6) = 1. Put r = ordq (2) and ρ = vq (2r − 1). Lifting gives
    n1 = ρ + vq (M ).
    The two large powers yield 0 < n2 log q − m1 log 2 < (27/26)q −N . Laurent’s lower bound gives
    an effective bound on M for fixed q. If q | M , then qr | M , giving absolute bounds q < 106 and
    M < 4 · 106 . The finite check in Section 5.5 excludes this branch.
    It remains to consider q ∤ M and n1 = ρ ≥ 2 even. With E = lcm(2, r), we have
    E | M,
    
    gcd(E, N ) = 1,
    
    a=
    
    2E − 1
    | A,
    qρ
    
    qN ≡ 1
    
    (mod a).
    
    Thus one prime-power factor of a at which q has order sharing a prime divisor with E would exclude
    every N for that q. Section 8 computes products of power-residue symbols that can certify such a
    factor without factoring a. The open step is to force an order obstruction for every remaining q.

## User

## Assistant

Yes. Since M is even, 2^M ≡ 1 (mod 3). And q > 3 means dividing 2^M − 1 by q^n₁ removes no factors of 3. So **3 | A**. The implication then goes the other way through the second gap equation: q^N − 1 = 2^m₂ A gives q^N ≡ 1 (mod 3), and N odd gives q ≡ 1 (mod 3).

In fact, A contains the full power of 3 in 2^M − 1. In the remaining case, where 3 ∤ N, lifting on both sides gives

```text
v₃(A) = 1 + v₃(M) = v₃(q − 1).
```

The prime 3 is primitive at exponent 2, so it contributes no primitive factor at M > 2. But it illustrates what A is absorbing: every prime power in 2^M − 1 other than the q-part must occur in q^N − 1 with the same multiplicity. At 3 that forces a valuation of q − 1. At the other Mersenne factors it also forces the order of q to divide N.

    \section{An order obstruction from power reciprocity}
    \label{sec:reciprocity}
    
    Keep $q\nmid M$, $n_1=\rho$ even, $E=\operatorname{lcm}(2,r)$ and
    $a=(2^E-1)/q^\rho$. Since $a\mid A$, an order
    $\operatorname{ord}_{\ell^f}(q)$ with $\ell^f\mid a$ cannot share a
    prime divisor with $E$. At a prime $\ell$, the $s^b$-th power-residue
    symbol detects such an obstruction when $s\mid E$ and $s^b\mid\ell-1$.
    It describes Frobenius in the Kummer extension obtained by adjoining
    an $s^b$-th root of $q$ to $\mathbb Q(\zeta_{s^b})$
    \cite[\S\S2,4]{StevenhagenKummer}.
    
    \subsection{A product computable at q}
    
    Take $m=s^b\mid r$ with $s$ prime and put
    \[
    B=2^{E/m},\qquad
    H_s=\Phi_m(B)=\frac{2^E-1}{2^{E/s}-1},\qquad a_s=H_s/q^\rho.
    \]
    The denominator in the quotient for $H_s$ is prime to $q$, so
    $a_s\mid a$. In $K=\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)$, set $\beta=B-\zeta_m$.
    The norm of $\beta$ is $H_s$. Let $J$ be the ideal obtained from
    $(\beta)$ by removing the factors above $q$ and $s$.
    At every prime ideal $P\mid J$ above $\ell$, $\zeta_m$ reduces
    to $B$ and has order $m$. The residue field is $\mathbb F_\ell$.
    Thus $(q/J)_m\ne1$ forces $s\mid\operatorname{ord}_{\ell}(q)$
    for some $\ell\mid a_s$.
    
    In the remaining case, for odd $s\mid r$ we have $s\mid A$ and $s\nmid N$.
    Equation~\eqref{eq:valuation-coupling} gives
    \[
    v_s(q-1)=v_s(2^{\operatorname{ord}_s(2)}-1)+v_s(M)
      \ge 1+v_s(r).
    \]
    Hence $q$ is an $m$-th power in $\mathbb Q_s$ by the $s$-adic logarithm.
    For $s=2$, $q\equiv1\pmod8$ gives $r\mid(q-1)/2$, so
    $q\equiv1\pmod{2m}$. Write $q=u^{m/2}$ in $\mathbb Q_2$ with
    $u\in1+4\mathbb Z_2$, using the logarithm on $1+4\mathbb Z_2$.
    Adjoining an $m$-th root of $q$ to $K$ locally at $2$ amounts to
    adjoining $\sqrt u$, giving a trivial or unramified extension.
    Since $\beta$ is a unit there, the local symbol equals $1$.
    Together the congruences give $E\operatorname{rad}(r)\mid q-1$,
    where $\operatorname{rad}(r)$ is the product of the distinct primes dividing $r$.
    
    With the symbol convention of Sharifi \cite[\S3, eq.~(5)]{SharifiCycl},
    global reciprocity expresses $(q/J)_m$ as the product of
    $(\beta,q)_m$ over the primes above $q$. The local contribution above
    $s$ is trivial by the preceding calculation, and for $m=2$ the real
    contribution is trivial by positivity. This adapts the norm and
    reciprocity calculation in Sharifi \cite[\S\S4,8]{SharifiCycl}.
    
    Reduce the resulting symbol modulo the prime where $\zeta_m$ maps
    to $B$. For $1<i<m$ with $\gcd(i,m)=1$, let $u_i i\equiv1\pmod m$.
    The result is
    \[
    T_m=
    \left(
    \frac{a_s}{\Phi'_m(B)}
    \prod_{\substack{1<i<m\\ \gcd(i,m)=1}} (B-B^i)^{u_i}
    \right)^{(q-1)/m}\pmod q.
    \]
    Indeed, at the prime above $q$ where $\zeta_m$ maps to $B$, $\beta$
    has valuation $\rho$ and $\beta/q^\rho$ reduces to
    $a_s/\Phi'_m(B)$, by dividing the norm by the other conjugate factors.
    The tame symbol uses this unit with sign $(-1)^\rho=1$.
    At the other primes the unit is $B-B^i$. Raising the corresponding
    residue symbol to $u_i$ expresses it in the common reduction
    $\zeta_m\mapsto B$. Thus every remaining solution must have $T_m=1$
    for all prime powers $m\mid r$.
    
    For $m=2$ this requires $a_2$ to be a square modulo $q$.
    For $m=3$ it requires $a_3(2B+1)$ to be a cube modulo $q$.
    For example, $q=3511$ has $r=1755$ and $\rho=2$.
    Here $a_3(2B+1)\equiv-14\pmod q$ and $T_3=756$.
    This prime is already excluded by earlier congruences.
    The open question is whether the remaining hypotheses force some
    $T_m\ne1$, or an individual order obstruction when the symbols cancel.

    \section{Orders modulo the factors of \texorpdfstring{$2^E-1$}{2\string^E-1}}
    \label{sec:orders}
    
    By \eqref{eq:gap}, \eqref{eq:remaining}, and \eqref{eq:gcd},
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:order-test}
    a=\frac{2^E-1}{q^\rho}\mid A,\qquad
    \gcd(\ord_{\ell^f}(q),E)=1
    \quad\text{for every prime power }\ell^f\mid a.
    \end{equation}
    The order condition follows because the order divides $N$.
    Both $a$ and $E$ are determined by $q$, so one failure of
    \eqref{eq:order-test} excludes that $q$ for all $M,N$.
    
    Power reciprocity can sometimes detect a failure without factoring $a$.
    Take a prime power $m=s^b$ dividing $r$ and put
    \[
    B=2^{E/m},\qquad
    a_s=\frac{\Phi_m(B)}{q^\rho}
    =\frac{2^E-1}{q^\rho(2^{E/s}-1)}.
    \]
    The integer $a_s$ divides $a$ since $r\nmid E/s$. Write
    $K=\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)$ and $\beta=B-\zeta_m$, so
    $\operatorname{Norm}_{K/\mathbb Q}(\beta)=\Phi_m(B)$.
    Let $J$ be the part of $(\beta)$ prime to $sq$. At a prime ideal
    dividing $J$ above $\ell$, $\zeta_m$ reduces to $B$ of order $m$ in
    $\mathbb F_\ell$. By \eqref{eq:order-test}, $q$ has order coprime to
    $s$ there, so the $m$-th power residue symbol $(q/J)_m$ must equal $1$.
    
    To compute this symbol at $q$, first consider the places above $s$.
    For odd $s$, we have $s\mid q-1$, $s\mid r\mid M$, and $s\nmid N$
    by \eqref{eq:gcd}. Lifting in \eqref{eq:gap} gives
    $v_s(q-1)=v_s(2^{\ord_s(2)}-1)+v_s(M)\ge b+1$.
    Thus $q$ is an $m$-th power in $\mathbb Q_s$ by the $s$-adic logarithm.
    For $s=2$, $q\equiv1\pmod8$ gives $r\mid(q-1)/2$, hence
    $q\equiv1\pmod{2m}$. The logarithm on $1+4\mathbb Z_2$ then gives
    $q=u^{m/2}$ for some $u\in1+4\mathbb Z_2$. Adjoining an $m$-th root
    of $q$ to $K$ locally at $2$ is equivalent to adjoining $\sqrt u$,
    which is trivial or unramified. Since $\beta$ is a unit at $2$, its
    local symbol is $1$. The real symbol when $m=2$ is trivial by positivity.
    In particular the restrictions at $s$ give
    $E\prod_{s\mid r,\ s\text{ prime}}s\mid q-1$.
    
    With the convention in \cite[\S3, (5)]{SharifiCycl}, reciprocity
    expresses $(q/J)_m$ as the product of the local symbols $(\beta,q)_m$
    above $q$. These primes correspond to the reductions
    $\zeta_m\mapsto B^i$ for $i$ coprime to $m$. At $i=1$, $\beta$ has
    valuation $\rho$, and its unit part reduces to $a_s/\Phi_m'(B)$ by
    the norm identity. At the other primes it has residue $B-B^i$.
    The tame symbol raises these units to $(q-1)/m$ and the sign from
    the valuation is $(-1)^\rho=1$. To express the symbol at
    $B^i$ in the reduction $\zeta_m\mapsto B$, raise it to the inverse
    $u_i$ of $i$ modulo $m$. The resulting product gives
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:T}
    \left(
    \frac{a_s}{\Phi_m'(B)}
    \prod_{\substack{1<i<m\\(i,m)=1}}(B-B^i)^{u_i}
    \right)^{(q-1)/m}\equiv1\pmod q,
    \qquad i u_i\equiv1\pmod m.
    \end{equation}
    For example, if $2\mid r$, taking $m=2$ requires
    $(2^{E/2}+1)/q^\rho$ to be a square modulo $q$.
    
    The open step is to find a prime-power factor in \eqref{eq:order-test}
    whose order shares a prime divisor with $E$, for every $q$ surviving
    the preceding reductions. A failure of \eqref{eq:T} for any $m$ supplies
    such a factor. When the product in \eqref{eq:T} is $1$, the individual
    symbols may still be nontrivial.

    # Cyclotomic reciprocity calculations
    
    These calculations develop the relative-norm suggestion following [Sharifi, *On cyclotomic polynomials, power residues, and reciprocity laws*](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~sharifi/publ/cycl.pdf). The reciprocity convention is his equation (5). The deductions below are for our equations; they are not applications of his prime-value theorems.
    
    ## Local conditions supplied by the equations
    
    Retain
    
    ```text
    r = ord_q(2),  E = lcm(2,r),  rho = v_q(2^r − 1),
    a = (2^E − 1)/q^rho,
    Aq^rho = 2^M − 1,  A2^m₂ = q^N − 1,
    r | M,  gcd(E,N) = 1,  rho ≥ 2 even.
    ```
    
    Let s be an odd prime dividing r. Since s divides q−1 and s does not divide N,
    
    ```text
    v_s(q−1) = v_s(A) = eta_s + v_s(M) ≥ 1 + v_s(r),
    eta_s = v_s(2^ord_s(2) − 1) ≥ 1.
    ```
    
    Here s divides A, so ord_s(2) divides M and lifting applies. No assumption eta_s=1 is needed. Consequently, for m=s^b dividing r,
    
    ```text
    q ≡ 1 (mod s^(b+1)),
    q is an m-th power in Q_s.
    ```
    
    The second assertion follows from the s-adic logarithm on 1+sZ_s. All m-th norm-residue symbols with q therefore equal 1 at primes above s.
    
    For s=2, q≡1 (mod 8) gives r | (q−1)/2. Thus m=2^b dividing r implies q≡1 (mod 2m). If q≡1 (mod 4m), q is an m-th power in Q_2. Otherwise write q=u^(m/2), where u≡5 (mod 8); adjoining an m-th root of q gives the unramified quadratic extension after adjoining the m-th roots of unity. Its norm-residue character is trivial on units. This includes b=1. The cyclotomic expressions used below are units at 2.
    
    In particular, the remaining equations imply the compact necessary condition
    
    ```text
    E rad(r) | q−1.
    ```
    
    ## A norm whose factors need not be computed
    
    Choose a prime power m=s^b dividing r. Put
    
    ```text
    B = 2^(E/m),
    H_s = Φ_m(B) = (2^E − 1)/(2^(E/s) − 1),
    a_s = H_s/q^rho.
    ```
    
    The integer H_s is independent of b. We have a_s | a, and B has order m modulo q. In K=Q(ζ_m), let β=B−ζ_m. Then Norm(β)=H_s. There is exactly one prime above q dividing β, with valuation rho: the prime where ζ_m reduces to B. Let J be the ideal obtained from (β) by removing its prime factors above q and s.
    
    At every prime P dividing J, the residue field is F_ell for some ell dividing a_s, and ζ_m reduces to B. Thus ell≡1 (mod m). If
    
    ```text
    (q/J)_m ≠ 1,
    ```
    
    some such ell satisfies s | ord_ell(q). This contradicts ord_ell(q) | N and gcd(E,N)=1.
    
    ## The calculation at q
    
    All expressions in this paragraph are modulo q. For each i with 1<i<m and gcd(i,m)=1, choose u_i satisfying i*u_i≡1 (mod m). Define
    
    ```text
    W_m = (-1)^rho · a_s / Φ'_m(B)
          · product_(1<i<m, gcd(i,m)=1) (B − B^i)^u_i,
    
    T_m = W_m^((q−1)/m).
    ```
    
    Changing the representatives u_i does not change T_m. Under the local conditions above, T_m is the reduction of (q/J)_m at ζ_m=B. Hence
    
    ```text
    T_m ≠ 1  ⇒  s | ord_ell(q) for some ell | a_s  ⇒  contradiction.
    ```
    
    **Proof of the formula.** Global reciprocity expresses (q/J)_m as the product of (β,q)_m at the primes above q; the symbols above s are trivial by the preceding local calculation. For m=2 the real symbol is also trivial, since β and q are positive.
    
    At the prime where ζ_m reduces to B^i, with i≠1, β is a unit with residue B−B^i. At the exceptional prime,
    
    ```text
    β/q^rho ≡ a_s/Φ'_m(B) (mod q).
    ```
    
    This follows by removing that factor from Φ_m(B)=product_i(B−ζ_m^i). At a prime P above q, the tame symbol (β,q)_m is the ((q−1)/m)-th power of the unit part of (-1)^v_P(β)β. Raising the contribution at the i-th embedding to u_i expresses every contribution using the same root ζ_m. Their product is the stated W_m. No generator for J is required.
    
    Thus the test uses the Mersenne quotient modulo q and cyclotomic expressions modulo q. It does not require the factorization of H_s, or a choice of M or N. The script also computes the same product independently by lifting the roots of unity modulo q^(rho+2).
    
    ## Small values of m
    
    For rho even, the first cases simplify to
    
    | m | W_m modulo q | necessary condition |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | 2 | a_2 | a_2 is a square modulo q |
    | 3 | a_3(2B+1) | a_3(2B+1) is a cube modulo q |
    | 4 | −4a_2 | a_2 is a fourth power modulo q |
    
    For m=3, use B²+B+1=0. For m=4, use B²=−1; since q≡1 (mod 8), −4 is a fourth power modulo q.
    
    ## Calculations
    
    The [full table](cyclotomic-reciprocity-tables.md) compares the q-adic calculation with direct power-residue symbols at the prime factors. All 23 comparisons satisfying the local condition agree. There are 41 complete-factor calculations and 46 independent comparisons between the derivative formula and the q-adic calculation.
    
    Two checks have rho=2:
    
    * **q=1093, r=E=364, m=2.** Here a_2=(2^182+1)/1093²≡101 (mod 1093), and 101^546≡−1. The complete factorization independently gives the same quadratic symbol.
    * **q=3511, r=1755, E=3510, m=3.** Here B=2^1170≡2754, a_3=(B²+B+1)/3511²≡2302, and W_3≡−14. Consequently T_3=(-14)^1170≡756≠1. No factorization of this 705-digit H_3 was used. Independently, 262657 is a primitive Mersenne factor at exponent 27 and 3511^87552≡512≠1 modulo 262657.
    
    These two primes already fail other restrictions from the notes. Their role here is to check the calculation with an even valuation, rather than extrapolate from rho=1.
    
    For **q=274177, r=128, m=128**, the local condition is the boundary case q≡1 (mod 256), q≢1 (mod 512). The calculation gives T_m=8, corresponding to ζ_128³. Directly,
    
    ```text
    2^64+1 = 274177 · 67280421310721,
    274177^((67280421310721−1)/128) ≡ 8 (mod 67280421310721).
    ```
    
    Products can cancel. For **q=433, m=8**, the individual exponents at ell=17,241,38737 are 6,2,0 modulo 8. Their sum is 0, so T_8=1 despite the two nontrivial symbols. The same q has T_9=27≠1.
    
    ## Remaining question
    
    Can all these T_m equal 1 when rho is even and the remaining conditions on q and r hold? The formula makes this a question about the residues of a_s and cyclotomic expressions modulo q, without first factoring a. Proving that some T_m is nontrivial would supply the desired obstruction for all N. No such uniform nonvanishing statement is established here.
    
    For further calculation, simplify W_m using relations between cyclotomic units, starting with m=8,9 and odd primes. A trivial product can be examined through the separate relative norms Norm_(Q(ζ_t)/Q(ζ_m))(2−ζ_t), for m | t | E; the code implements those as well.
    
    ```sh
    gp -fq -s 64M check_cyclotomic_reciprocity.gp
    ```
    
    The functions are in [cyclotomic_reciprocity.gp](cyclotomic_reciprocity.gp).

    \cite[\S\S3--6]{SUnitAlgorithms} give explicit archimedean and
    $\ell$-adic bounds, lattice reduction, and sieves for $S$-unit equations
    over number fields. A use here would first require a reduction to
    controlled fields and prime supports. The original equality gives a

    two-variable equation $x+y=1$. In a cyclotomic-field approach the
    uncontrolled primes in $A$ remain the obstacle to fixing that support.
    
    \section{An order obstruction from power reciprocity}
    \label{sec:reciprocity}
    
    \subsection{What the order obstruction would prove}
    
    Work in the remaining case $q>3$, $A>1$ and $q\nmid M$. Keep
    $r=\operatorname{ord}_q(2)$, $\rho=v_q(2^r-1)=n_1$ even, and
    $E=\operatorname{lcm}(2,r)$. Then
    \[
    a=\frac{2^E-1}{q^\rho}\mid A,\qquad \gcd(E,N)=1.
    \]
    Since $A2^{m_2}=q^N-1$, every $\operatorname{ord}_{\ell^f}(q)$ with
    $\ell^f\mid a$ divides $N$. If a prime divisor $s$ of $E$ divides
    one of these orders, that $q$ is excluded for all $M,N$.
    
    For the reciprocity argument, take $m=s^b\mid r$ with $s$ prime and
    $b\ge1$. At a prime $\ell\mid a$ with $m\mid\ell-1$, we can test
    whether $q$ is an $m$-th power modulo $\ell$:
    \[
    q^{(\ell-1)/m}\not\equiv1\pmod\ell
    \quad\Longrightarrow\quad s\mid\operatorname{ord}_{\ell}(q).
    \]
    Indeed, an order prime to $s$ would divide the part of $\ell-1$
    prime to $s$, hence would divide $(\ell-1)/m$.
    We will compute a product of these residue symbols without
    listing the primes $\ell$ individually.
    
    \subsection{Which factors enter the product}
    
    Set $B=2^{E/m}$. The identity for a prime-power cyclotomic polynomial
    gives a divisor of $2^E-1$:
    \[
    H_s=\Phi_m(B)
      =\frac{B^{s^b}-1}{B^{s^{b-1}}-1}
      =\frac{2^E-1}{2^{E/s}-1},
    \qquad a_s=\frac{H_s}{q^\rho}.
    \]
    The integer $H_s$ is the same at each level $b$ for a fixed $s$.
    Since $r\nmid E/s$, its denominator $2^{E/s}-1$ is prime to $q$.
    Thus $H_s$ contains all of $q^\rho$ and $a_s\mid a$.
    
    Let $K=\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)$ and $\beta=B-\zeta_m$. We have
    $\operatorname{Norm}_{K/\mathbb Q}(\beta)=H_s$.
    Let $J$ be the part of the ideal $(\beta)$ prime to $sq$.
    At each prime ideal $P\mid J$ above a rational prime $\ell$,
    $\zeta_m$ reduces to $B$. Since $\ell\ne s$, this reduction
    has order $m$. In particular $m\mid\ell-1$, and the residue field
    is $\mathbb F_\ell$ because the residue of $\zeta_m$ lies in it.
    
    The $m$-th power-residue symbol $(q/P)_m$ is the root of unity
    that reduces to $q^{(\ell-1)/m}$ at $P$. It is also the action
    of Frobenius on an $m$-th root of $q$ in the Kummer extension of $K$
    \cite[\S\S2,4]{StevenhagenKummer}. The product
    \[
    (q/J)_m=\prod_{P\mid J}(q/P)_m^{v_P(\beta)}
    \]
    therefore has a direct interpretation. If it differs from $1$,
    some factor symbol differs from $1$, and its prime $\ell\mid a_s$
    gives the order obstruction.
    
    \subsection{Moving the product to the primes above q}
    
    With the convention of Sharifi \cite[\S3, eq.~(5)]{SharifiCycl},
    the product of the local norm-residue symbols $(\beta,q)_{m,P}$
    over all places is $1$. At a prime $P$ away from $s$ and $q$,
    the local symbol is $(q/P)_m^{-v_P(\beta)}$. Multiplying over
    those primes gives $(q/J)_m^{-1}$, so $(q/J)_m$ equals the product
    of the symbols above $s$ and $q$ and at the archimedean places.
    This follows the use of cyclotomic norms in Sharifi
    \cite[\S\S4,8]{SharifiCycl}.
    
    For odd $s$, we have $s\mid q-1$ since $s\mid r$.
    Also $s\nmid N$ since $s\mid E$, so $s\mid A$ and
    $v_s(A)=v_s(q-1)$. Equation~\eqref{eq:valuation-coupling} gives
    \[
    v_s(q-1)=v_s(2^{\operatorname{ord}_s(2)}-1)+v_s(M)
      \ge 1+v_s(r)\ge b+1.
    \]
    On $1+s\mathbb Z_s$, taking an $s^b$-th power corresponds under the
    logarithm to multiplication by $s^b$ on $s\mathbb Z_s$.
    Thus $q$ is an $m$-th power in $\mathbb Q_s$, and the symbols above
    $s$ are trivial.
    
    For $s=2$, the congruence $q\equiv1\pmod8$ makes $2$ a square
    modulo $q$. Hence $r\mid(q-1)/2$ and $q\equiv1\pmod{2m}$.
    The logarithm on $1+4\mathbb Z_2$ gives $q=u^{m/2}$ for
    some $u\in1+4\mathbb Z_2$. Locally, adjoining an $m$-th root of $q$
    to $K$ is equivalent to adjoining $\sqrt u$. Over $\mathbb Q_2$,
    $\sqrt u$ belongs to the base field when $u\equiv1\pmod8$ and
    generates an unramified quadratic extension when $u\equiv5\pmod8$.
    The extension over the completion of $K$ is thus unramified or
    trivial. In either case the symbol is $1$ on the unit $\beta$.
    The divisibility conditions on $q-1$ obtained here give
    $E\operatorname{rad}(r)\mid q-1$, where $\operatorname{rad}(r)$
    is the product of the distinct primes dividing $r$.
    
    The archimedean contribution is trivial by positivity for $m=2$
    and because all places are complex for $m>2$. This leaves
    \[
    (q/J)_m=\prod_{P\mid q}(\beta,q)_{m,P}.
    \]
    
    \subsection{Evaluating the product modulo q}
    
    The residue of $B$ modulo $q$ has order $m$. Since $m\mid q-1$,
    $q$ splits completely in $K$. Write $P_i$ for the prime above $q$
    where $\zeta_m$ reduces to $B^i$, for $1\le i<m$ with
    $\gcd(i,m)=1$.
    
    \paragraph{The unit at each prime.}
    At $P_i$ for $i\ne1$, $\beta$ is a unit with residue $B-B^i$.
    At $P_1$, $\beta$ contains the entire contribution of $q$ to
    the norm, so $v_{P_1}(\beta)=\rho$. To compute its unit part,
    divide the norm identity $\Phi_m(B)=\prod_i(B-\zeta_m^i)$ over
    the same values of $i$ by $q^\rho$
    and reduce at $P_1$. The other factors reduce to $B-B^i$.
    Here $\Phi_m'(B)$ is the formal derivative of $\Phi_m(X)$
    evaluated at $X=B$. Over $\mathbb F_q$ we have
    \[
    \Phi_m(X)=(X-B)\prod_{\substack{1<i<m\\ \gcd(i,m)=1}}(X-B^i).
    \]
    Differentiating and setting $X=B$ leaves the product of the other
    factors, so $\Phi_m'(B)=\prod_{i\ne1}(B-B^i)$ in $\mathbb F_q$,
    with the product over the same values of $i$. This is nonzero
    because $B$ has order $m$. Thus the residues of the unit parts are
    \[
    U_i=
    \begin{cases}
    a_s/\Phi_m'(B), & i=1,\\
    B-B^i, & i\ne1,
    \end{cases}
    \qquad\text{in }\mathbb F_q^\times.
    \]
    At $P_i$ the tame symbol $(\beta,q)_{m,P_i}$ reduces to
    $U_i^{(q-1)/m}$. The sign $(-1)^{v_{P_i}(\beta)}$ in the tame
    symbol is $1$ because the only nonzero valuation is the even $\rho$.
    
    \paragraph{Putting the symbols in a common reduction.}
    Suppose the symbol at $P_i$ is $\zeta_m^{k}$. It reduces to
    $B^{ik}$ at $P_i$, but to $B^k$ at $P_1$.
    Thus to express the symbol in the reduction at $P_1$, raise the
    residue computed at $P_i$ to $u_i$, where $i u_i\equiv1\pmod m$.
    With all factors expressed at $P_1$, the product becomes
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:reciprocity-test}
    T_m=
    \left(
    \frac{a_s}{\Phi'_m(B)}
    \prod_{\substack{1<i<m\\ \gcd(i,m)=1}}(B-B^i)^{u_i}
    \right)^{(q-1)/m}
    \quad\text{in }\mathbb F_q^\times.
    \end{equation}
    The reduction is injective on the $m$-th roots of unity.
    Thus every solution requires $T_m=1$ for each prime power $m\mid r$.
    The computation
    uses $a_s$ modulo $q$, which can be obtained by evaluating
    $\Phi_m(B)$ modulo $q^{\rho+1}$ before dividing by $q^\rho$.
    
    \subsection{The quadratic and cubic tests}
    
    For $m=2$, the product in \eqref{eq:reciprocity-test} is empty
    and $\Phi'_2(B)=1$. The condition $T_2=1$ says that $a_2$ is a
    square modulo $q$.
    
    For $m=3$, the two residues of $\zeta_3$ above $q$ are $B$ and $B^2$,
    with $u_2=2$. Since $B^2+B+1=0$ in $\mathbb F_q$,
    \[
    B-B^2=2B+1=\Phi'_3(B).
    \]
    The expression raised to $(q-1)/3$ in \eqref{eq:reciprocity-test}
    is therefore $a_3(2B+1)$. In a solution this must be a cube modulo $q$.
    
    For $q=3511$ we have $r=1755$, $\rho=2$ and $E=3510$.
    Using $B=2^{1170}$ gives
    \[
    B\equiv2754,\qquad
    a_3=\frac{B^2+B+1}{3511^2}\equiv2302\pmod{3511}.
    \]
    Thus $a_3(2B+1)\equiv-14$ and $T_3=(-14)^{1170}\equiv756\pmod{3511}$.
    The nontrivial product guarantees a prime divisor of $a_3$ at which
    the order of $3511$ is divisible by $3$. For this example we can
    check one such prime directly. We have $\operatorname{ord}_{262657}(2)=27$,
    so $262657\mid a_3$, and $3511^{87552}\equiv512\pmod{262657}$.
    The prime $3511$ already fails
    the earlier congruences on $q$. It illustrates the calculation with
    the even valuation $\rho=2$.
    
    When $T_m=1$, the individual symbols may cancel. For $q=433$ and
    $m=8$, the three exponents of $\zeta_8$ in the product are $6,2,0$.
    The product is $1$ even though two factors already give an
    order obstruction. The open question is whether the remaining hypotheses
    force a nontrivial product for some $m$, or an individual order
    obstruction when the products are trivial.
    
    \subsection{Computational supplements}
    
    \begin{itemize}
    \item \path{md/mersenne-tables.md} gives orders, the factors used in $D_E$,
    and Frobenius in the cyclotomic fields for illustrative $q$.
    The GAP source is \path{scripts/mersenne_tables.g}. For the cyclotomic
    Frobenius formula see Milne \cite{MilneANT}.
    \item \path{md/order-obstructions.md} checks all prime choices with
    $E\le256$ using \path{scripts/check_order_obstruction.g} and
    \path{scripts/mersenne-factors-256.g}. There are 395 certificates among
    396 choices, with $q=3$, $a=1$ the exception. All have $\rho=1$.
    \item \path{md/cyclotomic-reciprocity.md} gives the derivation and examples.
    \path{md/cyclotomic-reciprocity-tables.md} compares the calculation at $q$
    with direct symbols at the prime factors and includes examples
    with $\rho=2$. The PARI/GP functions are in
    \path{scripts/cyclotomic_reciprocity.gp}. The tables come from
    \path{scripts/check_cyclotomic_reciprocity.gp}.
    \end{itemize}

    For a different route to a bound on N , Corvaja’s short survey [Cor10, §1] explains the Subspace
    Theorem bounds for gcds of powers and the extension to a fixed finitely generated multiplicative
    group. In our case
    A = gcd(2M − 1, q N − 1) > 3q N −1 .
    The strict inequality follows from 2m2 ≤ (q − 1)/3. An effective bound, valid for our family and
    uniform in q, of the form

    θ < 1,
    
    with fixed θ, K, would give N < (K + 1)/(1 − θ). This is a target, not a quoted theorem. Fixedgroup results do not supply uniformity as q varies, and their ineffectivity also matters for a finite
    computation. The survey connects this approach with complex analysis and the support problem.
    For computational algebraic number theory, Alvarado et al. [AKM+ , §§3–6] give explicit
    archimedean and ℓ-adic bounds, lattice reduction, and sieves for S-unit equations over number
    fields. A use here would first require a reduction to controlled fields and prime supports. The original equality gives a four-term unit relation over S = {2, q}, not directly their two-variable equation

    \subsection{Choosing the cyclotomic factor}
    
    To select primes for the test, set $B=2^{E/m}$ and take the
    cyclotomic value
    \[
    H_s=\Phi_m(B)
      =\frac{2^E-1}{2^{E/s}-1},
    \qquad a_s=\frac{H_s}{q^\rho}.
    \]
    Since $m\mid r$, the order of $B$ modulo $q$ is
    $r/\gcd(r,E/m)=m$. The equality uses $\gcd(m,E/r)=1$,
    as $E/r=2$ only when $r$ is odd.
    In particular, $2^{E/s}=B^{m/s}\not\equiv1\pmod q$. Thus $H_s$
    contains the full $q$-part of $2^E-1$ and $a_s\mid a$.
    
    Work in $K=\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)$ with $\zeta_m$ a primitive $m$-th
    root of unity. Set $\beta=B-\zeta_m$, whose norm to $\mathbb Q$
    is $H_s$, and let $J$ be the part of $(\beta)$ prime to $sq$.
    If $P\mid J$ lies above $\ell$, then $\zeta_m$ reduces to $B$
    at $P$. Since $\ell\ne s$, the reduction preserves its order $m$.
    This gives $m\mid\ell-1$ and residue field $\mathbb F_\ell$.
    
    The $m$-th power-residue symbol $(q/P)_m$ is the root of unity
    that reduces to $q^{(\ell-1)/m}$ at $P$. Equivalently, it is the
    factor by which Frobenius multiplies an $m$-th root of $q$ in the
    Kummer extension of $K$ \cite[\S\S2,4]{StevenhagenKummer}.
    Multiplying with the multiplicities in $J$ gives
    \[
    (q/J)_m:=\prod_{P\mid J}(q/P)_m^{v_P(\beta)}.
    \]
    If $(q/J)_m\ne1$, some symbol $(q/P)_m\ne1$. The order test
    then gives $s\mid\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)$ at its rational prime
    $\ell\mid a_s$.
    
    \subsection{Reciprocity and the local terms}
    
    Reciprocity expresses $(q/J)_m$ in terms of local symbols above
    $q$ and $s$ and at the archimedean places.
    In Sharifi's convention, the local norm-residue symbols
    $(\beta,q)_{m,v}$ have product $1$ over all places $v$ of $K$.
    At finite places away from $sq$, the local symbol is $1$ off
    $J$ and is $(q/P)_m^{-v_P(\beta)}$ on $J$. Hence
    \[
    (q/J)_m =
    \biggl(\prod_{P\mid q}(\beta,q)_{m,P}\biggr)
    \biggl(\prod_{P\mid s}(\beta,q)_{m,P}\biggr)
    \biggl(\prod_{v\mid\infty}(\beta,q)_{m,v}\biggr).
    \]
    This is the product formula used in Sharifi's calculation with
    cyclotomic norms \cite[\S3, eq.~(5) and \S\S4,8]{SharifiCycl}.
    
    The archimedean factors are $1$. For $m=2$ this follows from $q>0$,
    and for $m>2$ all the archimedean places are complex. The
    congruences on $q$ also make the factors above $s$ equal $1$.
    
    \paragraph{Odd $s$.}
    Since $s\mid r\mid q-1$ and $s\nmid N$, the gap equations give
    $v_s(A)=v_s(q-1)>0$. By \eqref{eq:valuation-coupling},
    \[
    v_s(q-1)=v_s(2^{\operatorname{ord}_s(2)}-1)+v_s(M)
      \ge b+1.
    \]
    The $s$-adic logarithm sends $1+s\mathbb Z_s$ to $s\mathbb Z_s$
    and sends $q$ into $s^{b+1}\mathbb Z_s$. Dividing $\log q$ by
    $s^b$ gives the logarithm of an $m$-th root of $q$ in $\mathbb Q_s$.
    Thus the factors above $s$ equal $1$.
    
    \paragraph{$s=2$.}
    Since $q\equiv1\pmod8$, we have $r\mid(q-1)/2$ by quadratic
    reciprocity, so $q\equiv1\pmod{2m}$. The logarithm on
    $1+4\mathbb Z_2$ gives $q=u^{m/2}$ for $u\in1+4\mathbb Z_2$.
    Adjoining an $m$-th root of $q$ over a completion of $K$ at $2$
    amounts to adjoining $\sqrt u$. Over $\mathbb Q_2$ this gives
    the trivial extension for $u\equiv1\pmod8$ and the unramified
    quadratic extension for $u\equiv5\pmod8$. The extension remains
    unramified after passing to the completion of $K$. Units are
    norms in an unramified extension, and $\beta=B-\zeta_m$ is a unit
    at $2$ because $B$ is even. Thus the factors above $2$ equal $1$.
    
    The residue-symbol product has now reduced to
    \[
    (q/J)_m=\prod_{P\mid q}(\beta,q)_{m,P}.
    \]
    The congruences used at $s$, taken at the largest power $s^b\mid r$
    for every prime $s\mid r$, also give $E\operatorname{rad}(r)\mid q-1$.
    Here $\operatorname{rad}(r)$ is the product of the distinct primes
    dividing $r$.
    
    \subsection{Evaluating the product modulo q}
    
    The primitive $m$-th roots in $\mathbb F_q$ are the $B^i$ with
    $1\le i<m$ and $\gcd(i,m)=1$. They give the primes $P_i$ above
    $q$ in $K$, with $\zeta_m\equiv B^i\pmod{P_i}$. The completion
    at each $P_i$ has residue field $\mathbb F_q$ and uniformizer $q$.
    
    \paragraph{The residues of the unit parts.}
    Write $U_i$ for the residue at $P_i$ of $\beta/q^{v_{P_i}(\beta)}$.
    For $i\ne1$, $\beta$ is already a unit, so $U_i=B-B^i$.
    Only $P_1$ divides $\beta$, so its valuation is
    $v_{P_1}(\beta)=v_q(H_s)=\rho$.
    
    To find $U_1$, divide the norm identity $H_s=\prod_i(B-\zeta_m^i)$
    by $q^\rho$ and reduce at $P_1$. This gives
    \[
    a_s=U_1\prod_{i\ne1}(B-B^i)\qquad\text{in }\mathbb F_q.
    \]
    The product on the right is $\Phi_m'(B)$, the formal derivative
    of $\Phi_m(X)$ evaluated at $B$. Indeed, over $\mathbb F_q$,

    from differentiating $X-B$ survives. The factors $B-B^i$ are
    nonzero, and we obtain
    \[
    U_1=\frac{a_s}{\Phi_m'(B)}\qquad\text{in }\mathbb F_q.
    \]
    
    \paragraph{Multiplying the symbols.}
    The tame formula gives $(\beta,q)_{m,P_i}\equiv U_i^{(q-1)/m}$

    \right)^{(q-1)/m}
    \quad\text{in }\mathbb F_q^\times.
    \end{equation}
    Every solution requires $T_m=1$ for each prime power $m\mid r$.
    This test uses $a_s$ only modulo $q$. Compute $\Phi_m(B)$ modulo
    $q^{\rho+1}$, then divide by $q^\rho$.

## User

why is gcd(E,N) 1 in section 8.1

## Assistant

It follows from **gcd(M, N, q − 1) = 1**, proved in Section 6.1. Since r = ord_q(2) divides both M and q − 1, this gives gcd(r, N) = 1. And since N is odd, adjoining the factor 2 to form E = lcm(2, r) preserves coprimality.

The argument in Section 6.1 is that if a prime s divides both M and N, the cyclotomic factorization gives p ≡ 1 (mod s). If s also divided q − 1, the representation p = 2^m₂ + q^n₂ would then give 2^m₂ ≡ 0 (mod s), impossible since s is odd. So this restriction on E holds even when M and N have a common factor.

    \section{An order obstruction from power reciprocity}
    \label{sec:reciprocity}
    
    \subsection{The order test}
    
    Work in the remaining case $q>3$, $A>1$ and $q\nmid M$. Keep
    $r=\operatorname{ord}_q(2)$, $\rho=v_q(2^r-1)=n_1$ even, and
    $E=\operatorname{lcm}(2,r)$. Then
    \[
    a=\frac{2^E-1}{q^\rho}\mid A,\qquad \gcd(E,N)=1.
    \]
    Since $A2^{m_2}=q^N-1$, the order of $q$ modulo any prime power
    $\ell^f\mid a$ divides $N$. To exclude $q$ for all $M,N$, it is enough
    to find one such order with a prime divisor in common with $E$.
    
    Fix a prime power $m=s^b$ dividing $r$. If $\ell\mid a$ is prime and
    $m\mid\ell-1$, then
    \[
    q^{(\ell-1)/m}\not\equiv1\pmod\ell
    \quad\Longrightarrow\quad s\mid\operatorname{ord}_{\ell}(q).
    \]
    An order prime to $s$ would divide $(\ell-1)/m$, since we only
    removed factors of $s$ from $\ell-1$. Reciprocity lets us test a
    product over several such primes without factoring $a$.
    
    \subsection{Choosing the cyclotomic factor}
    
    To select primes for the test, set $B=2^{E/m}$ and take the
    cyclotomic value
    \[
    H_s=\Phi_m(B)
      =\frac{2^E-1}{2^{E/s}-1},
    \qquad a_s=\frac{H_s}{q^\rho}.
    \]
    Since $m\mid r$, the order of $B$ modulo $q$ is
    $r/\gcd(r,E/m)=m$. The equality uses $\gcd(m,E/r)=1$,
    as $E/r=2$ only when $r$ is odd.
    In particular, $2^{E/s}=B^{m/s}\not\equiv1\pmod q$. Thus $H_s$
    contains the full $q$-part of $2^E-1$ and $a_s\mid a$.
    
    Work in $K=\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)$ with $\zeta_m$ a primitive $m$-th

    file changes: Completed · 1 changes
    Add: /home/erpage159/fluid/research/math/nt/prime-power-sum-pf/scripts/inspect_reciprocity.sage
    # Load in Sage with load("scripts/inspect_reciprocity.sage").
    # Try inspect_reciprocity(433, 8, factor_ideals=True), then add t=24.
    # For rho=2 without factoring the norm, try inspect_reciprocity(3511, 3).
    
    def cyclotomic_block(z, E, m, t):
        """Relative norm with the choice of root satisfying zeta_t^(E/m) = z."""
        h = t // m
        root = z^inverse_mod(E // t, m)
        # Inclusion-exclusion over divisors coprime to m.
        return prod(
            (2^(h // d) - root^inverse_mod(d, m))^moebius(d)
            for d in divisors(h) if gcd(d, m) == 1 and moebius(d) != 0
        )
    
    
    def inspect_reciprocity(q, m, t=None, factor_ideals=False):
        """Compare the local contributions at q with the selected ideal product."""
        q, m = ZZ(q), ZZ(m)
        if q <= 2 or not q.is_prime() or m < 2 or len(factor(m)) != 1:
            raise ValueError("Use an odd prime q and a prime power m.")
        s = factor(m)[0][0]
        r = Zmod(q)(2).multiplicative_order()
        E = lcm(2, r)
        if r % m:
            raise ValueError("m must divide ord_q(2).")
        if q % (2*m if s == 2 else s*m) != 1:
            raise ValueError("The local term at s needs a separate calculation.")
    
        K = CyclotomicField(m)
        z = K.gen()
        B = 2^(E // m)
        element = B - z
        if t is not None:
            t = ZZ(t)
            if t <= 0 or E % t or (E // t) % s == 0:
                raise ValueError("t must divide E and contain its full s-part.")
            element = cyclotomic_block(z, E, m, t)
    
        at_q = []
        for i in range(1, m):
            if gcd(i, m) != 1:
                continue
            P = K.ideal(q, z - power_mod(B, i, q))
            F = P.residue_field()
            v = element.valuation(P)
            unit = F(element / q^v)
            residue = ((-1)^v * unit)^((q - 1) // m)
            k = discrete_log(residue, F(z), ord=m)
            at_q.append(dict(i=i, valuation=v, unit=ZZ(unit), exponent=k))
    
        exponent = sum(row["exponent"] for row in at_q) % m
        result = dict(q=q, r=r, E=E, m=m, t=t, at_q=at_q,
                      exponent=exponent, T=power_mod(B, exponent, q))
        if factor_ideals:
            factors = []
            for P, v in K.ideal(element).factor():
                ell = P.smallest_integer()
                if ell in (q, s):
                    continue
                F = P.residue_field()
                residue = F(q)^((F.cardinality() - 1) // m)
                k = discrete_log(residue, F(z), ord=m)
                factors.append(dict(ell=ell, valuation=v, exponent=k))
            if sum(row["valuation"] * row["exponent"] for row in factors) % m != exponent:
                raise ArithmeticError("The product at the prime factors differs from the product at q.")
            result["factors"] = factors
        return result

## Assistant

The goal is a uniform order obstruction. For each remaining q, we want to force a prime ℓ dividing `a = (2^E − 1)/q^ρ` at which the order of q shares a prime divisor with E. One such ℓ excludes **every** p, M, and N for that q: the order must divide N, but gcd(E,N) = 1. An effective bound on the q for which this argument fails would also give a finite target, since the logarithmic bound already handles fixed q.

I rewrote [§8.1](/home/erpage159/fluid/research/math/nt/prime-power-sum-pf/prime_power_notes.tex:1871) to explain why we take the product. In a solution, each relevant power-residue symbol must equal 1. Multiplying the symbols over a chosen cyclotomic divisor gives a single quantity. If it differs from 1, some prime factor violates the order condition. Reciprocity is what lets us compute that product at the **known prime q** instead of finding all the prime factors first.

Two concrete ways to pursue this came out of the calculation:

- **Keep the cyclotomic factors separate.** For q = 433 and m = 8, the grouped product is 1. The separate products for Φ₈(2) and Φ₂₄(2) are ζ₈⁶ and ζ₈². Each certifies an obstruction, and they cancel when combined. This gives a reason to study the separate relative norms algebraically.
- **Use the gap equations to simplify the residue condition.** When 3 divides r, the cubic test simplifies to **h = M/E must be a cube modulo q**. The cubic expression is `−Ba`, which the gap equations identify modulo q with `B·2^(−m₂)/h`. Since 2 is already a cube modulo q in this branch, only the class of h matters. This gives a way to combine reciprocity with the restrictions on M when a uniform obstruction in q alone is hard to force.

I added a [Sage worksheet](/home/erpage159/fluid/research/math/nt/prime-power-sum-pf/scripts/inspect_reciprocity.sage) and verified both the cancellation example and the cubic calculation at q = 3511. In `pixi run sage`, try:

```python
load("scripts/inspect_reciprocity.sage")
inspect_reciprocity(433, 8, factor_ideals=True)
inspect_reciprocity(433, 8, t=24, factor_ideals=True)
inspect_reciprocity(3511, 3)
```

Joye et al. give a model for explicit symbol calculations at a fixed degree, 11, using reciprocity and norm-Euclidean division. Our remaining problem is to prove nontriviality for the particular cyclotomic values that arise as q varies. The Sage methods used in the worksheet are `valuation(P)` and `P.residue_field()`. [Joye et al.](https://marcjoye.github.io/papers/JLNN21eleventh.pdf) · [Sage valuations](https://doc.sagemath.org/html/en/reference/number_fields/sage/rings/number_field/number_field_element.html) · [Sage residue fields](https://doc.sagemath.org/html/en/reference/number_fields/sage/rings/number_field/number_field_ideal.html)

The [rebuilt notes](/home/erpage159/fluid/research/math/nt/prime-power-sum-pf/obj/prime_power_notes.pdf#page=27) include both deductions.

    \subsection{The ratio before taking d-th powers}
    For any common divisor $d>1$, write $M=ad$, $N=bd$ and
    $U=2^a$, $V=q^b$. Keep the smaller terms in the equality:
    \[
    p=2^{m_2}U^d+q^{n_1}=2^{m_2}+q^{n_1}V^d,
    \qquad
    R:=\frac{q^{n_1}}{2^{m_2}}=\frac{U^d-1}{V^d-1}.
    \]
    Thus $1<U/V<R^{1/d}$. More precisely, with
    $\delta=a\log2-b\log q>0$,
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:smaller-ratio}
    \boxed{d\delta=\log R-\Lambda,\qquad
    0<\Lambda<\frac{27}{26}q^{-bd}.}
    \end{equation}
    For fixed $q$, both $n_1$ and $m_2$ are fixed, so $R$ is fixed.
    Increasing $d$ requires a closer ratio $2^a/q^b$ and the
    exponentially accurate equality \eqref{eq:smaller-ratio}.
    
    The congruences on $q$ also constrain $R$. With
    $u=(q-1)/2^{m_2}$,
    \[
    R=\frac{u q^{n_1}}{q-1},\qquad
    \log R=(n_1-1)\log q+\log u+\log\frac q{q-1},
    \]
    where $3\mid u$ and $0<\log(q/(q-1))<1/(q-1)$.
    Consequently
    \[
    \frac{(n_1-1)\log q+\log u-(27/26)q^{-N}}d
    <\delta<
    \frac{(n_1-1)\log q+\log u+1/(q-1)}d.
    \]
    Every odd product forced to divide $q-1$ also divides $u$, giving
    a corresponding lower bound on this ratio. For a common prime $d$,

    2^{m_2+a}+q^{n_1}\equiv1\pmod d,\qquad
    2^{m_2}+q^{n_1+b}\equiv1\pmod d.
    \]
    These follow by reducing the $d$-th powers modulo $d$.

    $17\nmid\gcd(M,N)$. Consequently gaps are coprime whenever

    def cyclotomic_block(z, E, m, t):
        """Relative norm with the choice of root satisfying zeta_t^(E/m) = z."""
        h = t // m
        root = z^inverse_mod(E // t, m)
        # Inclusion-exclusion over divisors coprime to m.
        return prod(

    def inspect_reciprocity(q, m, t=None, factor_ideals=False):
        """Compare the local contributions at q with the selected ideal product."""
        q, m = ZZ(q), ZZ(m)
        if q <= 2 or not q.is_prime() or m < 2 or len(factor(m)) != 1:
            raise ValueError("Use an odd prime q and a prime power m.")
        s = factor(m)[0][0]
        r = Zmod(q)(2).multiplicative_order()
        E = lcm(2, r)
        if r % m:
            raise ValueError("m must divide ord_q(2).")
        if q % (2*m if s == 2 else s*m) != 1:
            raise ValueError("The local term at s needs a separate calculation.")
    
        K = CyclotomicField(m)
        z = K.gen()
        B = 2^(E // m)
        element = B - z
        if t is not None:
            t = ZZ(t)
            if t <= 0 or E % t or (E // t) % s == 0:
                raise ValueError("t must divide E and contain its full s-part.")
            element = cyclotomic_block(z, E, m, t)
    
        at_q = []
        for i in range(1, m):
            if gcd(i, m) != 1:
                continue
            P = K.ideal(q, z - power_mod(B, i, q))
            F = P.residue_field()
            v = element.valuation(P)
            unit = F(element / q^v)
            residue = ((-1)^v * unit)^((q - 1) // m)
            k = discrete_log(residue, F(z), ord=m)
            at_q.append(dict(i=i, valuation=v, unit=ZZ(unit), exponent=k))
    
        exponent = sum(row["exponent"] for row in at_q) % m
        result = dict(q=q, r=r, E=E, m=m, t=t, at_q=at_q,
                      exponent=exponent, T=power_mod(B, exponent, q))
        if factor_ideals:
            factors = []
            for P, v in K.ideal(element).factor():
                ell = P.smallest_integer()
                if ell in (q, s):
                    continue
                F = P.residue_field()
                residue = F(q)^((F.cardinality() - 1) // m)
                k = discrete_log(residue, F(z), ord=m)
                factors.append(dict(ell=ell, valuation=v, exponent=k))
            if sum(row["valuation"] * row["exponent"] for row in factors) % m != exponent:
                raise ArithmeticError("The product at the prime factors differs from the product at q.")
            result["factors"] = factors
        return result

    +def gap_candidate(q, exact_bits=0):
    +    """Recover h=M/E modulo q^rho and check one higher congruence.

    +        raise ValueError("Use a prime q > 3.")

    +    E = lcm(2, r)
    +    c = (q - 1).valuation(2)
    +    rho = 0
    +    while power_mod(2, E, q^(rho + 1)) == 1:
    +        rho += 1
    +    result = dict(q=q, r=r, E=E, rho=rho, m2=c)
